title: Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics
text:
Preface
These are the lecture notes for ASTRO 442, an introduction to the fluid dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics of astrophysical systems. They are written to be self-contained: the textbook, Clarke and Carswell’s Principles of Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics (Clarke and Carswell 2007), is optional further reading. Each chapter ends with pointers to the relevant sections of the textbook.

title: Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics
text:
How to use these notes

One chapter per lecture topic. Canvas lists which chapter goes with each lecture.
Everything is numbered by chapter. Equation (9.14) is the fourteenth numbered equation of Chapter 9, and Exercise 8.4 is the fourth exercise of Chapter 8. When you ask a question about the notes, quote these numbers.
In-class worksheets appear near the end of each chapter, followed by the exercises. Homework assignments on Canvas list the exercises to solve, for example “Exercises 2.1, 7.3”.
Units. We use SI units, together with a few units that are customary in astronomy: number densities in \(\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), mass densities in \(\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\), opacities in \(\mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}\), large energies in erg, magnetic fields in gauss (given in parentheses after the value in tesla), and pc, AU, \(M_\odot\), eV. Many astrophysics books and papers use Gaussian units for electromagnetism: 22  Introduction to Plasma explains how to translate their formulas.
Optional material is set apart in boxes titled “Going further”; you can skip it on a first reading.

title: 1  Fluids as Continua
text:
1.1 Fluid elements
Astrophysical systems contain very large numbers of elementary particles. However, for most applications, we are only interested in the dynamics of the gas or plasma on scales that are large compared to the typical length scale of interaction between its constituent particles. In this context, it is convenient to treat matter as a continuum. That is, instead of keeping track of the momentum and position of each particle in the system, we describe it using equations for the evolution of macroscopic, average quantities.
We imagine matter as being composed of fluid elements. These are parcels of gas, or plasma, that have a characteristic size that is much smaller than the scales in which we are interested, but that still contain a large enough number of fluid constituents, molecules, or ions, so that it makes sense to talk about their properties, such as temperature. In other words, we require a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) to be a parcel of matter that can be considered to be in thermodynamic equilibrium. We will call fluid a system that is composed of fluid elements. As we will see later, the equations of motion for fluids do not explicitly depend on the size or shape of the fluid elements, so we will not attempt to define them more precisely. The only requirement is that fluid elements should exist. We will also discuss later what happens when the concept of fluid element breaks down. For the moment, we will assume that the system we are studying can be decomposed in fluid elements and we will derive equations of motion for these fluid elements.
How large should a fluid element be? The particles in a fluid element need to collide with each other frequently, so that they can exchange energy and momentum and reach thermodynamic equilibrium. The average distance traveled by a particle between two collisions is called the mean free path \[
\lambda = \frac{1}{n \sigma},
\tag{1.1}\] where \(n\) is the number density (Equation 1.3) and \(\sigma\) is the cross section for collisions. Fluid elements need to be much larger than \(\lambda\), but also much smaller than the length scale \(L\) over which the properties of the system change. This is possible only if \[
\lambda \ll L .
\tag{1.2}\] The ratio \(\lambda / L\) is called the Knudsen number. In other words, the fluid approximation requires the Knudsen number to be small.
For plasmas, the mean free path does not tell the whole story. Magnetic fields force charged particles to gyrate around the field lines, so they cannot drift freely across the field lines even in the absence of collisions. For this reason, plasmas can sometimes be treated as fluids even when \(\lambda\) is large. We will come back to this point in Chapter 22.
We define the number density of a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) to be \[
n = \frac{\text{``number of particles in $\mathcal{V}$''}}{\text{``volume of
$\mathcal{V}$''}} \qquad [\mathrm{m}^{- 3}] .
\tag{1.3}\] As the system evolves, the number of particles inside the volume element \(\mathcal{V}\) remains constant, but the size of the volume changes, so \(n\) depends on the fluid element and on time.
An associated concept is that of the mass density (or simply density) \[
\rho = \frac{\text{``mass contained in $\mathcal{V}$''}}{\text{``volume of
$\mathcal{V}$''}} \qquad [\mathrm{kg} \, \mathrm{m}^{- 3}] .
\tag{1.4}\] We use SI units in these notes, but we follow the astrophysical custom of quoting number densities in \(\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) and mass densities in \(\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\), with \(1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}} = 10^6\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\) and \(1\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} = 10^3\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\). Note that we always convert them to SI before we use them in a formula. If the gas is composed of identical particles of mass \(m\), then \(\rho = mn\). For mixtures with many constituents \[
\rho = \sum_{i = 1}^N m_i n_i = \sum_{i = 1}^N m_i Y_i n = \mu m_u n,
\tag{1.5}\] where we have introduced the particle number fractions \(Y_i = n_i / n\), the atomic mass unit \(m_u \approx 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}\), and the mean molecular weight \[
\mu = \sum_{i = 1}^N Y_i \frac{m_i}{m_u} ,
\tag{1.6}\] which is the average mass of the particles in units of \(m_u\). Note that \(\mu\) is dimensionless. For example, \(\mu \approx 1\) for atomic hydrogen, while \(\mu \approx 1/2\) for fully ionized hydrogen, since there are one proton and one electron per atom. We can also decompose \(\rho\) in terms of the mass densities of the different species \(\rho_i = m_i n_i\): \[
\rho = \sum_{i = 1}^N \rho_i = \sum_{i = 1}^N X_i \rho .
\tag{1.7}\] The \(X_i = \rho_i / \rho\) are the mass fractions. \(Y_i\) measures the relative contribution of each species to the number density, while \(X_i\) measures the relative contribution to the mass density. In general, \(X_i \neq Y_i\), unless all particle species have the same mass.
We also assume that each element has a well-defined velocity \[
\mathbf{v}= \text{``velocity of $\mathcal{V}$''} \qquad [\mathrm{m}
\, \mathrm{s}^{- 1}]
\tag{1.8}\] and temperature \[
T = \text{``temperature of $\mathcal{V}$''} \qquad [\mathrm{K}] .
\tag{1.9}\] With these definitions in place, we are now ready to state explicitly the assumptions that we are making when we treat a gas or a plasma as a fluid. Consider region \(\mathcal{R}\) filled with matter. We say that this system can be treated as a fluid if the following assumption holds.
This assumption tells us that it makes sense to say that there is a single value of density, temperature, and velocity at each point. This assumption is violated, for example, in systems in which different particle species move independently. Such systems can sometimes be described as multi-fluids, that is systems in which there are different kinds of fluid elements that interact with each other. Plasmas in weakly collisional regimes can sometimes be treated as multi-fluids. A gas of photons in vacuum, instead, cannot be treated as a (multi-)fluid, since at each point in space there are photons traveling in infinitely many different directions.
The assumption also implies that sufficiently small parcels of material are in thermodynamic equilibrium, so that fluid elements have a well defined temperature. This is also called local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) condition. This condition is violated in some impulsive phenomena, such as in shock waves. Violations of LTE can sometimes be included in the fluid model. We will see two examples later: the effect of viscosity and heat conduction and the treatment of shocks. In other cases, it is necessary to describe non-LTE effects using a combination of fluid and non-fluid models. For example, to simulate the effect of cosmic rays on the dynamics of clouds in the interstellar medium it is necessary to solve separate equations for the cosmic rays, which cannot be treated as a fluid, and for the rest of the matter, for which the fluid approximation holds very well.
It is important to note that whether or not the fluid assumption holds is not an absolute statement, but also depends on the time and length scale of interest. For example, the dynamics of dark matter in the Bullet cluster (Figure 1.1) cannot be described using the fluid approximation. This is because dark matter does not flow with a single velocity. On the other hand, on cosmological scales, dark matter dynamics can be reasonably well described as a pressure-less fluid, as long as streams of dark matter do not cross. The Zel’dovich approximation is a famous application of this model.

title: 1  Fluids as Continua
text:
TipExample



Consider a cloud of atomic hydrogen in the interstellar medium with number density \(n \sim 1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}} = 10^{6}\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). The cross section for collisions between hydrogen atoms is \(\sigma \sim 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{m^2}\), so the mean free path is \(\lambda \sim 10^{13}\,\mathrm{m}\), or about \(70\,\mathrm{AU}\). This is much smaller than the typical size of interstellar clouds, \(L \sim 1\,\mathrm{pc} \approx 3 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}\). So \(\lambda / L \sim 3 \times 10^{-4}\) and the cloud can be treated as a fluid.







Assumption 1.1 (Fluid assumption) Every point \(P \in \mathcal{R}\) belongs to one fluid element, with given values of density \(\rho\), composition \(\{ Y_i \}\), velocity \(\mathbf{v}\), and temperature \(T\).










Figure 1.1: The Bullet cluster is the product of the head-on collision of two galaxy clusters (optical data). The gas in the two clusters has interacted producing a shock-wave (X-ray data in red) and trails the two groups of galaxies. Dark matter (blue halos) is nearly collisionless, so the two dark matter clouds associated with the clusters have passed through each other. title: 1  Fluids as Continua
text:
1.2 The continuity equation
We now consider a system that can be described as a fluid. We wish to derive equations to predict how \(\rho\), \(\mathbf{v}\), and \(T\) evolve for all fluid elements. To this aim, we will use three fundamental laws in classical physics: 1) the law of conservation of mass; 2) Newton’s second law; and 3) the first law of thermodynamics. The law of conservation of mass gives rise to the continuity equation, which we will now derive.






Figure 1.2: Fluid element stretching in the \(x\)-direction.



Consider the infinitesimal fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) shown in Figure 1.2. Let \(\mathrm{d} x\) be the size of the fluid element along the \(x\)-direction at some time \(t\). Let \(v_x\) be the \(x\)-component of the velocity. If we take the origin to be the center of the fluid element, the velocity with which the left face is moving is \(v_x \left( - \tfrac{\mathrm{d} x}{2} \right)\), while the velocity of the right face is \(v_x \left( \tfrac{\mathrm{d} x}{2} \right)\). For the moment, we assume \(v_y = v_z = 0\). The initial volume of \(\mathcal{V}\) is \(V = \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} y \mathrm{d} z\). At time \(t + \mathrm{d} t\), \(\mathcal{V}\) is deformed and has volume \[
V' = \left( \mathrm{d} x + \left[ v_x \left( \tfrac{\mathrm{d} x}{2} \right) - v_x
\left( - \tfrac{\mathrm{d} x}{2} \right) \right] \mathrm{d} t \right) \mathrm{d} y
\mathrm{d} z = \left( \mathrm{d} x + \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d}
t \right) \mathrm{d} y \mathrm{d} z,
\tag{1.10}\] so the relative rate in the change of volume of \(\mathcal{V}\) is \[
\frac{1}{V}  \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{1}{V}  \frac{V' - V}{\mathrm{d}
t} = \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} .
\tag{1.11}\] In an analogous way, we can find the rate of change of an infinitesimal volume \(V\) if \(v_y\) and \(v_z\) are nonzero: \[
\frac{1}{V}  \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} +
\frac{\partial v_y}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} = \nabla
\cdot \mathbf{v}.
\tag{1.12}\] We have derived this equation for a cubical fluid element. However, it turns out that this equation holds for infinitesimal fluid elements of any shape. The extension of this result to finite (as opposed to infinitesimal) regions is a special case of the Reynolds transport theorem, which states that \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} V_\Omega}{\mathrm{d} t} = \oint_{\partial \Omega} \mathbf{v} \cdot
\mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} A = \int_{\Omega} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{1.13}\] where \(\Omega\) is some extended region comoving with the flow, \(V_\Omega\) is its volume, \(\partial \Omega\) is the surface enclosing \(\Omega\), \(\mathbf{n}\) is the outwards pointing normal to it, and \(\mathrm{d} A\) and \(\mathrm{d} V\) are the area and volume elements.
The second equality follows from the Gauss divergence theorem. To see why the theorem holds, we can think of \(\Omega\) as being composed of many infinitesimal fluid elements. Each of them changes its volume at the rate \((\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}) \mathrm{d} V\) (Equation 1.12), so the rate of change of \(V_\Omega\) is obtained by summing over all of them, which gives the volume integral of \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}\). The geometrical interpretation of the first equality is illustrated in Figure 1.3. The rate of change of the volume of \(\Omega\) is equal to the surface integral of the component of the velocity normal to its boundary. This makes sense, because the tangential part of the velocity only slides the boundary along itself, while the normal component moves it outwards or inwards. Because \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}\) determines the rate of change of the fluid element volumes, it is also called the expansion.






Figure 1.3: The instantaneous rate of change in the volume of a region is equal to the flux of the velocity field through its boundary.



If we denote by \(\mathcal{M}\) the mass of a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\), and use the fact that \(\mathcal{M}\) is conserved, then we find \[
\rho = \frac{\mathcal{M}}{V} \Longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} =
- \frac{\mathcal{M}}{V^2}  \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t} = -
\frac{\mathcal{M}}{V}  \frac{1}{V}  \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \rho
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} .
\tag{1.14}\] We can rearrange the terms to obtain \[
\boxed{\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{v}}
\tag{1.15}\] This is the continuity equation, the first of the fundamental equations of motion for fluids. Note that \(\mathrm{d} / \mathrm{d} t\) denotes the rate of change of a quantity as we follow a fluid element. We will see in Chapter 5 how this is related to the rate of change at a fixed point in space.
The continuity equation can also be written in terms of \(n\), as long as the number of particles in each fluid element is conserved, that is, in the absence of ionization, recombination, or reactions: \[
\frac{1}{n}  \frac{\mathrm{d} n}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\tag{1.16}\] The continuity equation also holds separately for the \(n_i\) and \(\rho_i\) of each species in the fluid, as long as there are no reactions converting between the species, i.e., \(\dot{X}_i = \dot{Y}_i = 0\), and all species move with the same velocity.






TipExample



A flow in which all fluid elements have the same velocity has \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= 0\), since \(\mathbf{v}\) is a constant, so the density of each fluid element does not change (\(\mathrm{d} \rho / \mathrm{d} t = 0\)).








TipExample



Consider a planar flow \(\mathbf{v}= (- y, x, 0)\) [arbitrary units]. This is an example of a rotating flow, as shown in the visualization below:






Figure 1.4: Velocity field \(\mathbf{v}= (-y, x, 0)\).



This flow also preserves the density of each fluid element: \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \frac{\partial v_x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial
v_y}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial (- y)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial
(x)}{\partial y} = 0.
\tag{1.17}\]








TipExample



In cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\), a generic rotating flow with rotational axis along \(z\) takes the form \[
\mathbf{v}= v_{\phi}  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} .
\tag{1.18}\] Rotating flows preserve the volume of fluid elements if \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \frac{1}{R}  \frac{\partial (R
v_{R})}{\partial R} + \frac{1}{R}  \frac{\partial
v_{\phi}}{\partial \phi} + \frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} =
\frac{1}{R}  \frac{\partial v_{\phi}}{\partial \phi} = 0.
\tag{1.19}\] That is, as long as all fluid elements with fixed \((R, z)\) rotate with the same angular frequency.


Flows for which \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= 0\) everywhere are said to be incompressible. An important property of incompressible flows is that the net flux of the velocity field across any closed surface should vanish: \[
\oint_{\partial \Omega} \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} A =
\int_{\Omega} \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V = 0.
\tag{1.20}\] We can interpret this result graphically by introducing the velocity field lines, also called streamlines. These are curves \((x (s), y (s), z (s))\) satisfying \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} s} = v_x, \quad \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} s} = v_y,
\quad \frac{\mathrm{d} z}{\mathrm{d} s} = v_z .
\tag{1.21}\] In an incompressible flow there are no sources or sinks for the streamlines. This means that every streamline that enters a closed surface must also exit from it (Figure 1.5).






Figure 1.5: Streamlines in an incompressible flow (left) leave every closed surface they enter. Flows with expansion or compression (right) can have sources or sinks of streamlines. Note the analogy with the solenoidal geometry of magnetic field lines in magnetism.

title: 1  Fluids as Continua
text:
1.3 Radial flows
Most astrophysical transients are the result of explosions that generate approximately radial outflows. As such, an important class of flows are those for which the gas is flowing in the radial direction: \[
\mathbf{v}= v_r  \hat{\mathbf{r}} .
\tag{1.22}\] These are called radial flows. In the previous equation, \(v_r\) can depend on \(r\) and on the direction \((\theta, \phi)\).
Using the divergence in spherical coordinates (Appendix A), we find that radial flows are generically compressible: \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} &{}={} && \frac{1}{r^2}  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}
(r^2 v_r) + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta}  \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} (\sin
\theta v_{\theta}) \\
&&& + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta}  \frac{\partial
v_{\phi}}{\partial \phi}  \\
&{}={} && \frac{1}{r^2}  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}  (r^2 v_r) \\
&{}={} && \frac{\partial v_r}{\partial r} + \frac{2}{r} v_r .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{1.23}\] This expression vanishes only if \(v_r \propto 1 / r^2\), which is singular at the origin. So radial flows that are regular at the origin are always compressible.
Note that the radial direction, \(\hat{\mathbf{r}}\), is not well defined at the origin, since all directions are radial there. This implies that \(v_r (r = 0) = 0\). This regularity condition also ensures that the fluid element at the origin is not “broken” (transported in different directions), but only stretched.
An important example of radial flow is that of a homologously expanding (or contracting) sphere of gas. Here, “homologous” means that the relative rate of change of the volume of each fluid element, \(\frac{1}{V} \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t}\), is equal for all fluid elements. To see how this works, we consider a sphere of gas that at time \(t = 0\) has a constant density \(\rho_0\). The assumption of constant density is not necessary, as all calculations will remain valid even for variable density, but it will make the results more transparent.
To see what this implies for the velocity, note that for a radial flow the condition that \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}\) is the same for all fluid elements reads \(\partial_r v_r + 2 v_r / r = 3 H\), where \(H\) does not depend on \(r\). The solutions of this equation are \(v_r = H r + B / r^2\). The regularity condition at the origin requires \(B = 0\), so \(v_r \propto r\).
Accordingly, in a homologous flow, the velocity of fluid elements that are at \(r = q\) at \(t = 0\) is given by \[
v_r (r = q, t = 0) = Hq,
\tag{1.24}\] where \(H\) is a constant. At later times, we assume that each fluid element continues to move with the velocity it had initially. In other words, we are assuming that fluid elements are not subject to any force and they coast at their original velocity. This is Newton’s first law applied to the fluid elements.
To find the change in density in the system, we could be tempted to write \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \frac{1}{r^2}  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}  (r^2
v_r) \overset{!!!}{=} \frac{1}{r^2}  \frac{\partial}{\partial r}  (r^3 H) = 3 H,
\tag{1.25}\] but this is incorrect. The issue is that at any time \(t \neq 0\), the velocity of a fluid element at the location \(r\) is not \(Hr\). Instead, its velocity is \(Hq\), where \(q\) is the position that that fluid element had at time \(t = 0\).
To find it, we consider the equation of motion of the fluid element originally located at \(r = q\): \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} r (t ; q)}{\mathrm{d} t} = Hq, \qquad r (0 ; q) = q.
\tag{1.26}\] This can be integrated to find \[
r (t ; q) = q + Hqt.
\tag{1.27}\] Solving for \(q\) gives \[
q = \frac{r}{1 + Ht} .
\tag{1.28}\] This means that \[
v_r (r, t) = \frac{rH}{1 + Ht} \neq rH.
\tag{1.29}\] The continuity equation gives \[
\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= -
3 \frac{H}{1 + Ht} .
\tag{1.30}\] Note that the expansion (or compression if \(H < 0\)) rates depend only on \(H\) and \(t\) and not on the initial position of the fluid element \(q\). In other words, all fluid elements are expanding/contracting at the same rate.
To make this result more transparent, we define \(R (t)\) to be the radius of the expanding/contracting gas sphere at time \(t\). Evidently, \(\dot{R} (t) = HR_0\) and \(R (t) = R_0 (1 + Ht)\). So Equation 1.30 can be written as \[
\boxed{\frac{\dot{\rho}}{\rho} = - 3 \frac{\dot{R}}{R}}
\tag{1.31}\] This equation can be integrated to find \(\rho \propto R^{-3}\). This should not be surprising, because the mass of the sphere, \(\frac{4 \pi}{3} \rho R^3\), is conserved. The expansion is illustrated in Figure 1.6.






Figure 1.6: Homologous expansion of a sphere of gas, at \(t = 0\) and at two later times. Each marked fluid element keeps its initial velocity (arrows), which is proportional to its initial distance from the centre. The pattern of fluid elements is the same at all times, only scaled up, and the density (shading) decreases as \(R^{-3}\).



The flows produced by many types of astronomical explosions can be described well as homologously expanding flows at sufficiently late times, typically once the gas has expanded to several times its initial radius. This is because at early times pressure gradients accelerate the gas, converting internal energy into kinetic energy. As the gas expands, it cools adiabatically and the pressure forces become negligible. Afterwards, the fluid elements are not subject to any net force, so they coast at a fixed velocity. Fluid elements that started from a small region then end up at \(r \approx v t\), which is a homologous flow. This is the basis for the models of supernova light curves that we will discuss in Chapter 3.






TipExample



Consider a supernova that ejects \(M = 10\,M_\odot\) of gas, with the outer layers moving at \(v = 5000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). After one year, the radius of the ejecta is \(R \approx v t \approx 1.6 \times 10^{14}\,\mathrm{m}\), or about \(1000\,\mathrm{AU}\), so their mean density is \[
\bar{\rho} = \frac{3 M}{4 \pi R^3} \approx 1 \times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}} = 1 \times 10^{-15}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}.
\tag{1.32}\] This corresponds to about \(10^9\) particles per \(\mathrm{cm^3}\). Since \(R \propto t\) at late times, the density decreases as \(t^{-3}\), so after ten years it is a thousand times smaller.

What is the mean molecular weight of this gas?

Find \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}\) using the expression for the divergence of \(\mathbf{v}\) in spherical coordinates: \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = {} & \frac{1}{r^2}  \frac{\partial}{\partial
r}  (r^2 v_r) \\
& + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta}  \frac{\partial}{\partial
\theta} (\sin \theta v_{\theta}) \\
& + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta}
\frac{\partial v_{\phi}}{\partial \phi},

Is the flow incompressible if \(v_r = \mathrm{const}\)?

Exercise 1.1 (Differential rotation of a star) A spherical star of radius \(R_*\) is differentially rotating with angular velocity \[
\Omega (R) = \frac{\Omega_0}{1 + \left( \frac{R}{R_*} \right)^2},
\tag{1.34}\] where \(R\) is the cylindrical radius.

Is the flow incompressible? Why?

title: 2  Thermodynamics Refresher
text:
2.1 Equation of state for ideal gases
In our discussion so far, we have considered a gas to be a set of fluid elements, each with its own macroscopic velocity \(\mathbf{v}\). However, gases are actually composed of particles, each with its own microscopic velocity. How do we reconcile these two pictures? For simplicity, let’s consider a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) containing a single species of atoms, each having mass \(m\). Let \(\mathbf{u}_i\) be the velocity of the \(i\)th particle. Then we can decompose \(\mathbf{u}_i\) as \[
\mathbf{u}_i =\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}_i,
\tag{2.1}\] where \[
\mathbf{v}= \langle \mathbf{u} \rangle = \frac{1}{N}  \sum_{i = 1}^N
\mathbf{u}_i,
\tag{2.2}\] is the average velocity and \(\mathbf{w}_i\) is the peculiar velocity of each particle. By definition \(\langle \mathbf{w} \rangle = 0\).
Because the random component of the velocity averages to zero, it does not impact the continuity equation. To see this, consider the net mass crossing the grayed surface in Figure 2.1. Over any given \(\mathrm{d} t\), only the particles in the region with volume \(\langle u_x \rangle \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A\) cross the surface, so the mass crossing the surface is \[
nm \langle u_x  \rangle \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A = \rho v_x \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A .
\tag{2.3}\] However, the random motion of particles contributes to a net momentum flux. This is because each particle contributes a momentum \(mu_x\), so the momentum flux is \[
F \mathrm{d} t = nm \langle u_x^2 \rangle \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A = \rho v_x^2 \mathrm{d}
t \mathrm{d} A + \rho \langle w_x^2 \rangle \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A.
\tag{2.4}\] Note that the momentum flux per unit time has units of \[
[F] = [\rho v_x^2 \mathrm{d} A] = \mathrm{kg} \, \mathrm{m} \, \mathrm{s}^{- 2} = \mathrm{N},
\tag{2.5}\] where \(\mathrm{N}\) (newton) is the SI unit of force, so the quantity \(\rho \langle w_x^2 \rangle\) is a force per unit area. Pressure is measured in pascal, \(1\,\mathrm{Pa} = 1\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}\). If the random motions are isotropic, that is, if they have no preferred direction, then \(\langle w_x^2 \rangle = \langle w_y^2 \rangle = \langle w_z^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{3} \langle | \mathbf{w} |^2 \rangle\). Accordingly, we define as gas pressure the quantity \[
p = \frac{1}{3} \rho \langle | \mathbf{w} |^2 \rangle .
\tag{2.6}\] The factor \(1 / 3\) can be understood to come from the fact that pressure forces are the result of random motion in three directions. In analogy, the quantity \(\rho v_x^2\) is called the ram pressure. If you are swimming in a river the ram pressure is the force that tries to drag you along with the flow, while the pressure is responsible for the buoyancy you experience.
For a monoatomic gas with particles of mass \(m\), the rms velocity can be computed using the equipartition theorem1: \[
m \langle | \mathbf{w} |^2 \rangle = 3 k_B T,
\tag{2.7}\] where \(T\) is the temperature in kelvin and \(k_B\) is the Boltzmann constant, \[
k_B = 1.380649 \times 10^{- 23} \, \mathrm{J} \, \mathrm{K}^{- 1} .
\tag{2.8}\] Combining this with Equation 2.6 we find the equation of state for an ideal gas: \[
\boxed{p = nk_B T.}
\tag{2.9}\] Often, the equation of state for ideal gases is written in terms of the ideal gas constant \(\mathcal{R}\) as \[
p = \frac{\mathcal{R}}{N_A m} \rho T,
\tag{2.10}\] where \(N_A\) is Avogadro’s number. Since \(n = \frac{\rho}{m}\), we see that \(\mathcal{R}\) is just an alias for \(N_A k_B\). For mixtures of monoatomic gases, Equation 2.9 remains unchanged, with \(n\) now being the number density of particles of any species, while Equation 2.10 becomes \[
p = \frac{\mathcal{R}}{N_A \mu m_u} \rho T = \frac{\rho k_B T}{\mu m_u},
\tag{2.11}\] where \(m_u\) is the atomic mass unit and \(\mu\) is the mean molecular weight (Equation 1.6): \[
\mu = \frac{\rho}{n m_u} .
\tag{2.12}\] Thermal motion is not only a source of pressure, but also a reservoir of energy for the gas. In other words, because of their motion, the particles in the gas have average kinetic energy per unit mass \[
\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2} \langle | \mathbf{w} |^2 \rangle = \frac{3}{2 m}
k_B T \Longrightarrow k_B T = \frac{2}{3} m \varepsilon .
\tag{2.13}\] Using this definition we can eliminate the temperature from the ideal-gas equation of state: \[
p = \frac{2}{3} \rho \varepsilon,
\tag{2.14}\] where we have used the definition \(\rho = nm\).
The last equation is a particular case of a \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state: \[
\boxed{p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon,}
\tag{2.15}\] where \(\Gamma = \frac{5}{3}\) for a monoatomic gas. The \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state is a good approximation also for non monoatomic gases or mixture of gases, for which Equation 2.14 does not hold. For example, air can be described with a \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state with \(\Gamma = 1.4\). Another example is given by radiation-dominated gases, which we discuss below. Note that it is possible to rewrite Equation 2.15 as \[
p = (\Gamma - 1) u,
\tag{2.16}\] where \(u = \rho \varepsilon\) is the internal energy density, measured in \(\mathrm{J} / \mathrm{m}^3\).

title: 2  Thermodynamics Refresher
text:
2.2 The first law of thermodynamics
The first law of thermodynamics applied to a fluid element of volume \(V\) and mass \(\mathcal{M}\) reads \[
\mathrm{d} E = \delta Q - \delta W.
\tag{2.17}\] It states that the amount of energy in the fluid element increases by the amount of heat absorbed by the fluid element, \(\delta Q\), and decreases by the amount of mechanical work done, \(\delta W\).
For a perfect fluid, the mechanical work is given by \[
\delta W = p \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{2.18}\] where \(V\) is the volume of the fluid element. In the case of nonperfect fluids, there are corrections that arise from the anisotropic components of the stress tensor.
For a reversible process, the amount of absorbed heat is given by \[
\delta Q = T \mathrm{d} S.
\tag{2.19}\] In many cases, it is convenient to work with the first law of thermodynamics using specific (per unit mass) quantities: \[
\varepsilon = \frac{E}{\mathcal{M}}, \qquad w = \frac{W}{\mathcal{M}},
\qquad q = \frac{Q}{\mathcal{M}}, \qquad s = \frac{S}{\mathcal{M}}, \qquad v
= \frac{V}{\mathcal{M}} = \frac{1}{\rho} .
\tag{2.20}\] Note that here \(v\) denotes the specific volume, that is, the volume per unit mass, and not the velocity. In terms of the specific quantities, the first law reads \[
\mathrm{d} \varepsilon = \delta q - \delta w = T \mathrm{d} s - p \mathrm{d} v = T
\mathrm{d} s + \frac{p}{\rho^2} \mathrm{d} \rho .
\tag{2.21}\] In the case of adiabatic flows \(\delta q = 0\), the first law simplifies to \[
\mathrm{d} \varepsilon = \frac{p}{\rho^2} \mathrm{d} \rho .
\tag{2.22}\] For a \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state \(\varepsilon = \frac{p}{(\Gamma - 1) \rho}\), so we find \[
\frac{1}{\rho} \mathrm{d} p - \frac{p}{\rho^2} \mathrm{d} \rho = (\Gamma - 1)
\frac{p}{\rho^2} \mathrm{d} \rho \Longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{p} = \Gamma
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\rho} .
\tag{2.23}\] If \(\Gamma\) is constant, this can be integrated to yield \[
\boxed{p = K \rho^{\Gamma},}
\tag{2.24}\] where \(K\) is an integration constant. Equation 2.24 represents a so-called polytropic equation of state. Note that for an adiabatic flow, \(K\) is constant with time in each fluid element, but \(K\) does not have to be the same in each fluid element. A comparison between Equation 2.24 and Equation 2.15 shows that \[
K = (\Gamma - 1) \rho^{1 - \Gamma} \varepsilon .
\tag{2.25}\] For an ideal gas, \(K\) is a function of the specific entropy only, so we can think of \(K\) as a measure of the entropy of a fluid element.






TipExample



Consider a fluid element of monoatomic ideal gas (\(\Gamma = 5/3\)) that is compressed adiabatically, so that its density doubles. Since \(K\) is constant, the pressure increases by a factor \(2^{5/3} \approx 3.2\). From the ideal-gas law, \(T \propto p / \rho \propto \rho^{\Gamma - 1}\), so the temperature increases by a factor \(2^{2/3} \approx 1.6\).


Note that, if \(K\) is the same for all fluid elements, Equation 2.24 is barotropic, that is, the pressure depends only on the density. In this case, this equation of state, together with the continuity equation and the equation for the velocity (Euler’s equation, Chapter 4), form a closed system of equations, using which it is, in principle, possible to compute all quantities in the flow. If \(K\) differs between fluid elements, the system is still closed, since \(K\) is constant along each fluid element (\(\mathrm{d} K / \mathrm{d} t = 0\)). However, the polytropic equation of state cannot be applied if \(\delta q \neq 0\), due to the presence of heating or cooling of the gas. Even if the flow is adiabatic (\(\delta q = 0\)), there are irreversible thermodynamic processes that operate in shocks. When this happens, the steps we took to get  Equation 2.24 from Equation 2.21 are no longer valid, because in irreversible processes the entropy of a fluid element increases even if no heat is exchanged, \(T \mathrm{d} s > \delta q\). In all these situations, it is necessary to derive a new equation, in addition to the equation of state and the velocity and continuity equations, to close the system. In the presence of heating and cooling, this is the energy equation discussed below. Shocks require a different treatment, which we will discuss in Chapter 6 and Chapter 11.

title: 2  Thermodynamics Refresher
text:
2.3 Radiation pressure
Gas-pressure is not the only relevant source of pressure in astrophysical flows. Radiation pressure is another important component. While gas pressure arises due to the random (or thermal) component of the velocity of particles, radiation pressure arises as a result of momentum deposition by photons in optically thick conditions, in which radiation can be considered to be isotropic and in thermal equilibrium with the gas. We can derive the radiation pressure using a similar method as for the gas pressure, if we assume that photons carry momentum. However, to relate the radiation pressure to the temperature we need to use thermodynamics, and the value of the constant of proportionality can only be derived using quantum mechanics.
Consider a region filled with radiation and let \(u\) be the energy density in radiation. We assume that the radiation field is isotropic, meaning that there is an equal probability to find a photon traveling in each direction. In other words, the energy density of photons per unit solid angle of direction is \(J = \frac{u}{4 \pi}\). Let’s compute the flux of momentum crossing an area \(\mathrm{d} A\) with normal \(\hat{\mathbf{n}}\) (shown in Figure 2.2).






Figure 2.2: Area element for the calculation of the radiation pressure.



Each photon with energy \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ph}}\) carries a momentum \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ph}} / c\). Over the time interval \(\mathrm{d} t\) photons in the volume \(\mathrm{d} V = c \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A \cos \theta\) will cross \(\mathrm{d} A\), each carrying a normal component of the momentum equal to \((\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ph}} / c) \cos \theta\), so the overall flux of momentum is \[
\int J (\cos \theta)^2 \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A \mathrm{d} \Omega = \frac{u \mathrm{d} t
\mathrm{d} A}{4 \pi} \int_0^{2 \pi} \mathrm{d} \phi \int_0^{\pi} \mathrm{d} \theta \sin \theta
(\cos \theta)^2 = \frac{1}{3} u \mathrm{d} t \mathrm{d} A \Longrightarrow
\boxed{p = \frac{1}{3} u.}
\tag{2.26}\] So we have found that the radiation pressure can be described with a \(\Gamma\)-law equation of state with \(\Gamma = 4 / 3\). However, to be able to actually compute the pressure, we need to find a relation between \(u\), \(p\), and the temperature \(T\). Consider the following thought experiment (Figure 2.3):






Figure 2.3: Blackbody enclosure.



The first and second law of thermodynamics read \[
\delta Q = \mathrm{d} E + p \mathrm{d} V, \quad T \mathrm{d} S = \delta Q.
\tag{2.27}\] The energy can be written in terms of the energy density as \(E = uV\), so \[
\mathrm{d} E = V \mathrm{d} u + u \mathrm{d} V = V \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\mathrm{d} T} \mathrm{d} T + u
\mathrm{d} V
\tag{2.28}\] Solving Equation 2.27 for \(\mathrm{d} S\) and using Equation 2.26 to eliminate \(p\), we find \[
\mathrm{d} S = \frac{V}{T}  \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\mathrm{d} T} \mathrm{d} T + \frac{4}{3}
\frac{u}{T} \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{2.29}\] We can rewrite the previous equation as: \[
\left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial T} \right)_V = \frac{V}{T}  \frac{\mathrm{d}
u}{\mathrm{d} T}, \qquad \left( \frac{\partial S}{\partial V} \right)_T =
\frac{4}{3}  \frac{u}{T} .
\tag{2.30}\] Since \(\mathrm{d} S\) is an exact differential: \[
\frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial V \partial T} = \frac{1}{T}  \frac{\mathrm{d}
u}{\mathrm{d} T} = \frac{4}{3}  \frac{1}{T}  \frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\mathrm{d} T} -
\frac{4}{3}  \frac{u}{T^2} = \frac{\partial^2 S}{\partial T \partial V} .
\tag{2.31}\] Combining the terms we find \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} u}{\mathrm{d} T} = 4 \frac{u}{T} \Longrightarrow \boxed{u =
aT^4 .}
\tag{2.32}\] The constant of integration is the radiation constant. It can be derived using quantum mechanics: \[
a \cong 7.5657 \times 10^{- 16} \, \mathrm{J} \, \mathrm{m}^{- 3} \, \mathrm{K}^{- 4}
.
\tag{2.33}\] The radiation constant is related to the Stefan–Boltzmann constant \(\sigma\) by \[
a = \frac{4 \sigma}{c},
\tag{2.34}\] where \(c\) is the speed of light.
In general, both radiation and gas pressure can be present. For example, for ionized stellar matter the pressure and energy densities can be computed as \[
p = \frac{\rho k_B T}{\mu m_u} + \frac{1}{3} aT^4, \qquad u = \rho \varepsilon =
\frac{3}{2}  \frac{\rho k_B T}{\mu m_u} + aT^4 .
\tag{2.35}\]






TipExample



Consider the center of the Sun, where \(\rho \approx 150\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} = 1.5 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\) and \(T \approx 1.5 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{K}\). For fully ionized solar matter \(\mu \approx 0.6\), so the gas pressure is \[
p_{\mathrm{gas}} = \frac{\rho k_B T}{\mu m_u} \approx 3 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{Pa},
\tag{2.36}\] while the radiation pressure is \[
p_{\mathrm{rad}} = \frac{1}{3} a T^4 \approx 1.3 \times 10^{13}\,\mathrm{Pa}.
\tag{2.37}\] So radiation contributes only about \(0.04\%\) of the pressure at the center of the Sun. As we will see in Chapter 3, the situation is very different in the ejecta of supernovae, which are radiation dominated.

title: 2  Thermodynamics Refresher
text:
2.4 Energy equation
The first law of thermodynamics can be used to derive the energy equation for a perfect fluid. We start from the first law written for the energy per unit mass \[
\mathrm{d} \varepsilon = \delta q + \frac{p}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\rho} .
\tag{2.38}\] Dividing both terms by \(\mathrm{d} t\), multiplying by \(\rho\), and using the continuity equation (Equation 1.15) gives \[
\boxed{\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} = \rho \dot{q} - p
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}.}
\tag{2.39}\] The first term on the RHS contains the net heating rate per unit mass, \(\dot{q} = \dot{q}_{\mathrm{heat}} - \dot{q}_{\mathrm{cool}}\). For example,  \(\dot{q}_{\mathrm{heat}}\) might represent the energy generation due to nuclear burning in the gas, while \(\dot{q}_{\mathrm{cool}}\) might be the energy lost by emitting radiation. The second term is the so-called pdV term. It represents the energy spent by doing work on the environment, or on other fluid elements. A list of common heating and cooling processes in astrophysics is given in Clarke and Carswell (2007), Section 4.5.

For a reversible process in a gas with fixed composition, the first law of thermodynamics reads \[
\mathrm{d} E = T \mathrm{d} S - p \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{2.40}\] Define the specific (per unit mass) quantities: \[
\varepsilon = \frac{E}{\mathcal{M}}, \qquad w = \frac{W}{\mathcal{M}},
\qquad q = \frac{Q}{\mathcal{M}}, \qquad s = \frac{S}{\mathcal{M}},
\qquad v = \frac{V}{\mathcal{M}} = \frac{1}{\rho} .
\tag{2.41}\]

Find an expression for \(\mathrm{d} \varepsilon\) in terms of \(T, s, p, \rho\).
Consider an ideal-gas with \(p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon\) undergoing an adiabatic process (\(\delta q = 0\)).

p = K \rho^{\Gamma} .
\tag{2.42}\]

2.6 Exercises

Exercise 2.1 (Equation of state of an H/He plasma) Consider a mixture of ionized hydrogen and helium with \(X_{\mathrm{H}} = 70\%\) and \(X_{\mathrm{He}} = 30\%\). The pressure is given by \[
p = p_{\mathrm{ions}} + p_e + p_{\mathrm{rad}},
\tag{2.43}\] where \(p_{\mathrm{ions}}\) is the partial pressure of the ions, \(p_e\) is the partial pressure of the electrons, and \(p_{\mathrm{rad}}\) is the radiation pressure. Treat ions and electrons as ideal monoatomic gasses (with the appropriate mean molecular weights), and assume that the radiation is in thermal equilibrium with the gas.

Write a code to compute \(p_{\mathrm{ions}}\), \(p_e\), and \(p_{\mathrm{rad}}\) for any given density \(\rho\) and temperature \(T\).
Plot \(p_{\mathrm{ions}}\), \(p_e\), and \(p_{\mathrm{rad}}\) as a function of temperature for \(\rho = 150\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\) (central density of the Sun) and for \(\rho = 10^{-24}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\) (ISM density). At what temperature does radiation become dominant in each case?

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.1 Observational facts
Supernovae are among the most energetic and luminous transients in the sky. They are the result of the explosion of massive stars, or of accreting white dwarfs at the end of their lives. Here, we use the tools of fluid mechanics we have developed so far to construct a simple model for these and similar explosive transients, such as novae and kilonovae. Our goal is to understand the basic physics, not to develop precise models, or to discuss all the nuances of the problem, for which we refer to the specialized literature.
Observationally, supernovae are characterized by a fast rise in the luminosity, on a timescale of a few days. They peak on a timescale of days to weeks and then decline over a timescale of months. A famous example of a core-collapse supernova light curve is given by the SN 1987A light curve in Figure 3.1. At peak magnitude, supernovae have luminosity \(L \sim 10^{10} L_{\odot}\), where \(L_{\odot}\) is the luminosity of the Sun. They remain bright for weeks to months, before beginning to fade. At peak, their typical effective temperature is \(T_{\mathrm{eff}} \sim 2 T_{\odot} \approx 12{,}000\,\mathrm{K}\), \(T_{\odot}\) being the effective temperature of the Sun. For a black body, the Stefan–Boltzmann law gives a relation between temperature and luminosity: \[
L = 4 \pi R^2 \sigma T^4,
\tag{3.1}\] where \(\sigma\) is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant \[
\sigma = \frac{ac}{4} = 5.6704 \times 10^{-8} \, \mathrm{W} \, \mathrm{m}^{- 2}
\, \mathrm{K}^{- 4} .
\tag{3.2}\] Assuming in first approximation supernovae to be black body emitters, this implies that the characteristic radius of a supernova at peak magnitude is \[
R_p \sim 2.5 \times 10^4 R_{\odot} \approx 10^{13} \, \mathrm{m} .
\tag{3.3}\] This is about twenty times larger than the radius of the largest stars. The duration of the peak is of a few weeks, say \(\sim 2 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{s}\), so the total energy release in photons is \[
\mathcal{E}_r \sim (2 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{s}) \times 10^{10} L_{\odot} \approx 8 \times
10^{49}\,\mathrm{erg} .
\tag{3.4}\] Here and in the rest of the chapter, we follow the custom of quoting large energies in erg and luminosities in \(\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}\), with \(1\,\mathrm{erg} = 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{J}\). From the observation of Doppler shifted emission and absorption lines, we know that the typical velocities are in the range of \(2{,}000\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{- 1}\) to \(10{,}000\,\mathrm{km}\,\mathrm{s}^{- 1}\). These velocities are consistent with the estimated length and temporal scales of the supernova phenomenon: \[
v \sim \frac{10^{13} \, \mathrm{m}}{10^6\,\mathrm{s}} = 10^7 \, \mathrm{m} \, \mathrm{s}^{- 1} =
10^4 \, \mathrm{km} \, \mathrm{s}^{- 1} .
\tag{3.5}\] The associated kinetic energy is \[
K \sim \frac{1}{2} Mv^2 \approx 10^{51}  \left( \frac{M}{M_{\odot}} \right)
\mathrm{erg} \gg \mathcal{E}_r .
\tag{3.6}\]
From these basic observational facts, we know that supernovae must be powered by objects with large surface areas and require large energies. All these numbers already suggest that supernovae could be powered by the explosion of stars. This is most dramatically confirmed by the disappearance of stars previously observed at the location of supernovae.

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.2 Shock breakout
Our supernova model begins with a star of radius \(R_0\) in which a large amount of energy \(\mathcal{E}\), much larger than the gravitational binding energy of the star, is injected. The source of this energy might be gravitational, in the case of core-collapse supernovae, or thermonuclear, but the outcome is similar: the progenitor is disrupted and matter starts expanding with large velocities. To fix our ideas, we will consider the explosion of a red supergiant with \(R_0 \sim 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}\), however all our results can be rescaled for other radii.
Immediately after the energy has been injected into the star, kinetic and internal energy are expected to be in equipartition \(K \sim E \sim \mathcal{E} \sim 10^{51}\,\mathrm{erg} = 10^{44}\,\mathrm{J}\), so we can estimate the temperature, assuming the gas to be radiation dominated: \[
E = \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3_0 aT^4 .
\tag{3.7}\] This estimate gives a temperature of \[
T \approx 4.2 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{K} \left( \frac{R_0}{10^{12} \, \mathrm{m}}
\right)^{- 3 / 4}  \left( \frac{E}{10^{51}\,\mathrm{erg}} \right)^{1 / 4} .
\tag{3.8}\] The energy is injected close to the center of the star and it is carried outwards by a shock wave (Chapter 11), which reaches the surface of the star after a time \(\sim R_0 / v \sim 10^5\,\mathrm{s}\), about a day (see Equation 3.32 below). When this happens, the hot radiation behind the shock is able to escape. This is the so-called shock breakout, which is the first light emanating from the supernova. Because of the high temperature, the radiation spectrum at breakout peaks in the UV and X-ray bands.
We can check if the assumption of radiation dominated gas is consistent by computing the ratio of radiation pressure to gas pressure: \[
\beta = \frac{\frac{1}{3} aT^4}{nk_B T} = \frac{a}{3 k_B}  \frac{T^3}{n}
\approx \frac{a}{3 k_B}  \frac{4 \pi R^3_0}{3}  \frac{\mu m_u}{M} T^3,
\tag{3.9}\] where we have approximated \(n\) with the average number density, \(n = \rho / (\mu m_u)\) (Equation 1.5), and \(M\) is the mass of the progenitor. We find \(\beta\): \[
\beta \approx 4.8 \times 10^3 \mu  \left( \frac{1
M_{\odot}}{M} \right)  \left( \frac{R_0}{10^{12} \, \mathrm{m}} \right)^{3 / 4}
\left( \frac{E}{10^{51}\,\mathrm{erg}} \right)^{3 / 4},
\tag{3.10}\] confirming that radiation dominates at early times. As we will see later, for homologous expansion, \(E \sim R^{- 1}\), so \(\beta\) is independent of the radius to which the ejecta has expanded, and matter remains radiation dominated.

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.3 Radiation diffusion
After the breakout, the star is full of radiation, but the photons need to make their way out of the explosion debris, before they can reach our telescopes. The dominant source of opacity is Thomson scattering on free electrons, but photons can also be absorbed and then re-emitted through various free-free, bound-free, and bound-bound processes. Their path out of the ejecta can be described as a random walk, such as the one illustrated in Figure 3.2.






Figure 3.2: Random walk of a photon in the supernova ejecta.



Consider a photon emitted at some location \(S\) deep inside the supernova ejecta. The photon is not able to escape immediately. Instead, it propagates over a distance \(\lambda_1\) before interacting with matter, either because it is scattered, or because it is absorbed and subsequently re-emitted in a different direction. The photon then moves in a new straight line over another distance \(\lambda_2\) and interacts again. This process is repeated \(N\) times (7 in the figure). We want to estimate how many steps are necessary for the photon to escape.
Let \(\mathbf{r}_1\), \(\mathbf{r}_2\), etc., be the displacement vectors between emission and absorption locations. We want to compute the total displacement \[
\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{r}_1 +\mathbf{r}_2 +\mathbf{r}_3 + \cdots,
\tag{3.11}\] and compare \(| \mathbf{R} |\) with the size of the expanding ejecta cloud \(R\). Since the direction of each step is random \[
\langle \mathbf{R} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{r}_1 +\mathbf{r}_2
+\mathbf{r}_3 + \cdots \rangle = \langle \mathbf{r}_1 \rangle + \langle
\mathbf{r}_2 \rangle + \langle \mathbf{r}_3 \rangle + \cdots = 0.
\tag{3.12}\] However, the mean square of the displacement does not vanish: \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\langle \mathbf{R}^2 \rangle &{}={} && \langle (\mathbf{r}_1 +\mathbf{r}_2
+\mathbf{r}_3 + \cdots) \\
&&& \quad \cdot (\mathbf{r}_1 +\mathbf{r}_2 +\mathbf{r}_3 +
\cdots) \rangle \\
&{}={} && \langle \mathbf{r}_1^2 \rangle + \langle \mathbf{r}_2^2 \rangle +
\langle \mathbf{r}_3^2 \rangle + \cdots \\
&&& + 2 \langle \mathbf{r}_1 \cdot
\mathbf{r}_2 \rangle + 2 \langle \mathbf{r}_1 \cdot \mathbf{r}_3 \rangle +
\cdots
\end{alignedat}
\tag{3.13}\] The mixed products disappear, since the orientation of the displacement vectors is random, but \[
\langle \mathbf{r}_i^2 \rangle = \lambda^2 > 0,
\tag{3.14}\] up to a factor of order unity, where \(\lambda\) is the photon mean free path. We conclude that \[
\langle \mathbf{R}^2 \rangle = N \lambda^2 .
\tag{3.15}\] Equating this to the size \(R\) of the supernova, we find that the number of interactions experienced by the photon before escaping is \[
N = \left( \frac{R}{\lambda} \right)^2 .
\tag{3.16}\] Neglecting the time between absorption and re-emission, the time required for the photon to escape, the so-called radiative diffusion time, is given by \[
\tau_d = N \frac{\lambda}{c} = \frac{R^2}{\lambda c} .
\tag{3.17}\] The mean free path can be expressed as \(\lambda = 1 / (\kappa \rho)\), where \(\kappa\) is the opacity (compare with Equation 1.1, \(\kappa \rho\) plays the role of \(n \sigma\)), and \(\rho = \frac{3 M}{4 \pi R^3}\), so \[
\tau_d = \frac{\kappa \rho}{c} R^2 = \frac{3}{4 \pi}  \frac{\kappa M}{Rc} .
\tag{3.18}\] Our calculation did not account for geometrical effects, but captured the essence of the problem. A more careful numerical calculation reveals that the characteristic radiation diffusion time scale is \[
\boxed{\tau_d = \frac{\kappa M}{\beta Rc}},
\tag{3.19}\] where \(\beta\) is a geometrical factor, not to be confused with the ratio of radiation to gas pressure. For spherical geometry, \(\beta \approx 13.8\).
Note that, since \(R = R_0 + vt \approx vt\), the diffusion time scale decays with time. On the other hand, the hydrodynamic time scale \(\tau_h = R / \dot{R} \approx t\) increases with time. Most of the radiation will escape at the time at which \(t_p = \tau_d (t_p)\), which is also the time at which diffusion and hydrodynamic time scales become equal: \[
\boxed{t_p = \left( \frac{\kappa M}{\beta cv} \right)^{1 / 2} .}
\tag{3.20}\] This is the peak time of the bolometric luminosity. For Thomson scattering in a hydrogen-rich, ionized gas \(\kappa = 0.4\,\mathrm{cm}^2\,\mathrm{g}^{- 1}\), that is, \(0.04\,\mathrm{m^2\,kg^{-1}}\) (as is customary, we quote opacities in \(\mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}\)), so \[
t_p = 1.4 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{s} \left( \frac{M}{M_{\odot}} \right)^{1 / 2}
\left( \frac{\kappa}{0.4\,\mathrm{cm}^2\,\mathrm{g}^{- 1}} \right)^{1 / 2}
\left( \frac{v}{10^4 \, \mathrm{km} \, \mathrm{s}^{- 1}} \right)^{- 1 / 2} .
\tag{3.21}\] The characteristic radius of the supernova at this time is \[
R_p = R_0 + t_p v \approx t_p v \sim 10^{13} \, \mathrm{m} .
\tag{3.22}\] This time scale and characteristic radius are in good agreement with observations. These formulae also show that the typical duration of the rise time of the supernova is proportional to the square root of the mass and of the opacity, and inversely proportional to the square root of the velocity. This implies that the explosion of less massive stars produces faster transients, while more massive stars produce light curves that evolve over longer timescales. These relations are key to interpret not only supernovae, but also other explosive transients, such as kilonovae. For SN 1987A the inferred velocity from spectroscopy is \(v \sim 3000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\) and the peak time is \(t_p \approx 100\,\mathrm{days}\) (Figure 3.1), so we can estimate \(M \approx 10 M_{\odot}\). This gives an explosion energy of \(\mathcal{E}= \frac{1}{2} Mv^2 \sim 10^{51}\,\mathrm{erg}\). These estimates are only correct to within an order of magnitude, since they neglect important effects, such as recombination, which we discuss below.

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.4 Ejecta expansion
We describe the supernova outflow as a single fluid element undergoing homologous expansion (Section 1.3), the so-called “one-zone approximation”. Accordingly, the equation for energy balance in the ejecta is (Equation 2.39) \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} + p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \rho
\dot{q} .
\tag{3.23}\] For the moment, we neglect radioactive heating, so \(\dot{q}\) only accounts for the loss of energy due to the escape of photons. Using the fact that \(\rho = M / V\) and \(M\) is constant, we can rewrite this as \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} (\varepsilon M)}{\mathrm{d} t} + pV \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= M
\dot{q} .
\tag{3.24}\] The first term is just the time derivative of the total internal energy in the ejecta \(E = \varepsilon M\), while the term on the RHS is minus the total luminosity, \(L = - M \dot{q}\), since \(\dot{q}\) only accounts for the energy lost by the escape of photons. Using the fact that \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \frac{1}{V} \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t}\) (Equation 1.12), the second term in the LHS can be rewritten as \[
pV \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= p \frac{\mathrm{d} V}{\mathrm{d} t},
\tag{3.25}\] so the energy equation becomes \[
\dot{E} + p \dot{V} = - L.
\tag{3.26}\] This is, of course, just the first law of thermodynamics applied to the entire supernova.
Using dimensional arguments, we can estimate the luminosity as \[
\boxed{L \approx \frac{E}{\tau_d}},
\tag{3.27}\] where \(E\) is the total thermal energy in the ejecta and \(\tau_d\) is the radiative diffusion time. This formula is valid when \(t \gtrsim \tau_d\), that is after the peak of the light curve, because photons are trapped for \(t \ll \tau_d\). We should be careful with the interpretation of the results we will find using Equation 3.27. For example, we will find that the light curve decays for all times, but, as previously discussed, we actually expect the supernova light curve to rise and then decline. However, Equation 3.27 is only valid after the peak.
It is useful to rewrite the pdV term as \[
p \dot{V} = pV \frac{\dot{V}}{V} = 3 pV \left( \frac{\dot{R}}{R} \right) = 3
pV \frac{1}{\tau_h},
\tag{3.28}\] where we have used the hydrodynamical timescale \(\tau_h = R / \dot{R} = R / v\), and the fact that \[
\frac{\dot{V}}{V} = 3 \frac{\dot{R}}{R} .
\tag{3.29}\] For a radiation dominated gas, \(p = u / 3\) (Equation 2.26), so \[
p = \frac{1}{3} \rho \varepsilon \Longrightarrow 3 pV = M \varepsilon = E.
\tag{3.30}\] Combining the last two equations with Equation 3.27, we obtain \[
\dot{E} + \frac{E}{\tau_h} = - \frac{E}{\tau_d} \Longrightarrow
\boxed{\frac{\dot{E}}{E} = - \left( \frac{1}{\tau_h} + \frac{1}{\tau_d}
\right) .}
\tag{3.31}\] Remember that this expression is only valid for \(t \gtrsim \tau_d\). Also note that both \(\tau_h\) and \(\tau_d\) depend on time.
At the time of break out, the hydrodynamical time scale is \[
\tau_{h, 0} = \frac{R}{v} = 10^5\,\mathrm{s} \left( \frac{R_0}{10^{12}
\, \mathrm{m}} \right)  \left( \frac{v}{10^4 \, \mathrm{km} \, \mathrm{s}^{- 1}}
\right)^{- 1} .
\tag{3.32}\] The radiation diffusion time scale can be estimated using \(\kappa \approx 0.4\,\mathrm{cm}^2\,\mathrm{g}^{- 1}\) to be \[
\tau_{d, 0} = 2 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{s} \left( \frac{M}{M_{\odot}} \right)
\left( \frac{R_0}{10^{12} \, \mathrm{m}} \right)^{- 1} \gg \tau_{h, 0} .
\tag{3.33}\] So at early times radiation is trapped in the expanding ejecta, however most of the thermal energy is “lost” to pdV work (it is converted to kinetic energy) on a time scale \(t \sim \tau_h\), before it has a chance to escape as radiation. Indeed, at early times we can neglect the radiative losses to find \[
\frac{\dot{E}}{E} + \frac{\dot{R}}{R} = 0 \Longrightarrow ER \sim
\mathrm{const} \Longrightarrow E \sim \frac{1}{R} .
\tag{3.34}\] So after matter has expanded by a factor \(10\), the thermal energy is reduced to a tenth of the initial value. This explains why \(\mathcal{E}_r \ll \mathcal{E}\) in supernovae. Indeed, since \(R_p \sim 10 R_0\) (Equation 3.22), we expect \(\mathcal{E}_r \sim \mathcal{E} / 10 \sim 10^{50}\,\mathrm{erg}\), in agreement with Equation 3.4.
To calculate the bolometric light curve, we write the energy as \[
\frac{\dot{E}}{E} + \frac{\dot{R}}{R} = - \frac{1}{\tau_d (t)}
\Longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} \ln (ER)}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{1}{\tau_d (t)} .
\tag{3.35}\] and expand \(\tau_d (t)\) as: \[
\tau_d (t) = \tau_{d, p}  \frac{R_p}{R_p + vt} = \tau_{d, p}  \frac{R_p /
v}{R_p / v + t} = \frac{\tau_{d, p} \tau_{h, p}}{\tau_{h, p} + t},
\tag{3.36}\] where \(\tau_{d, p}\) and \(\tau_{h, p}\) are the diffusion and hydrodynamic time scale at the peak of the light curve, respectively, and where we now measure \(t\) from the time of the peak.
In this way we find \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \ln (ER)}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{t + \tau_{h, p}}{\tau_{d, p}
\tau_{h, p}} \Rightarrow ER = (E_p R_p) \exp \left( - \frac{\tau_{h, p} t +
t^2 / 2}{\tau_{d, p} \tau_{h, p}} \right) .
\tag{3.37}\] The last expression gives the expression for the luminosity, because \[
L = \frac{E}{\tau_d} = \left( \frac{\beta c}{\kappa M} \right) ER,
\tag{3.38}\] so \[
\boxed{\begin{aligned} L = {} & \left( \frac{\beta cE_p R_p}{\kappa M} \right) \exp \left( -
\frac{\tau_{h, p} t + t^2 / 2}{\tau_{d, p} \tau_{h, p}} \right) \\
& \mathrm{for}\ t \geq 0 .\end{aligned}}
\tag{3.39}\] The luminosity at peak can be estimated as \[
\begin{aligned}
L_0 &= \frac{\beta cE_p R_p}{\kappa M} = \frac{E_p}{\tau_{d, p}} \\
&\approx 5.2 \times 10^{43}\,\mathrm{erg}\,\mathrm{s}^{- 1}  \left(
\frac{E_p}{10^{50}\,\mathrm{erg}} \right) \\
&\qquad \times \left( \frac{R_p}{10^{13}
\, \mathrm{m}} \right) \left( \frac{M_{\odot}}{M} \right)  \left( \frac{0.4
\mathrm{cm}^2\,\mathrm{g}^{- 1}}{\kappa} \right)
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.40}\] For the explosion of a red supergiant with \(M \sim 10 M_{\odot}\), we have \(R_p \sim 10 R_0 \sim 10^{13}\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(E_p \sim \mathcal{E} / 10 \sim 10^{50}\,\mathrm{erg}\), so this formula predicts \(L_0 \sim 5 \times 10^{42}\,\mathrm{erg}\,\mathrm{s}^{- 1}\), comparable to the luminosity of Type II-P supernovae (Figure 3.5). For SN 1987A, whose progenitor was a compact blue supergiant with \(R_0 \approx 3 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{m}\), this estimate is about ten times smaller than the observed peak. As we will see below, the light curve of SN 1987A is powered by radioactive decays.
This shows that, in absence of radioactive heating, or when radioactive heating is subdominant, the luminosity declines rapidly after having peaked at \(t = t_p\). At late times, \(t \gtrsim \tau_{h, p}\), the luminosity decreases as \(\exp (- t^2 / \tau_{\mathrm{lc}}^2)\), where the characteristic decay time for the light curve is given by \[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_{\mathrm{lc}} &= \sqrt{2 \tau_{d, p} \tau_{h, p}} \\
&\approx 2 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{s} \left( \frac{\kappa}{0.4\,\mathrm{cm}^2\,\mathrm{g}^{- 1}} \right)^{1/ 2}  \left( \frac{M}{M_{\odot}} \right)^{1 / 2} \\
&\qquad \times \left( \frac{v}{10^4
\, \mathrm{km} \, \mathrm{s}^{- 1}} \right)^{- 1 / 2} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.41}\] Note that \(\tau_{\mathrm{lc}}\) does not depend on the expansion radius, but remains constant. Since \(\tau_{d, p} = t_p\) and \(\tau_{h, p} \approx t_p\), we also have \(\tau_{\mathrm{lc}} \approx \sqrt{2} t_p\), which explains why Equation 3.41 and Equation 3.21 have the same scaling.
This simple model with no radioactive heating already predicts several key properties of supernovae and other explosive transients. It shows that the luminosity is proportional to the explosion energy per unit mass and to the radius of the progenitor, and inversely proportional to the opacity. Indeed, using \(E_p \approx \mathcal{E} R_0 / R_p\) in Equation 3.40, we find \(L_0 \approx \beta c \mathcal{E} R_0 / (\kappa M)\). It also shows that the typical duration of the transient is proportional to the square root of the mass and of the opacity, and inversely proportional to the square root of the velocity. For example, we have found that the explosion of less massive stars produces faster transients, while more massive stars produce light curves that evolve over longer timescales.

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.5 Radioactive heating
The radioactive decay of \(^{56}\,\mathrm{Ni}\) to \(^{56}\,\mathrm{Co}\) and of \(^{56}\,\mathrm{Co}\) to \(^{56}\,\mathrm{Fe}\) powers the light curve of supernovae. These decays produce \(\gamma\)-rays and positrons. Some of these particles escape from the ejecta, so their energy does not contribute to the optical light curve. However, especially in the first weeks, the majority of the decay products are reprocessed into thermal radiation. After having included this new heating source, the first law of thermodynamics is: \[
\dot{E} + p \dot{V} = \dot{Q}_{\mathrm{heat}} - L,
\tag{3.42}\] where \(\dot{Q}_{\mathrm{heat}}\) is the energy deposited by the radioactive decays in \(\mathrm{erg}\,\mathrm{s}^{- 1}\).
Proceeding as before, we can introduce a heating time scale \[
\tau_{\mathrm{heat}} = \frac{E}{\dot{Q}_{\mathrm{heat}}},
\tag{3.43}\] and obtain the energy equation \[
\frac{\dot{E}}{E} + \frac{\dot{R}}{R} = \frac{1}{\tau_{\mathrm{heat}}} -
\frac{1}{\tau_d} \Longrightarrow \boxed{\frac{\mathrm{d} \ln (E R)}{\mathrm{d}
t} = \frac{1}{\tau_{\mathrm{heat}}} - \frac{1}{\tau_d} .}
\tag{3.44}\] With the inclusion of radioactive heating, the light curve changes qualitatively. In particular, the luminosity can continue to grow even after \(t \gtrsim \tau_d\) and reach a higher maximum. To see this, we use the fact that \(E R = (\kappa M / \beta c) L \propto L\) (Equation 3.38), which implies that the peak is reached when the RHS of Equation 3.44 vanishes: \[
\frac{1}{\tau_{\mathrm{heat}}} = \frac{1}{\tau_d} \Longrightarrow
\frac{\dot{Q}_{\mathrm{heat}}}{E} = \frac{1}{\tau_d} \Longrightarrow
\boxed{\dot{Q}_{\mathrm{heat}} = \frac{E}{\tau_d} = L.}
\tag{3.45}\] This shows that the luminosity at peak equals the heating rate. This is a key result in supernova theory called “Arnett’s rule”1. Since the energy released by each nuclear decay is known from laboratory experiments, Arnett’s rule provides a way to estimate the amount of radioactive material produced by the supernova. Type Ia supernovae (Figure 3.4), which are the result of the thermonuclear explosion of white dwarfs, are an example of supernovae in which radioactivity plays the dominant role in the light curve over all times and for which Arnett’s rule can be applied.
The effect of radioactive heating is illustrated in Figure 3.3, which shows the solution of the one-zone model, Equation 3.44 with \(L = E / \tau_d\), for the explosion of a red and of a blue supergiant. The explosion of the compact blue supergiant would be very faint without radioactive heating, because most of its thermal energy is lost to \(p \mathrm{d} V\) work. With radioactive heating, the light curve has a broad peak after about four months, which is qualitatively similar to the one of SN 1987A (Figure 3.1). Note that the peak is reached when the luminosity equals the heating rate, as predicted by Arnett’s rule.






Figure 3.3: Light curves from the one-zone model for the explosion of a red supergiant (\(R_0 = 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}\)) and of a compact blue supergiant (\(R_0 = 3 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{m}\)), with \(M = 10\,M_\odot\), \(v = 3000\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\), and an initial thermal energy of \(5 \times 10^{50}\,\mathrm{erg}\). The dashed line includes the heating by the decay of \(0.07\,M_\odot\) of \(^{56}\)Ni, whose rate is shown by the dotted line. The model is not accurate at early times, before the peak (see text).









Figure 3.4: Sample of Type Ia thermonuclear supernova light curves: data and theoretical models. From Arnett (1996); © Princeton University Press, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.6 Recombination and nebular phase
After the peak of the light curve, as the explosion debris expand and cool, other physical effects start to become important. First, a larger fraction of gamma rays and positrons escape and/or are not thermalized. Secondly, ions begin to recombine. This removes the free electrons that were responsible for the Thomson opacity from the gas which then becomes transparent in the infrared/optical bands. Thus, as matter recombines, radiation quickly escapes, rapidly cooling down the material. This process launches a recombination wave into the supernova debris. The photons we see at this stage are no longer coming from the outer edge of the ejecta, but instead are emitted at a photosphere that is very close to the recombination front.
Recombination of hydrogen and helium is important for many classes of supernovae, including for SN 1987A, but their impact is particularly spectacular in hydrogen rich, Type II-P supernovae. Because recombination of hydrogen happens at a fixed temperature2, the luminosity can be estimated as \[
L = 4 \pi R_r^2 (t) \sigma T^4_r,
\tag{3.46}\] where \(T_r \approx 6000\,\mathrm{K}\) is the recombination temperature (a constant), and \(R_r (t)\) is the position of the recombination front (which nearly coincides with the photosphere). In Type II-P supernovae, \(R_r (t) \sim \mathrm{const}\) for \(\sim 100\) days and the bolometric luminosity plateaus to a nearly constant value (P stands for plateau). A prototypical example is SN 1999em, shown in Figure 3.5.






TipExample



Consider the plateau of SN 1999em. If we take the radius of the recombination front to be \(R_r \sim 10^{13}\,\mathrm{m}\), as estimated in Equation 3.22, and \(T_r \approx 6000\,\mathrm{K}\), Equation 3.46 gives \[
L \approx 4 \pi \left( 10^{13}\,\mathrm{m} \right)^2 \sigma \left( 6000\,\mathrm{K} \right)^4 \approx 9 \times 10^{34}\,\mathrm{W} = 9 \times 10^{41}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}},
\tag{3.47}\] or \(\log L \approx 42.0\), in good agreement with the plateau in Figure 3.5.


After the recombination wave has swept through the ejecta, the supernova enters the so called nebular phase. In this stage there is no longer a photosphere, because the material is transparent. The black body approximation fails, because radiation is produced by various decays and matter is no longer in thermodynamic equilibrium. Often, the luminosity decays exponentially, with characteristic time scale equal to the mean lifetime of \(^{56}\,\mathrm{Co}\), \(\tau \approx 111\) days (its half life is 77 days), so it is possible to fit the decay tail to estimate the amount of radioactive material. This has to be done carefully, accounting for the thermalization efficiency of positrons and gamma-rays.






Figure 3.5: Bolometric light curve for SN 1999em, a classical example of a Type II-P supernova. Data from Elmhamdi et al. (2003); figure courtesy of Viktoriya Morozova, used with permission and not covered by the license of these notes.

3.7 In-class worksheet

Consider the explosion of a red supergiant with radius \(R_0 = 10^{12}\,\mathrm{m}\) and mass \(M \sim 10\,M_\odot\). At time \(t = 0\), we inject a large amount of energy into the star, \(\sim 10^{51}\,\mathrm{erg} = 10^{44}\,\mathrm{J}\).
Constants: \(a = 7.6 \times 10^{-16}\,\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}\,K^{-4}}\), \(k_B = 1.4 \times 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J/K}\), \(h = 6.6 \times 10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}\).

Find the temperature of the gas, and determine the waveband in which the black body emission peaks.
Show that the gas is radiation dominated. Compute \(\beta = P_{\mathrm{rad}} / P_{\mathrm{gas}}\).

Given the mean free path \(\lambda = 1 / (\kappa \rho)\), and the definition of the photon diffusion time through a system of size \(R\), \(\tau_d = R^2 / \lambda c\), find the time needed for a photon to escape the Sun, after being created in the core. Take \(\kappa \sim 25\,\mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}\).
Show that: \[
\tau_d (t) = \frac{\tau_d (0) \tau_h (0)}{\tau_h (0) + t} .
\tag{3.48}\]

title: 3  Core-Collapse Supernovae
text:
3.8 Exercises

Exercise 3.1 (The Katz integral) Consider a homologously expanding radioactive cloud of debris, with radius \(R \approx v t\), launched by an explosion of some kind, e.g., a supernova.

Assume that the gas is described by the gamma-law equation of state \[
p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon .
\tag{3.49}\] Show that the first law of thermodynamics becomes \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} E}{\mathrm{d} t} = - L + \dot{Q} - 3 (\Gamma - 1)
\frac{E}{t},
\tag{3.50}\] where \(L\) is the luminosity (energy radiated away in erg/s), and \(\dot{Q}\) is the radioactive heating rate in erg/s.
Show that the following exact relation holds under suitable assumptions: \[
\int_0^t L (t') t' \mathrm{d} t' = \int_0^t \dot{Q} (t') t' \mathrm{d} t' .
\tag{3.51}\] The quantity on the LHS is called the Katz integral and can be determined observationally. Discuss the validity of the approximations made to derive this result.
The radioactive heating can be written as \[
\dot{Q} = M (t)  \frac{q}{\tau},
\tag{3.52}\] where \(q\) is the radioactive energy release in J/kg, \(\tau\) is the radioactive decay timescale, and \(M (t) = M_0 \mathrm{e}^{- t / \tau}\) is the mass of the radioactive material at time \(t\). Show how \(M_0\) can be estimated from the Katz integral, assuming \(q\) and \(\tau\) to be known from nuclear physics experiments.

title: 4  The Euler Equation
text:
4.1 Internal stresses
Up to this point we have described the motion of fluids in which the velocity field is prescribed, or known. Now we derive the equation of motion for fluids. The acceleration of a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) with mass \(\mathcal{M}\) is given by Newton’s law: \[
\mathcal{M} \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} =\mathbf{F},
\tag{4.1}\] where \(\mathbf{F}\) is the sum of all forces (the net force) acting on \(\mathcal{V}\). To derive an equation that does not explicitly make reference to the fluid elements, we can divide Equation 4.1 by the volume of \(\mathcal{V}\) to find \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} =\mathbf{f},
\tag{4.2}\] where \(\mathbf{f}\) is the force per unit volume acting on the fluid: \[
[\mathbf{f}] = \mathrm{N} \, \mathrm{m}^{- 3} = \mathrm{kg} \, \mathrm{m}^{- 2}
\, \mathrm{s}^{- 2},
\tag{4.3}\] where \(\mathrm{N}\) is the newton, the SI unit of force (Equation 2.5). There are two types of forces that can act on a fluid element: external and internal forces. In astrophysical applications, gravity is the most common external force. The force per unit volume (body force) due to gravity is \[
\mathbf{f}_g = \rho \mathbf{g}= - \rho \nabla \Psi,
\tag{4.4}\] where \(\mathbf{g}\) is the gravitational acceleration and \(\Psi\) is the gravitational potential (Chapter 7). The internal forces are due to the interaction of \(\mathcal{V}\) with other fluid elements.
Consider a container with water at rest on the surface of the Earth. The container has been left undisturbed for sufficiently long time that the velocity of all fluid elements is zero. Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a fluid element of water somewhere away from the edge of the container. Clearly, \(\mathcal{V}\) is subject to the force of gravity. Since \(\mathcal{V}\) is not in contact with the container, the gravitational force cannot be balanced by a contact force with the walls of the container. Instead, the force on \(\mathcal{V}\) must be balanced by a force exchanged by \(\mathcal{V}\) with the neighboring fluid elements. This shows that the equation of motion of a fluid must include the acceleration due to its internal forces. What is their nature?
We consider an infinitesimal fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) in a fluid at rest, as illustrated in Figure 4.1. We can take the origin of the coordinate system to be the center of \(\mathcal{V}\) and its extent in the three directions to be \(\mathrm{d} x\), \(\mathrm{d} y\), and \(\mathrm{d} z\). We also take the \(z\) axis to point upwards, so that the gravitational acceleration is \(\mathbf{g} = - g \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), with \(g > 0\).
The fluid element is subject to forces applied by the rest of the fluid to its six square faces and to the force of gravity, which we can take to be applied to its center of mass, as shown in Figure 4.1. Our goal is to determine these forces. What distinguishes a fluid from a solid is that a fluid at rest cannot sustain shear stresses: if we try to shear it, it flows. So, for a fluid at rest, the surface forces must be perpendicular to each face. In a moving fluid, instead, these surface forces can in principle have many possible magnitudes and directions, and we cannot make much progress without knowing more about the nature of the fluid.
However, there is a class of fluids, known as perfect fluids, for which the internal forces are particularly simple. In a perfect fluid the surface forces are assumed to be always directed along the perpendicular to each face, also when the fluid is in motion (as is the case in Figure 4.1). The problem of finding the internal forces thus reduces to that of finding a scalar quantity, called the pressure, that gives the magnitude of the force per unit area across each face of the fluid element. One can show, by considering the forces acting on a small wedge of fluid, that this magnitude does not depend on the orientation of the face1: \[
p = \text{``force per unit area''} \qquad [\mathrm{Pa} = \mathrm{N} \, \mathrm{m}^{- 2}] .
\tag{4.5}\] In particular, for a perfect fluid the force exerted by the fluid on an infinitesimal surface with outward-directed area element \(\mathrm{d} \mathbf{A}\) is \[
\mathrm{d} \mathbf{F}= - p \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A}.
\tag{4.6}\] In most cases the pressure is positive \(p > 0\), so a fluid element, or equivalently an object immersed in a fluid, is subject to compression.
The concept of perfect fluid is an idealization of reality, but, in practice, liquids and gases can be considered as perfect fluids to very good approximation in most situations. More generally, because the force needs to transform under basis change in the same way as a vector, it can be shown that internal forces can be written as \[
\mathrm{d} \mathbf{F}=\mathbf{T} \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A},
\tag{4.7}\] where \(\mathbf{T}\) is a matrix that depends on the properties of the fluid, the so-called stress tensor of the fluid. The perfect fluid is the special case of this general theory in which \[
\mathbf{T}= - p\mathbf{I},
\tag{4.8}\] where \(\mathbf{I}\) is the identity matrix. We will encounter examples of non-perfect fluids later in the course (Chapter 21 and Chapter 18).

title: 4  The Euler Equation
