title: 4  The Euler Equation
text:
4.2 Euler’s equation
We can now consider the net acceleration of the fluid element in the vertical direction. There are three forces to consider: the force of gravity, and the forces at the bottom and at the top of \(\mathcal{V}\). The forces from the side do not contribute, since they are orthogonal to the \(z\)-direction. Putting everything together we find: \[
\mathcal{M} \frac{\mathrm{d} v_z}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \left[ p \left( z =
\tfrac{\mathrm{d} z}{2} \right) - p \left( z = - \tfrac{\mathrm{d} z}{2} \right)
\right] \mathrm{d} A +\mathcal{M}g_z,
\tag{4.9}\] where \(\mathrm{d} A = \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} y\), and \(\mathcal{M}= \rho V = \rho \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} y \mathrm{d} z\). Dividing both terms by \(V\) gives \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} v_z}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{1}{\mathrm{d} z}  \left[ p \left( z =
\tfrac{\mathrm{d} z}{2} \right) - p \left( z = - \tfrac{\mathrm{d} z}{2} \right)
\right] + \rho g_z = - \partial_z p + \rho g_z .
\tag{4.10}\] A similar derivation can be done for the momentum balance in the \(x\)- and \(y\)-directions to find \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p + \rho \mathbf{g}.
\tag{4.11}\] In the more general case, in which we consider an arbitrary volume force applied onto the fluid, we obtain the so-called Euler, or momentum equation for a perfect fluid: \[
\boxed{\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p
+\mathbf{f}.}
\tag{4.12}\] Note that it is the gradient of the pressure, and not the pressure directly that determines the mechanical response of the fluid. We will see that this has important implications in a number of situations. Also note that \(\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v} / \mathrm{d} t\) is the acceleration of the fluid element. In Chapter 5 we will rewrite Euler’s equation in terms of derivatives at fixed points in space.
In the case of non-perfect fluids, Equation 4.12 becomes \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{T}+\mathbf{f},
\tag{4.13}\] where we have introduced the divergence of a tensor, defined to be a vector with components \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{T}  = \left(\begin{array}{c}
\partial_x T_{x x} + \partial_y T_{x y} + \partial_z T_{x z}\\
\partial_x T_{y x} + \partial_y T_{y y} + \partial_z T_{y z}\\
\partial_x T_{z x} + \partial_y T_{z y} + \partial_z T_{z z}
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{4.14}\] The momentum equation, Equation 4.13, holds even for solids, which can rarely be described as perfect fluids, but for which the stress tensor can also be defined.






TipExample



Consider a liquid at rest (\(\mathbf{v}= 0\)) in a tank and subject to gravity. The tank is not pressurized, so the surface of the liquid is at the atmospheric pressure \(p_0\), in order to be in mechanical equilibrium with the air. Liquids are nearly incompressible, so, if the tank is not too deep, we can neglect the change of the density with depth and take \(\rho = \mathrm{const}\). What is the pressure at the bottom of the tank?
We can take \(z\) to be the vertical coordinate, pointing upwards, with \(z = 0\) being the bottom of the tank and \(z = d > 0\) being the surface of the liquid. The force balance in the \(z\)-direction is \[
\partial_z p = - \rho g,
\tag{4.15}\] where \(g > 0\) is the gravitational acceleration. Integrating this equation from the surface, we find \[
p (z) = p_0 + \int_z^d \rho g \mathrm{d} z' = p_0 + \rho g (d - z).
\tag{4.16}\] The pressure at the bottom of the tank is \(p_0 + \rho gd\). For water, \(\rho \approx 1\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} = 10^3\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), so for \(d = 10\,\mathrm{m}\) we find \(\rho g d \approx 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa}\), which is about one atmosphere. In other words, every \(10\,\mathrm{m}\) of water adds about one atmosphere of pressure.








TipExample



Consider a body of volume \(V\) fully immersed in a fluid at rest. What is the net force exerted by the fluid on the body?
The force is obtained by integrating Equation 4.6 over the surface \(\partial V\) of the body. Using a variant of the divergence theorem, \(\oint_{\partial V} p \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} = \int_V \nabla p \mathrm{d} V\), we find \[
\mathbf{F}_b = - \oint_{\partial V} p \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} = - \int_V \nabla p \mathrm{d} V .
\tag{4.17}\] The pressure in the fluid does not know about the body: it is the same pressure that would be there if the body were replaced by fluid. So, from Equation 4.11 with \(\mathbf{v} = 0\), \(\nabla p = \rho_f \mathbf{g}\), where \(\rho_f\) is the density of the fluid. If \(\rho_f\) is constant, we find \[
\mathbf{F}_b = - \rho_f V \mathbf{g} = \rho_f V g \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{4.18}\] The body is pushed upwards with a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. This is Archimedes’ principle. Note that only the gradient of \(p\) enters in this result. For example, increasing the atmospheric pressure \(p_0\) at the surface of the fluid does not change the force on the body.


Let’s recap our situation. We have started with the continuity equation (Equation 1.15), which describes the evolution of the density \(\rho\) given the velocity \(\mathbf{v}\). To find the velocity we have now derived an equation of motion for it, Euler’s equation, which however involves the pressure. As we have seen in Chapter 2, the pressure is given by the equation of state of the fluid, which depends on its density, temperature or entropy, and composition \[
p = p (\rho, T, \{ Y_i \}) .
\tag{4.19}\] This should not be surprising, because water and interstellar gas behave very differently, even though they satisfy the same equations. Their different dynamics is the result of the fact that they have different equations of state. To close the system, we also need an equation for the temperature, or the internal energy: this is the energy equation (Equation 2.39). There are some special cases, however, in which the pressure can be taken to be a function of only the density: \[
p = p (\rho) .
\tag{4.20}\] In this case we say that the equation of state is barotropic, and the continuity and Euler equations form a closed system, without the need for an energy equation. Some important cases that we will encounter in our course are

pressureless fluids, in which \(p = 0\);
isothermal gases, in which \(p = c_s^2 \rho\), where \(c_s > 0\) is a constant, which we will see is equal to the speed of sound in the gas;
polytropic gases, in which \(p = K \rho^{\Gamma}\) (Equation 2.24), where \(K\) and \(\Gamma\) are some known positive constants.

The pressureless approximation can sometimes be employed for highly supersonic flows, or for collisionless matter, such as dark matter or dust, when its velocity dispersion is small (that is, when it is cold). Note that collisionless matter can only be described as a fluid as long as it flows with a single velocity at each point. When different streams cross, the fluid approximation itself breaks down (Chapter 1). The isothermal and polytropic equations of state hold when temperature or entropy are constant in the gas, so the equation of state becomes barotropic. We will discuss this in more detail later.

4.3 In-class worksheet

A tank of water, open at the top, is accelerated horizontally with constant acceleration \(a\). Once the water has come to rest with respect to the tank, what is the shape of its free surface? Treat the water as incompressible.
Core-collapse supernovae are triggered when the iron core of a massive star exceeds the Chandrasekhar mass. Initially, the core is in hydrostatic equilibrium: \[
\partial_r p = - \frac{GM}{r^2} \rho,
\tag{4.21}\] where \(M = M (r)\) is the enclosed mass. After the core becomes unstable, it starts to contract. Show that, if \(\Gamma \approx 4 / 3\), and if the collapse is homologous and adiabatic, then the iron core remains close to hydrostatic equilibrium as it contracts, meaning that Equation 4.21 remains approximately true. [Hint: compare how the two sides of Equation 4.21 scale with the radius of the core.] What happens if \(\Gamma > 4/3\)? And if \(\Gamma < 4/3\)? In reality, the flow is no longer adiabatic, once it becomes supersonic, so the homologous collapse only describes the region with \(v < c_s\).

title: 4  The Euler Equation
text: Consider a small wedge-shaped fluid element of size \(\ell\). The surface forces acting on its faces are proportional to their areas, so they scale as \(\ell^2\), while body forces, such as gravity, and the inertia of the element are proportional to its volume, so they scale as \(\ell^3\). As \(\ell \to 0\), the surface forces must balance each other on their own. Because the areas of the faces of the wedge are related by geometry, this is only possible if the force per unit area is the same on all faces.↩︎

title: 5  Eulerian and Lagrangian Descriptions
text:
5.1 Motivation
Up to this point, we have considered the equation of motion for individual fluid elements. This is the so-called Lagrangian description of fluid mechanics. However, there are many problems in which it is more convenient to work with equations that describe the density, velocity, and temperature of the fluid at a specific point in space, and not for individual fluid elements. In other words, we want to solve for \(\rho (t, \mathbf{x})\) and \(\mathbf{v} (t, \mathbf{x})\), as opposed to \(\rho (t ; \mathcal{V})\) and \(\mathbf{v} (t ; \mathcal{V})\). This is the so-called Eulerian approach.
As motivation, we consider a celestial body of mass \(M\), for example a planet or a star, that is accreting matter at a constant rate \(\dot{M}\). \(M\) and \(\dot{M}\) are unknown, but we know density and velocity of the fluid at a given radius \(r_0\) from spatially resolved observations of an emission line. How can we estimate \(M\) and \(\dot{M}\)? We assume the in-falling matter to have no angular momentum, so that the flow is radial. We also neglect radiation pressure and fluid pressure (\(p = 0\)). We will consider the more general case in which pressure forces are included later in the course (Chapter 14). However, we remark that the pressureless approximation provides an accurate description of the flow when it is highly supersonic (close to the surface of the accretor).
The equations of motion for the gas (assuming spherical symmetry) are \[
\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{1}{r^2} \partial_r
(r^2 v), \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{GM}{r^2} .
\tag{5.1}\] In the new language we have just introduced, these are the Lagrangian equations of motion. That is, they describe the density and velocity of each fluid element. Note that, even though the problem describes a steady state system, we cannot drop the time derivatives, because each individual fluid element is not stationary, but it is in free fall.
Consider a fluid element that starts at rest at large distance from the accretor. Since the fluid elements are not subject to any force besides gravity, they are in free fall \[
v = - \sqrt{\frac{2 GM}{r}} .
\tag{5.2}\] Inserting this into the continuity equation yields: \[
\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{3 \sqrt{2 GM}}{2 r^{3 /
2}} .
\tag{5.3}\] Here, we need to be careful, because in the Lagrangian framework \(r = r (t)\), since we are traveling with each fluid element. So, before we can solve the continuity equation, we need to find \(r\) as solution of \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \sqrt{\frac{2 GM}{r}} .
\tag{5.4}\] This equation can be solved analytically assuming the initial radius to be \(r (0) = r_0\), but its solution is rather complex: \[
r (t) = \left( - \frac{3 \sqrt{2 GM} t}{2} + r_0^{3 / 2} \right)^{2 / 3} .
\tag{5.5}\] Plugging this back into the continuity equation, we find \[
\frac{1}{\rho}  \frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \frac{3 \sqrt{2 GM}}{3
\sqrt{2 GM} t - 2 r_0^{3 / 2}} .
\tag{5.6}\] This can be solved with initial conditions \(\rho (0) = \rho_0\) to yield \[
\rho (t) = \frac{2 r_0^{3 / 2} \rho_0}{2 r_0^{3 / 2} - 3 \sqrt{2 GM} t} .
\tag{5.7}\] After all of this work, we still do not have \(\rho\) as a function of radius: for that we need to solve \(t\) from Equation 5.5 and plug the result back into Equation 5.7. Note, however, that the denominator in Equation 5.7 is just \(2 r^{3 / 2}\), so \(\rho = \rho_0 (r_0 / r)^{3 / 2}\) along each fluid element. Since the flow is steady, every fluid element has density \(\rho_0\) when it crosses \(r_0\), so this is also \(\rho (r)\). We got there, but only after solving for the trajectory of each fluid element. We also still need to relate \(\rho_0\) to \(\dot{M}\)… Wouldn’t our lives have been much simpler if we could have solved directly for \(\rho (t, r)\)? As we will see shortly, the Eulerian formulation of fluid mechanics gives us \(\rho (r)\) directly, without ever computing a trajectory.

title: 5  Eulerian and Lagrangian Descriptions
text:
5.2 Advective derivative
We leave for a moment the problem of the spherical accretion, to develop the general theory of the Eulerian formulation of fluid mechanics. Let \(A (t ; \mathcal{V})\) be some quantity that is specific to a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\). For example, \(A\) could be the density or the velocity of the fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\). The same quantity can also be thought of as being a function of position: \[
A (t, \mathbf{x}) := A \left( t ; \text{``fluid element at location
$\mathbf{x}$ at time $t$''} \right) .
\tag{5.8}\] If the law of motion of each fluid element is known, then it is possible to compute \(A (t, \mathbf{x})\) from \(A (t ; \mathcal{V})\). We have done this in the case of the homologously expanding flow (Section 1.3), when we needed to compute \(v (t, r)\) given \(v (t, q)\), where \(q\) was the “label” we used to identify the fluid elements.
Consider a fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) with trajectory \(\mathbf{x} (t)\). Then, at time \(t\) \[
A (t ; \mathcal{V}) = A (t, \mathbf{x} (t)) .
\tag{5.9}\] We can differentiate both sides with respect to \(t\) to find \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{d} A (t ; \mathcal{V})}{\mathrm{d} t} =  \frac{\mathrm{d} A (t,
\mathbf{x} (t))}{\mathrm{d} t}  \\
& \quad = \frac{\partial A (t, \mathbf{x} (t))}{\partial t} + \biggl(
\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} t} \partial_x + \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{d} t}
\partial_y \\
& \qquad\qquad + \frac{\mathrm{d} z}{\mathrm{d} t} \partial_z \biggr) A (t, \mathbf{x}
(t))  \\
& \quad = \frac{\partial A (t, \mathbf{x} (t))}{\partial t} + \left(
\frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{x}}{\mathrm{d} t} \cdot \nabla \right) A (t, \mathbf{x}
(t)) \\
& \quad = \frac{\partial A (t, \mathbf{x} (t))}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot
\nabla) A (t, \mathbf{x} (t)),
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.10}\] where we used the chain rule for differentiation and the definition of velocity. Equation 5.10 gives us a way to relate the time derivative of a quantity defined with respect to fluid elements to the same quantity taken to be a function of spatial position and time. The reason why \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} A (t ; \mathcal{V})}{\mathrm{d} t} \neq \frac{\partial A (t,
\mathbf{x} (t))}{\partial t}
\tag{5.11}\] is that the partial derivative with respect to time considers the rate of change of \(A\) at a fixed location, but there are different fluid elements crossing that location as a function of time. This is illustrated in Figure 5.1. The operator \(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}\) that we have used so far is called the advective derivative (also material, or Lagrangian, derivative; many books write it as \(D / Dt\)), because it represents the rate of change of a quantity measured when riding along a fluid element.






Figure 5.1: Eulerian (left) and Lagrangian (right) descriptions of a flow. In the Eulerian description, we measure the rate of change of a quantity at a fixed point \(\mathbf{x}\), across which different fluid elements (1, 2, 3) pass over time. In the Lagrangian description, we follow a single fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\) along its trajectory.



Equation 5.10 can be written more succinctly as \[
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm{d} A}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial A}{\partial t}
+\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla A.}
\tag{5.12}\] To be mathematically precise, we should keep in mind that this relation represents the equivalence between two different mathematical operations performed on different objects. The \(A\) on the LHS is a function of only time for a fixed fluid element \(\mathcal{V}\), while the \(A\) on the RHS is a function of position and time and is not specific to any single fluid element.






TipExample



Consider a steady temperature field \(T (\mathbf{x}) = T_0 + \alpha x\), where \(T_0\) and \(\alpha\) are constants, in a fluid moving with uniform velocity \(\mathbf{v} = v_0 \hat{\mathbf{x}}\). At any fixed point, the temperature does not change: \(\partial_t T = 0\). However, each fluid element moves towards regions with higher temperature (if \(\alpha v_0 > 0\)), so its temperature increases at the rate \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} T}{\mathrm{d} t} = \partial_t T + \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla T = \alpha v_0 .
\tag{5.13}\]

title: 5  Eulerian and Lagrangian Descriptions
text:
5.3 Eulerian formulation of fluid mechanics
The Eulerian equations can be obtained from the Lagrangian equations by replacing all advective derivatives: \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} & \rightarrow \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} +
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \rho, \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} & \rightarrow \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot
\nabla) \mathbf{v}, \\
\frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} & \rightarrow \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial t} +
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \varepsilon .
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.14}\]
The continuity equation (Equation 1.15) becomes \[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \rho + \rho
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= 0.
\tag{5.15}\] In Cartesian coordinates, we can expand all derivatives as \[
\begin{aligned}
& (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \rho + \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} \\
& \quad = v_x
\partial_x \rho + v_y \partial_y \rho + v_z \partial_z \rho \\
& \qquad\qquad + \rho
\partial_x v_x + \rho \partial_y v_y + \rho \partial_z v_z  \\
& \quad = \partial_x (\rho v_x) + \partial_y  (\rho v_y) + \partial_z  (\rho
v_z) \\
& \quad = \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.16}\] So the continuity equation can be written as \[
\boxed{\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v})
= 0.}
\tag{5.17}\]
The velocity equation (Equation 4.12) can be written as \[
\boxed{\rho \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + \rho (\mathbf{v}
\cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}= - \nabla p + \mathbf{f}.}
\tag{5.18}\] The term \((\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}\) is the acceleration of a fluid element due to the fact that it moves to places where the velocity is different. For this reason, fluid elements can accelerate even in a steady flow, in which \(\partial_t \mathbf{v} = 0\). The spherical accretion flow of the next section is an example.
In the same way, the energy equation (Equation 2.39) becomes \[
\rho \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial t} + \rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \varepsilon = \rho \dot{q} - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} .
\tag{5.19}\] We will write these equations in conservative form in Chapter 6.

title: 5  Eulerian and Lagrangian Descriptions
text:
5.4 Pressureless spherical accretion
We are now ready to solve the problem of the spherical accretion of a pressureless fluid that we have attempted to solve at the beginning of this chapter. Because the Eulerian equations deal with quantities as a function of position and time, all time derivatives vanish for a steady flow and we find: \[
\partial_r  (r^2 \rho v) = 0, \qquad v \partial_r v = - \frac{GM}{r^2} .
\tag{5.20}\] The second equation can be written as \[
\frac{1}{2} \partial_r  (v^2 ) = - \frac{GM}{r^2},
\tag{5.21}\] which can be integrated to give, for an infalling flow that is at rest at large distances, \[
v (r) = - \sqrt{\frac{2 GM}{r}} .
\tag{5.22}\] The continuity equation shows that \[
r^2 \rho v = \mathrm{const} .
\tag{5.23}\] Apart from a \(4 \pi\) factor, this is the accretion rate, because the inflow of mass across a surface of radius \(r\) is (assuming spherical symmetry): \[
\dot{M} = - \oint r^2 \rho v \mathrm{d} \Omega = - 4 \pi r^2 \rho v.
\tag{5.24}\] So \[
\rho (r) = - \frac{\dot{M}}{4 \pi r^2 v} = \frac{\dot{M}}{4 \pi \sqrt{2 GM}
r^{3 / 2}} .
\tag{5.25}\] We can now solve for \(M\) using Equation 5.22 and for \(\dot{M}\) using Equation 5.25. Evaluating them at \(r_0\), where \(\rho = \rho_0\) and \(v = v_0\), we find \[
M = \frac{r_0 v_0^2}{2 G}, \qquad \dot{M} = 4 \pi r_0^2 \rho_0 | v_0 |,
\tag{5.26}\] which answers the question we asked at the beginning of the chapter.

What is the rate of change of the temperature, \(\partial_t T\), at a fixed point?

title: 5  Eulerian and Lagrangian Descriptions
text:
5.6 Exercises

Exercise 5.1 (Eulerian and Lagrangian frames) A fluid moves so that, at time \(t\), the position \(\mathbf{x}= (x_1, x_2, x_3)\) of a fluid element initially located at \(\mathbf{q}= (q_1, q_2, q_3)\) is \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
x_1 &{}={} && \frac{1}{2}  (q_1 + q_2) \mathrm{e}^t + \frac{1}{2}  (q_1 - q_2) \mathrm{e}^{- t},
\\
x_2 &{}={} && \frac{1}{2}  (q_1 + q_2) \mathrm{e}^t - \frac{1}{2}  (q_1 - q_2) \mathrm{e}^{- t}, \\
x_3 &{}={} && q_3 .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{5.27}\]

Find the initial position \((q_1, q_2, q_3)\) of a fluid element currently at \((x_1, x_2, x_3)\). [You need to invert Equation 5.27 to find \(\mathbf{q}= \mathbf{q} (t, \mathbf{x})\).]
Compute the velocity \(\dot{\mathbf{x}} (t ; \mathbf{q})\) and acceleration \(\ddot{\mathbf{x}} (t ; \mathbf{q})\) of the fluid elements.
Find the Eulerian velocity \(\mathbf{v} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \dot{\mathbf{x}} [t ; \mathbf{q} (t, \mathbf{x})]\) and acceleration \(\mathbf{a} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \ddot{\mathbf{x}} [t ; \mathbf{q} (t, \mathbf{x})]\).
Verify that \(\mathbf{a}= \partial_t \mathbf{v}+ (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}\).
Is the flow incompressible? Sketch the streamlines.

title: 6  Conservation Laws
text:
6.1 Momentum equation in conservation form
In this chapter, we wish to reformulate the hydrodynamics equations in a way that makes conservation of momentum and energy manifest. These equations will also be useful later on, when we discuss shock waves (Chapter 11). We start with the equation for the momentum.
The starting point is the velocity equation (Equation 4.13), which reads \[
\rho \left[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot
\nabla) \mathbf{v} \right] = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{T}+ \rho \mathbf{g}.
\tag{6.1}\] We can bring \(\rho\) inside the time derivative at the price of including new terms to the equation: \[
\rho \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + \rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla)
\mathbf{v} = \frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} -\mathbf{v}
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v} .
\tag{6.2}\] Using the continuity equation (Equation 5.17) we find \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + \rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla)
\mathbf{v} &= \frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} +\mathbf{v}
\nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}) \\
&\qquad + \rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.3}\] Let’s write down explicitly the last two terms in Cartesian coordinates: \[
\begin{aligned}
& \mathbf{v} \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}) + \rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla)
\mathbf{v} \\
& \quad = \mathbf{v} [\partial_x  (\rho v_x) + \partial_y  (\rho v_y)
+ \partial_z  (\rho v_z)] \\
& \qquad\qquad + \rho v_x \partial_x \mathbf{v}+ \rho v_y \partial_y \mathbf{v}+
\rho v_z \partial_z \mathbf{v} \\
& \quad = \partial_x  (\rho v_x \mathbf{v}) + \partial_y  (\rho v_y \mathbf{v})
+ \partial_z  (\rho v_z \mathbf{v})  \\
& \quad = \nabla \cdot [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}],
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.4}\] where we have recognized the second to last line as being the divergence of the tensor \[
\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v} := \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
v_x v_x & v_x v_y & v_x v_z\\
v_y v_x & v_y v_y & v_y v_z\\
v_z v_x & v_z v_y & v_z v_z
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{6.5}\] Putting everything together we can write the momentum equation \[
\frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [\rho
\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}-\mathbf{T}] = \rho \mathbf{g}.
\tag{6.6}\] In the special case in which \(\mathbf{T}= - p\mathbf{I}\) we obtain \[
\boxed{\frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot
[\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{I}] = \rho \mathbf{g}.}
\tag{6.7}\] The meaning of this equation is more clear if we integrate over some fixed region \(\Omega\) (not moving with the flow): \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \int_{\Omega} \rho \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V +
\int_{\Omega} \nabla \cdot [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{I}]
\mathrm{d} V = \int_{\Omega} \rho \mathbf{g} \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{6.8}\] Moving the second term to the RHS and using the divergence theorem, we find \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \int_{\Omega} \rho \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V = -
\int_{\partial \Omega} [\rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}) \mathbf{v}+
p\mathbf{n}] \mathrm{d} A + \int_{\Omega} \rho \mathbf{g} \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{6.9}\] where \(\partial \Omega\) is the surface bounding \(\Omega\) and \(\mathbf{n}\) its outward directed normal.
In words, Equation 6.9 states that the total momentum in some region changes due to the action of volumetric forces and because of the flux of momentum across the boundary. For example, if we take \(\Omega\) to be the region with \(x > 0\) and neglect gravity, then \(\partial \Omega\) is the \(y z\)-plane. If we also assume that this region is isolated, so that no momentum flows in or out through the surface at infinity, then Equation 6.9 becomes: \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t}  \int_{x > 0} \rho \left(\begin{array}{c}
v_x\\
v_y\\
v_z
\end{array}\right) \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} y \mathrm{d} z \\
& \quad = \int_{x = 0} \biggl[ \rho v_x
\left(\begin{array}{c}
v_x\\
v_y\\
v_z
\end{array}\right) + p \left(\begin{array}{c}
1\\
0\\
0
\end{array}\right) \biggr] \mathrm{d} y \mathrm{d} z.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.10}\] Note that the pressure across the \(x = 0\) surface only influences the \(x\)-component of the momentum.
The last equation also gives an alternative interpretation of pressure. We see that in the RHS the pressure has the same effect as the term \(\rho v_x v_x\). This term describes the flow of momentum through the \(y z\)-plane and is also called the ram pressure. This suggests that we can think of pressure not only as force per unit area, but also as a flux of momentum per unit area. This is the same interpretation that we found in Chapter 2, when we derived the pressure as the flux of momentum due to the random motion of the particles (Equation 2.4).

title: 6  Conservation Laws
text: Figure 6.1: Diagram illustrating the balance of momentum in \(\Omega\).

title: 6  Conservation Laws
text:
6.2 Energy equation
The energy equation (Equation 2.39) reads \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} = \rho \dot{q} - p \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{v}.
\tag{6.11}\] We can expand the advective derivative in Equation 6.11 to obtain the energy equation in the Eulerian frame (Equation 5.19): \[
\rho \frac{\partial \varepsilon}{\partial t} + \rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot
\nabla) \varepsilon = \rho \dot{q} - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\tag{6.12}\] Using a similar approach to what we have done before with the momentum equation, we bring the density into the time derivative to find \[
\frac{\partial (\rho \varepsilon)}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho
\varepsilon \mathbf{v}) = \rho \dot{q} - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\tag{6.13}\] The form of this equation is similar to that of the Eulerian continuity equation and to the momentum equation above. They are all examples of balance laws: equations describing the conservation of some quantity. A balance law reads: \[
\frac{\partial U}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}= S,
\tag{6.14}\] where \(U\), \(\mathbf{F}\), and \(S\) are called the conserved quantities, the fluxes, and the sources of the balance law, respectively. If \(S = 0\), then Equation 6.14 is said to be a conservation law. The name balance law is more clear if we convert the equation to integral form by integrating it over a fixed volume \(\Omega\): \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \int_{\Omega} U \mathrm{d} V + \int_{\Omega} \nabla
\cdot \mathbf{F} \mathrm{d} V = \int_{\Omega} S \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{6.15}\] Using the divergence theorem, we obtain \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \int_{\Omega} U \mathrm{d} V = \int_{\Omega} S \mathrm{d} V
- \int_{\partial \Omega} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} A.
\tag{6.16}\] This equation signifies that the total amount of a quantity \(U\) in the volume \(\Omega\) changes by the amount of \(U\) that flows in/out through the boundary \(\partial \Omega\), plus the amount of \(U\) created/destroyed by the source/sink term \(S\) (see Figure 6.2). Equations in the form of Equation 6.14 are also said to be in conservation form.






Figure 6.2: Graphical illustration of a balance law.



At this point, one might ask in what sense Equation 6.13 describes the conservation of the energy in the fluid. First, this equation does not contain any terms describing the work done on the system by external forces. Second, \(\varepsilon\) is only part of the energy in the flow: we are not including kinetic and potential energy. The issue is that Equation 6.13 only describes the evolution of the internal energy. Mechanical work done by gravity, or other forces, can only directly affect the mechanical energy of the fluid (its kinetic energy). The conversion between internal and kinetic energy is operated by the pdV term. We postpone for the moment the issue of the gravitational energy of the system (Chapter 7), which will turn out to be more complex than expected, to focus on the interplay between kinetic and internal energy.
To derive an equation for the kinetic energy, we start from the Euler equation \[
\rho \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + \rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla)
\mathbf{v}= - \nabla p +\mathbf{f}.
\tag{6.17}\] We multiply this equation by \(\mathbf{v}\) to find \[
\frac{1}{2} \rho \left[ \frac{\partial v^2}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot
\nabla) v^2 \right] = - \nabla p \cdot \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{f} \cdot
\mathbf{v}.
\tag{6.18}\] Once again, we can use the continuity equation to bring \(\rho\) inside the time derivative to find \[
\frac{\partial \left( \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 \right)}{\partial t} + \nabla
\cdot \left( \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 \mathbf{v} \right) = - \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla
p+\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\tag{6.19}\] Using the identity \[
\nabla \cdot (p\mathbf{v}) =\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla p + p \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{v},
\tag{6.20}\] we can rewrite this equation as \[
\frac{\partial \left( \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2 \right)}{\partial t} + \nabla
\cdot \left[ \left( \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right) \mathbf{v} \right] = p
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v} .
\tag{6.21}\] This is the wanted equation for the kinetic energy. We notice two things. First, this equation shows that pressure can be interpreted also as an energy density. Second, this equation has the same pdV term as the internal energy equation, but with opposite sign! This is the term describing the conversion of internal energy into kinetic energy and vice versa. Also note that the work done by external forces appears in the kinetic energy equation, but heating and cooling terms do not.
Adding Equation 6.19 to Equation 6.13 gives the equation describing conservation of the total energy (internal + kinetic): \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial \left[ \rho \left( \frac{1}{2} v^2 + \varepsilon
\right) \right]}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left[ \left(
\tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + \rho \varepsilon + p \right) \mathbf{v}
\right] \\
&\qquad = \rho \dot{q} +\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{6.22}\] This shows that the total energy in the fluid is conserved in absence of external forces and heating/cooling. If \(\mathbf{f}\) is a conservative force, it is possible to rewrite the energy equation in a way that is manifestly conservative by including the potential inside the time derivative. For example, consider gravity, \(\mathbf{f} = - \rho \nabla \Psi\), and assume that the potential \(\Psi\) does not depend on time, as is the case for an external, static potential. Then, using the continuity equation, \[
\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v} = - \rho \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla \Psi = - \nabla \cdot (\rho \Psi \mathbf{v}) + \Psi \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}) = - \nabla \cdot (\rho \Psi \mathbf{v}) - \frac{\partial (\rho \Psi)}{\partial t},
\tag{6.23}\] so that Equation 6.22 becomes \[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial \left[ \rho \left( \frac{1}{2} v^2 + \varepsilon + \Psi
\right) \right]}{\partial t} \\
&\qquad + \nabla \cdot \left[ \left(
\tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + \rho \varepsilon + p + \rho \Psi \right) \mathbf{v}
\right] = \rho \dot{q} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.24}\] If the gas is self-gravitating, instead, \(\Psi\) depends on time through the density, and this simple manipulation does not work. We will come back to this in Chapter 7.
We can now summarize the equations of hydrodynamics in conservation form (Equation 6.14). In the absence of heating and cooling, and with a body force \(\mathbf{f}\), we have:



Table 6.1: The equations of hydrodynamics in conservation form.

We will use these equations in Chapter 11 to derive the jump conditions across shock waves.

title: 6  Conservation Laws
text:
6.3 Heat conduction
Heat conduction can be included in Equation 6.22 by adding a heat flux \(\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}}\): \[
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{\partial \left[ \rho \left( \frac{1}{2} v^2 + \varepsilon \right)
\right]}{\partial t} \\
&\qquad + \nabla \cdot \left[ \left( \tfrac{1}{2} \rho
v^2 + \rho \varepsilon + p \right) \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}} \right] \\
&\qquad = \rho \dot{q} +\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.25}\] In many astrophysical applications, energy is transported mostly by photons, and the heat flux can be approximated as \[
\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}}= - \frac{c}{3 \rho \kappa_R} \nabla (aT^4),
\tag{6.26}\] where \(c\) is the speed of light, \(a\) the radiation constant (Equation 2.33), and \(\kappa_R\) is the so-called Rosseland mean opacity. The term in parentheses is an energy density. Indeed, it is the energy density of radiation for a black body (Equation 2.32): \[
u_{\mathrm{rad}} = aT^4 .
\tag{6.27}\] The opacity has units of \(\mathrm{m}^2 \, \mathrm{kg}^{- 1}\) (we quote it in \(\mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}\), as is customary), so \(\lambda = 1 / (\rho \kappa_R)\) has units of a length. Indeed, \(\lambda\) is the photon mean free path. Combining these two facts, we can write Equation 6.26 as \[
\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}}= - \frac{1}{3} \lambda c \nabla u_{\mathrm{rad}} = -\mathcal{D} \nabla
u_{\mathrm{rad}}, \qquad \mathcal{D} = \frac{\lambda c}{3} .
\tag{6.28}\] This is a special case of Fick’s law of diffusion: \[
\textbf{diffusive flux} = -\mathcal{D} \nabla \left(
\text{density of quantity being diffused} \right) .
\tag{6.29}\] The diffusion coefficient has units of \[
[\mathcal{D}] = \mathrm{m}^2 \cdot \mathrm{s}^{- 1} .
\tag{6.30}\] The time needed to diffuse over a distance \(R\) is \(\sim R^2 / \mathcal{D}\), which is the diffusion time we found in Equation 3.17 with the random-walk argument (up to a factor of 3).
If energy due to radiation was advected with velocity \(\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}}\), then \[
\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{heat}}= u_{\mathrm{rad}} \mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}} .
\tag{6.31}\] Comparing this to Equation 6.28 suggests that \[
v_{\mathrm{eff}} \sim \left( \frac{\lambda}{3 H} \right) c,
\tag{6.32}\] where \(H\) is the radiation energy density scale-height: \[
H = \frac{u_{\mathrm{rad}}}{| \nabla u_{\mathrm{rad}} |} .
\tag{6.33}\] In the interior of stars \(H \gg \lambda\), so radiation diffuses very slowly: the time it needs to cross the star is much longer than the light-crossing time.






TipExample



Consider the Sun. With an opacity \(\kappa \approx 25\,\mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}} = 2.5\,\mathrm{m^2\,kg^{-1}}\) and the mean density of the Sun, \(\bar{\rho} \approx 1.4\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} = 1.4 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\), the photon mean free path is \(\lambda \approx 3 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}\). Taking \(H \sim R_{\odot}\), Equation 6.32 gives \[
v_{\mathrm{eff}} \sim \frac{3 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}}{3 \times 7 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m}}\, c \approx 4 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},
\tag{6.34}\] or about \(40\,\mu\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). At this speed, energy takes \(R_{\odot} / v_{\mathrm{eff}} \sim 5 \times 10^5\) years to reach the surface from the center, while light would cross the Sun in about \(2\,\mathrm{s}\).


Close to the surface of stars \(H \lesssim \lambda / 3\) and Equation 6.28 predicts that radiant energy propagates faster than the speed of light. This is a symptom that the diffusion approximation breaks down. More generally, the transport of energy by radiation can be described using Equation 6.26 only if photons and matter are in local thermodynamic equilibrium. If the diffusion approximation cannot be used, matter and radiation need to be treated separately using the equations of radiation-hydrodynamics1.

text:
6.5 Exercises

Exercise 6.1 (Angular momentum) The angular momentum of a fluid element of mass \(\mathcal{M}\) is \(\mathcal{M}\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v}\), so the angular momentum density for a fluid is (upon division by \(\mathcal{V}\)): \[
\mathbf{j}= \rho \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v}.
\tag{6.37}\]

Starting from the momentum equation, derive a Lagrangian equation for the evolution of \(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v}\).
Show that, in absence of external forces, \(\mathbf{j}\) satisfies the conservation law \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{j}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [\mathbf{j}
\otimes \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{R}] = 0,
\tag{6.38}\] where \[
\mathbf{R}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
0 & - z & y\\
z & 0 & - x\\
- y & x & 0
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{6.39}\] [Hint. Write out explicitly the expression \(\mathbf{r} \times \nabla p\).]
Consider a fluid that is subject to an external force per unit volume \(\mathbf{f}\). How does \[
\mathbf{J}= \int \mathbf{j} \mathrm{d} V
\tag{6.40}\] evolve with time?
Show that, for an isolated fluid in an axisymmetric potential \(\Psi (R, z)\), the \(z\)-component of \(\mathbf{J}\) is conserved.

title: 7  The Gravitational Potential
text:
7.1 The gravitational potential
According to Newtonian mechanics, the gravitational acceleration can be written as the gradient of the gravitational potential \(\Psi\): \[
\mathbf{g} = - \nabla \Psi .
\tag{7.1}\] The potential can be interpreted as encoding the work needed to carry a particle of mass \(m\) from the position \(\mathbf{r}\) to infinity: \[
\begin{aligned}
W_{\mathrm{ext}} &= - m \int_{\mathbf{r}}^{\infty} \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\ell} = m \int_{\mathbf{r}}^{\infty} \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\ell} \\
&= m [\Psi (\infty) - \Psi (\mathbf{r})] .
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.2}\] Note that the potential is unique only up to an additive constant, typically chosen so that \(\Psi(\infty) = 0\). In this case, \(W_{\mathrm{ext}} = -m \Psi(\mathbf{r})\).

title: 7  The Gravitational Potential
text:
TipExample



The potential of a point mass \(M\) is \[
\Psi = - \frac{GM}{r} .
\tag{7.3}\] Its gradient is \[
\nabla \Psi = \frac{GM}{r^2} \nabla r = \frac{GM}{r^3} \mathbf{r} = \frac{GM}{r^2} \hat{\mathbf{r}} = - \mathbf{g},
\tag{7.4}\] where we have used \[
\begin{aligned}
& r = (x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{1 / 2} \\
& \quad \Longrightarrow \frac{\partial r}{\partial x} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{2 x}{(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{1 / 2}} = \frac{x}{r} \\
& \quad \Longrightarrow \nabla r = \frac{1}{r} (x, y, z) = \frac{\mathbf{r}}{r} = \hat{\mathbf{r}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.5}\]








TipExample



The gravitational potential generated by \(N\) point particles with masses \(m_i\) at positions \(\mathbf{r}_i\) is \[
\begin{aligned}
& \Psi = - \sum_{i = 1}^N \frac{G m_i}{| \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_i |} \\
& \quad \Longrightarrow \mathbf{g} = - \sum_{i = 1}^N \frac{G m_i}{| \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_i |^3} (\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_i) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.6}\]

title: 7  The Gravitational Potential
text:
7.2 Poisson equation
The gravitational potential is related to the mass density by the Poisson equation: \[
\boxed{\nabla^2 \Psi = 4 \pi G \rho .}
\tag{7.7}\] See Clarke and Carswell (2007) for a derivation, or Griffiths (2023, secs. 2.2–2.3) for the derivation of the analogous equation for the electrostatic potential.

7.2.1 Gauss theorem
Consider a region \(\Omega\) with boundary \(\partial \Omega\). Integrating Equation 7.7 over \(\Omega\) we find \[
\int_{\Omega} \nabla^2 \Psi \mathrm{d} V = 4 \pi G \int_{\Omega} \rho \mathrm{d} V = 4 \pi G M,
\tag{7.8}\] where \(M\) is the mass contained in \(\Omega\). Using the divergence theorem, \[
\int_{\Omega} \nabla \cdot [\nabla \Psi] \mathrm{d} V = \oint_{\partial \Omega} \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} = 4 \pi G M,
\tag{7.9}\] so that \[
\boxed{- \oint_{\partial \Omega} \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} = 4 \pi G M .}
\tag{7.10}\] Note that the flux of \(\mathbf{g}\) through \(\partial \Omega\) depends only on the mass enclosed in \(\Omega\). This result is Gauss theorem for gravitation and is analogous to the Gauss law for electrostatics. As you may already know from electrostatics, the Gauss theorem is very useful to find the gravitational field for mass distributions that are symmetric.






TipExample



Consider a spherically symmetric mass distribution and take \(\partial \Omega\) to be a sphere of radius \(r\). By symmetry, \(\mathbf{g} = - g \hat{\mathbf{r}}\), so \[
- \oint_{\partial \Omega} \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} = 4 \pi r^2 g \Longrightarrow g = \frac{G M (r)}{r^2},
\tag{7.11}\] where \(M (r)\) is the enclosed mass.




7.2.2 Spherically symmetric bodies
For a spherically symmetric body, we can integrate the Poisson equation with the boundary condition \(\Psi (\infty) = 0\): \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{1}{r^2} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \left( r^2 \frac{\partial \Psi}{\partial r} \right) = 4 \pi G \rho \\
& \quad \Longrightarrow \int_0^r \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( x^2 \frac{\partial \Psi}{\partial x} \right) \mathrm{d} x = \int_0^r 4 \pi G \rho x^2 \mathrm{d} x,
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.12}\] which gives \[
r^2 \frac{\partial \Psi}{\partial r} = G M (r) .
\tag{7.13}\] Integrating again, from \(r\) to infinity, and using \(\Psi (\infty) = 0\), we obtain \[
\Psi (r) = - \int_r^{\infty} \frac{G M (x)}{x^2} \mathrm{d} x \neq - \frac{G M (r)}{r} .
\tag{7.14}\] In words, it is not true that the potential depends only on the enclosed mass, when we are inside of a body. Of course, if \(r \geq R\), then \(M (x) = M = \mathrm{const}\) for all \(x > r\) and we recover the same potential as for a point particle \[
\Psi (r) = - \int_r^{\infty} \frac{G M}{x^2} \mathrm{d} x = \frac{G M}{x} \bigg|_r^{\infty} = - \frac{G M}{r} .
\tag{7.15}\] The fact that the potential at radius \(r\) depends on the mass at radii \(x > r\) is often a source of confusion, because it appears to be contradicting Gauss theorem, which states that the flux of the gravitational acceleration through a closed surface depends only on the enclosed mass. However, there is no contradiction, because gravitational acceleration and potential measure different things. The potential is related to the amount of work needed to carry a parcel of matter to infinity, so it necessarily depends on the mass distribution everywhere. This distinction is particularly important when computing the gravitational binding energy.

title: 7  The Gravitational Potential
text:
7.3 Gravitational binding energy
The gravitational energy of a fluid element of mass \(\rho \mathrm{d} V\), that is, minus the work required to bring this fluid element to infinity, is \([\Psi (\mathbf{r}) - \Psi (\infty)] \rho \mathrm{d} V = \Psi (\mathbf{r}) \rho \mathrm{d} V\). As such, the gravitational energy of a mass of fluid in a potential well with prescribed potential \(\Psi_{\mathrm{ext}}\), that is, minus the work necessary to transport it to infinity, is \[
W = \int \rho \Psi_{\mathrm{ext}} \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{7.16}\] However, in the case in which the potential is generated by the fluid itself, that is if the fluid is self-gravitating, the gravitational energy \(W\) has an additional factor \(1 / 2\): \[
W = \frac{1}{2} \int \rho \Psi \mathrm{d} V .
\tag{7.17}\] The origin of the factor \(1 / 2\) is explained by the following example.






TipExample



Consider two point particles of mass \(m\), \(A\) at \(x = a\) and \(B\) at \(x = - a\). The potential is \[
\Psi = - \frac{G m}{| \mathbf{r} - a \hat{\mathbf{x}} |} - \frac{G m}{| \mathbf{r} + a \hat{\mathbf{x}} |} .
\tag{7.18}\] The work done to carry \(A\) to infinity along the \(x\)-axis, in the field of \(B\), is \[
\begin{aligned}
W_{\mathrm{ext}, A} &= - m \int_{\mathbf{r}_A}^{\infty} \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\ell} = \int_a^{\infty} \frac{G m^2}{| x + a |^2} \mathrm{d} x \\
&= \frac{G m^2}{2 a} = - m \Psi_B (\mathbf{r}_A),
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.19}\] where \(\Psi_B\) is the potential generated by \(B\). Similarly, \(W_{\mathrm{ext}, B} = - m \Psi_A (\mathbf{r}_B)\).
What is the total work needed to unbind the system? Once \(A\) has been carried to infinity, \(B\) is free, so the work needed is only \(W_{\mathrm{ext}, A} = (W_{\mathrm{ext}, A} + W_{\mathrm{ext}, B}) / 2\). The gravitational energy of the system is then \[
W = - W_{\mathrm{ext}, A} = - \frac{1}{2} (W_{\mathrm{ext}, A} + W_{\mathrm{ext}, B}) = - \frac{G m^2}{2 a} .
\tag{7.20}\]


Generalizing the previous example to a system of \(N\) particles with masses \(\{ m_j \}\), we have \[
W = - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i \neq j} \frac{G m_i m_j}{| \mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j |}
= - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i \neq j} \underbrace{\rho_i \mathrm{d} V_i}_{\rho \mathrm{d} V} \underbrace{\frac{G m_j}{| \mathbf{r}_i - \mathbf{r}_j |}}_{- \Psi} .
\tag{7.21}\] In the continuum limit, the masses \(m_j\) are replaced by a mass density \(\rho\) and the summation becomes an integral: \[
\boxed{W = \frac{1}{2} \int_V \rho (\mathbf{r}) \Psi (\mathbf{r}) \mathrm{d} V .}
\tag{7.22}\]






TipExample



Consider a sphere of mass \(M\), radius \(R\), and constant density \(\rho\). What is the value of the gravitational potential \(\Psi\)?
From Equation 7.14, for \(r \geq R\) \[
\Psi (r) = - \int_r^{\infty} \frac{G M (x)}{x^2} \mathrm{d} x = - \frac{G M}{r},
\tag{7.23}\] while for \(r < R\) \[
\Psi (r) = - \int_r^R \frac{G M (x)}{x^2} \mathrm{d} x - \int_R^{\infty} \frac{G M}{x^2} \mathrm{d} x .
\tag{7.24}\] The last integral is equal to \(G M / R\). Inside the sphere \(M (x) = \frac{4}{3} \pi \rho x^3\), so \[
- \int_r^R \frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho x \mathrm{d} x = - \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho x^2 \right]_r^R = \frac{G M (r)}{2 r} - \frac{G M}{2 R} .
\tag{7.25}\] So, for \(r < R\), \[
\boxed{\Psi (r) = - \frac{3 G M}{2 R} + \frac{G M (r)}{2 r} .}
\tag{7.26}\] This potential is shown in Figure 7.1.






Figure 7.1: Gravitational potential of a sphere with constant density.



The gravitational energy is \[
\begin{aligned}
W &= 2 \pi \int_0^R \rho (r) \Psi (r) r^2 \mathrm{d} r \\
&= 2 \pi \int_0^R \left[ - \frac{3 G M}{2 R} \rho r^2 + \frac{1}{2} \frac{4}{3} \pi G \rho^2 r^4 \right] \mathrm{d} r \\
&= - \frac{G M}{R} \pi \rho R^3 + \frac{1}{10} (2 \pi) \left( \frac{4}{3} \pi \right) G \rho^2 R^5 \\
&= - \frac{3}{4} \frac{G M^2}{R} + \frac{3}{20} \left( \frac{4 \pi}{3} \rho R^3 \right)^2 \frac{G}{R} \\
&= \frac{G M^2}{R} \left[ - \frac{3}{4} + \frac{3}{20} \right] = - \frac{G M^2}{R} \left[ \frac{15 - 3}{20} \right] \\
&= - \frac{G M^2}{R} \frac{3 \cdot 4}{5 \cdot 4} = - \frac{3 G M^2}{5 R},
\end{aligned}
\tag{7.27}\] where we have used \(2 \pi = \frac{4}{3} \pi \cdot \frac{3}{2}\). We would have gotten the wrong result without the factor \(1 / 2\)!

7.5 Exercises

Exercise 7.1 (Homologous collapse and the Friedmann equation) A homogeneous gas sphere is collapsing under its self-gravity. Assume the velocity to be given by \[
\mathbf{v} (t, \mathbf{r}) = H (t) \mathbf{r},
\tag{7.29}\] where \(\mathbf{r}\) is the displacement of the fluid element from the center of the cloud.

Argue that the density remains constant throughout the sphere (although it is changing with time) and show that the momentum equation implies \[
\dot{H} (t) + H (t)^2 = - \frac{4 \pi G \rho (t)}{3} .
\tag{7.30}\] Assume the gas to be described by a barotropic EOS \(p = p (\rho)\).
Introduce the scale factor \(a (t)\) defined so that \[
\frac{\dot{a} (t)}{a (t)} = H (t) .
\tag{7.31}\] Show that \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \left( H^2 a^2 - \frac{8 \pi}{3} G \rho a^2
\right) = 2 Ha^2  \left( \dot{H} + H^2 + \frac{4 \pi G}{3} \rho \right)
= 0
\tag{7.32}\] and show that this implies that the dynamics is described by Friedmann equation \[
\dot{a} (t)^2 - \frac{8 \pi G \rho (t)}{3} a (t)^2 = - k,
\tag{7.33}\] where \(k\) is a constant of motion.
Show that \(\rho (t) \propto a (t)^{- 3}\) using the continuity equation. Use this to cast the Friedmann equation into the equation of a particle rolling down an effective potential \[
\frac{1}{2}  \dot{a} (t)^2 + U_{\mathrm{eff}} (a) =\mathcal{E}.
\tag{7.34}\] Sketch a graph for \(\rho (t)\) and \(a (t)\) as a function of time.

the initial acceleration of the particle, and
the time the particle takes to fall to the centre.

The two cases are:

the body is a point mass;
the body is a uniform sphere of radius \(R_0\).

title: 8  Hydrostatic Equilibrium and the Virial Theorem
text:
8.1 The virial theorem
We consider a self-gravitating cloud of gas in equilibrium, described by the momentum equation in conservation form (Equation 6.7) \[
\frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [\rho
\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{I}] = - \rho \nabla \Psi,
\tag{8.1}\] where \(\Psi\) is the gravitational potential. We consider the scalar moment of inertia \[
I = \frac{1}{2} \int_V \rho (\mathbf{r}) r^2 \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{8.2}\] where \(V\) is a volume that encloses the whole gas cloud. The time derivative of \(I\) is (using the continuity equation) \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\frac{\mathrm{d} I}{\mathrm{d} t} &{}={} && \frac{1}{2}  \int_V \frac{\partial
\rho}{\partial t} r^2 \mathrm{d} V \\
&{}={} && - \frac{1}{2} \int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho
\mathbf{v}) r^2 \mathrm{d} V \\
&{}={} && - \frac{1}{2} \int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}r^2) \mathrm{d} V \\
&&& + \frac{1}{2}  \int_V \rho \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla r^2 \mathrm{d} V.
\end{alignedat}
\tag{8.3}\] The total divergence term is equal to a boundary integral \[
\int_V \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}r^2) \mathrm{d} V = \int_{\partial V} \rho
\mathbf{v}r^2 \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} A,
\tag{8.4}\] but the latter vanishes since, by assumption, \(\rho \rightarrow 0\) at the boundary of \(V\). So we find \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} I}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{1}{2}  \int_V \rho \mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla
r^2 \mathrm{d} V = \int_V \rho \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{8.5}\] Here, we have used the fact that \(\nabla r =\mathbf{r}/ r\).
The second time derivative of \(I\) is \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 I}{\mathrm{d} t^2} &= \int_V \frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V \\
&\qquad - \int_V \nabla \cdot [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{I}] \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V \\
&\qquad - \int_V \nabla \cdot [\rho (\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{r}) \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{r}] \mathrm{d} V \\
&\qquad + \int_V [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{I}] : \nabla \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V,
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.6}\] where the notation \(\mathbf{A}: \mathbf{B}\) denotes the inner product between two tensors: \[
\mathbf{A}: \mathbf{B}= \sum_{i = 1}^3 \sum_{k = 1}^3 A_{i k} B_{k i} =
\mathrm{Trace} \left[ \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
A_{x x} & A_{x y} & A_{x z}\\
A_{y x} & A_{y y} & A_{y z}\\
A_{z x} & A_{z y} & A_{z z}
\end{array}\right)  \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
B_{x x} & B_{x y} & B_{x z}\\
B_{y x} & B_{y y} & B_{y z}\\
B_{z x} & B_{z y} & B_{z z}
\end{array}\right) \right] .
\tag{8.7}\] Once again, we can drop the total divergence terms, since, by the divergence theorem, they are equal to boundary integrals that vanish because \(\rho\) and \(p\) vanish at the boundary of \(V\). We find \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 I}{\mathrm{d} t^2} = - \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot
\mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V + \int_V [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+
p\mathbf{I}] : \nabla \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{8.8}\] The second term in the RHS is simpler than it looks, because \[
\nabla \mathbf{r}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\partial_x x & \partial_x y & \partial_x z\\
\partial_y x & \partial_y y & \partial_y z\\
\partial_z x & \partial_z y & \partial_z z
\end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 1 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right) =\mathbf{I}.
\tag{8.9}\] So everything simplifies to \[
\int_V [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ p\mathbf{I}] : \nabla \mathbf{r}
\mathrm{d} V = \int_V \rho v^2 \mathrm{d} V + 3 \int_V p \mathrm{d} V =: 2 K +
3 \Pi,
\tag{8.10}\] where \(K\) is the kinetic energy of the gas and \(\Pi\) is the integrated pressure.
The first term in the RHS of Equation 8.8 requires a little more work. First, we need to compute an expression for the gravitational potential in terms of the mass density \(\rho\). To do this, we remember that the gravitational potential generated by a distribution of point masses with mass \(m_i\) at locations \(\mathbf{r}_i\) is given by \[
\Psi (\mathbf{r}) = - \sum_{i = 1}^N \frac{Gm_i}{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_i
|} .
\tag{8.11}\] This can be generalized to the case of a mass density distribution by converting the sum into an integral \[
\Psi (\mathbf{r}) = - \int_V \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}')}{ |
\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |} \mathrm{d}^3 r' .
\tag{8.12}\] Inserting this into the first term in the RHS of Equation 8.8 yields \[
\int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d}^3 r = - \int_V
\mathrm{d}^3 r \rho (\mathbf{r}) \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \int_V \mathrm{d}^3
r'  \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}')}{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |} \cdot
\mathbf{r},
\tag{8.13}\] where we have used the notation \(\nabla_{\mathbf{r}}\) to remind ourselves that the derivatives are computed with respect to the unprimed position \(\mathbf{r}\). In particular, note that \(\rho (\mathbf{r}')\) in the integral is not affected by the derivative, since it is a function of \(\mathbf{r}'\) and not of \(\mathbf{r}\). The only term that we need to differentiate is the denominator: \[
\begin{aligned}
& \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \frac{1}{| \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |} \\
& \quad = \nabla_{\mathbf{r}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{(x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2 + (z - z')^2}} \\
& \quad = \frac{- 1}{[(x - x')^2 + (y - y')^2 + (z - z')^2]^{3 / 2}} \\
& \qquad\quad \times \left(\begin{array}{c}
x - x' \\
y - y' \\
z - z'
\end{array}\right) \\
& \quad = - \frac{\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'}{| \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.14}\] Inserting the last expression into Equation 8.13, we obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
& \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d}^3 r \\
& \quad = \int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r \int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r' \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}') \rho (\mathbf{r}) }{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}') \cdot \mathbf{r} \\
& \quad = \int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r \int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r' \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}') \rho (\mathbf{r}) }{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^2 \\
& \qquad + \int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r \int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r' \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}') \rho (\mathbf{r}) }{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}') \cdot \mathbf{r}' \\
& \quad = \int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r \int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r' \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}') \rho (\mathbf{r}) }{| \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |} \\
& \qquad + \int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r' \rho (\mathbf{r}') \mathbf{r}' \cdot \int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r \frac{G \rho (\mathbf{r}) (\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}') }{ | \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} \\
& \quad = - \int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r \Psi (\mathbf{r}) \rho (\mathbf{r}) \\
& \qquad - \int_V \rho (\mathbf{r}') \nabla_{\mathbf{r}'} \Psi (\mathbf{r}') \cdot \mathbf{r}' \mathrm{d}^3 r' .
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.15}\] We have used the fact that (note the difference in sign compared to Equation 8.14) \[
\nabla_{\mathbf{r}'}  \frac{1}{| \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |} =
\frac{\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}'}{| \mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}' |^3} .
\tag{8.16}\] The last term on the RHS of Equation 8.15 is identical to the LHS, so we find \[
- \int_V \rho \nabla \Psi \cdot \mathbf{r} \mathrm{d}^3 r= \frac{1}{2}
\int_V \mathrm{d}^3 r \Psi (\mathbf{r}) \rho (\mathbf{r}) = W,
\tag{8.17}\] \(W\) being the gravitational potential energy.
For a stationary configuration \(\mathrm{d}^2 I / \mathrm{d} t^2 = 0\), so Equation 8.8 yields the virial theorem: \[
\boxed{W + 2 K + 3 \Pi = 0.}
\tag{8.18}\] For an ideal gas \(p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon\) (Equation 2.15), so \[
\Pi = \int_V p \mathrm{d} V = (\Gamma - 1) \int_V \rho \varepsilon \mathrm{d} V =
(\Gamma - 1) U,
\tag{8.19}\] where \(U\) is the total internal energy. In this case, the virial theorem reads \[
\boxed{W + 2 K + 3 (\Gamma - 1) U = 0.}
\tag{8.20}\]

title: 8  Hydrostatic Equilibrium and the Virial Theorem
text:
8.2 Hydrostatic equilibria
A fluid is in hydrostatic equilibrium when \(\mathbf{v} = 0\), so that Euler’s equation reduces to \(\nabla p = - \rho \nabla \Psi\). For a spherical star, this reads \(\mathrm{d} p / \mathrm{d} r = - G M (r) \rho / r^2\), where \(M (r)\) is the mass enclosed within the radius \(r\) (see also Equation 4.21).
The virial theorem has an important consequence for the stability of hydrostatic equilibria. Consider a cloud of gas or star in hydrostatic equilibrium, that is with no large scale motion (no rotation). Then the virial theorem states that \[
W + 3 (\Gamma - 1) U = 0.
\tag{8.21}\] On the other hand, the energy of the cloud is \[
E = W + U.
\tag{8.22}\] The energy must be negative for the system to be bound, \(E \leq 0\). This implies \[
U \leq - W = 3 (\Gamma - 1) U \Longrightarrow [- 1 + 3 (\Gamma -
1)] U \geq 0,
\tag{8.23}\] since \(U \geq 0\), this requires \[
\Gamma \geq 4 / 3.
\tag{8.24}\] Monoatomic gas has \(\Gamma = 5 / 3\), so regular stars are stable. Matter dominated by relativistic particles, such as radiation or the relativistic degenerate electrons in white dwarfs and in the iron cores of massive stars, has \(\Gamma \approx 4 / 3\). Stars made of such matter are only marginally stable, and small effects that reduce \(\Gamma\) below \(4/3\) can make them collapse. This happens in the iron cores of massive stars, where electron captures reduce the pressure, triggering core-collapse supernovae (Chapter 3 and Section 4.3), and in very massive stars, where the production of electron–positron pairs triggers so-called pair-instability supernovae.
A surprising consequence of the virial theorem is that self-gravitating systems have negative specific heat. Consider a self-gravitating cloud (a protostar) emitting infrared radiation. As its energy \(E\) becomes more negative its gravitational binding energy \(- W\) must increase, because \(U \geq 0\). We can use Equation 8.21 and Equation 8.22 to solve for \(U\) in terms of \(E\): \[
U = - \frac{E}{3 \Gamma - 4} .
\tag{8.25}\] If \(\Gamma > 4 / 3\), Equation 8.25 predicts that \(U\) will increase as \(E\) becomes more negative. Meaning that the system heats up as it loses energy! Eventually the cloud contracts to the point that nuclear fusion starts occurring and a star is born. Nuclear burning prevents the star from heating up further.






TipExample



Could the Sun be powered by gravitational contraction alone? In this case, the Sun would radiate its gravitational binding energy, \(| W | \sim G M_{\odot}^2 / R_{\odot}\), over a time \[
t_{\mathrm{KH}} \sim \frac{G M_{\odot}^2}{R_{\odot} L_{\odot}} \approx 3 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{yr},
\tag{8.26}\] where \(L_{\odot} \approx 3.8 \times 10^{26}\,\mathrm{W}\) (\(3.8 \times 10^{33}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}\)) is the luminosity of the Sun. This is the so-called Kelvin–Helmholtz time. It is much shorter than the age of the Earth, about \(4.5 \times 10^9\) years, so the Sun must have another source of energy: nuclear fusion.








TipExample



The hot gas in a galaxy cluster is in approximate virial equilibrium in the gravitational potential of the cluster. Consider a cluster with mass \(M \sim 10^{15}\,M_{\odot}\) and radius \(R \sim 1\,\mathrm{Mpc}\), and assume, for simplicity, that the gas has the same distribution as the total mass. For a uniform sphere \(W = - \frac{3}{5} G M^2 / R\), while \(3 \Pi = 3 M k_B T / (\mu m_u)\), so the virial theorem gives \[
k_B T \sim \frac{G M \mu m_u}{5 R} \approx 5\,\mathrm{keV},
\tag{8.27}\] or \(T \sim 6 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{K}\), where we have taken \(\mu \approx 0.6\) for fully ionized gas. This is why galaxy clusters are bright X-ray sources, as in the case of the Bullet cluster (Figure 1.1).

title: 8  Hydrostatic Equilibrium and the Virial Theorem
text:
8.3 Application to star formation
Consider a spherical cloud of radius \(R\). For simplicity, we take its density \(\bar{\rho}\) to be uniform. Then the gravitational potential energy is \[
- W = G \int_0^R 4 \pi r \rho (r) M (r) \mathrm{d} r = \frac{16 \pi^2}{15} G \bar{\rho}^2 R^5 = \frac{3}{5} \frac{G M^2}{R},
\tag{8.28}\] where \(M = \frac{4 \pi}{3} \bar{\rho} R^3\) is the mass of the cloud and \[
M (r) = \int_0^r 4 \pi r'^2 \rho (r') \mathrm{d} r'
\tag{8.29}\] is the mass enclosed within the radius \(r\). For an ideal gas, the pressure is given by \[
p = \frac{k_B T}{\mu m_u} \rho,
\tag{8.30}\] where \(\mu\) is the mean molecular weight (Equation 1.6), \(m_u\) is the atomic mass unit, \(k_B\) is the Boltzmann constant and \(T\) is the temperature. We can assume \(T\) to be constant. This is a good approximation for optically thin clouds which can efficiently cool by emitting radiation. With this approximation \[
\Pi = \int_0^R 4 \pi r^2 p (r) \mathrm{d} r = \frac{4}{3} \pi c_s^2
\bar{\rho} R^3,
\tag{8.31}\] where \[
c_s^2 = \frac{k_B T}{\mu m_u}
\tag{8.32}\] is a constant. As we will see later, \(c_s\) turns out to be the sound speed of the gas (Chapter 9). The condition for collapse of the cloud is that \(3 \Pi < | W |\), which implies that collapse will occur for a cloud with \[
R > R_J, \qquad R_J^2 = \frac{15 c_s^2}{4 \pi G \bar{\rho}} .
\tag{8.33}\] \(R_J\) is called the Jeans length. Typical molecular clouds have \(R \gg R_J\), so instead of collapsing to an object with mass equal to the mass of the cloud, they fragment into smaller pieces. The mass of these fragments can be estimated as the mass contained within one Jeans length, the so-called Jeans mass1: \[
\begin{aligned}
M_J &= \frac{4 \pi}{3}  \bar{\rho} R_J^3 = \frac{15^{3 / 2} c_s^3}{3 (4 \pi
\bar{\rho})^{1 / 2} G^{3 / 2}} \\
&= \frac{15^{3 / 2} k_B^{3 / 2}}{3 (4 \pi)^{1 / 2} m_u^2
G^{3 / 2}}  \frac{T^{3 / 2}}{\mu^2 n^{1 / 2}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{8.34}\] Inserting the values of the constants, we find \[
M_J \approx 94\,M_{\odot}  \left( \frac{T}{\mathrm{K}} \right)^{3 / 2}
\left( \frac{\mathrm{cm}^{- 3}}{n} \right)^{1 / 2}  \frac{1}{\mu^2} .
\tag{8.35}\] For a typical molecular cloud with \(T = 10\,\mathrm{K}\), \(n = 100\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), and \(\mu = 2\) (for molecular hydrogen) the Jeans length is \(R_J \approx 1.5\,\mathrm{pc}\) and the Jeans mass is \(M_J \approx 70\,M_{\odot}\). This is much larger than the mass of a typical star. Note however that the Jeans mass decreases with increasing \(n\). So, as long as the gas can efficiently cool and remain at low temperature, the fragments collapse and undergo further fragmentation. In the dense cores of molecular clouds, with \(n \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), the Jeans mass is \(M_J \approx 7\,M_{\odot}\), and at even higher densities it approaches the mass of typical stars.
While the arguments we have given here give an order of magnitude estimate for the mass of protostars, star formation is strongly influenced by a number of factors that we have neglected. These include turbulence and magnetic fields. Moreover, star formation strongly depends on the ability of the gas to cool to low temperature, as shown by Equation 8.35.

title: 8  Hydrostatic Equilibrium and the Virial Theorem
text:
8.4 In-class worksheet
For a magnetic star the virial theorem becomes: \[
W + 2 K + 3 \Pi +\mathfrak{M}= 0,
\tag{8.36}\] where the new term is the magnetic energy of the star, which is \[
\mathfrak{M}= \frac{1}{2 \mu_0} \int B^2 \mathrm{d} V .
\tag{8.37}\]

Find the condition for stability of a nonrotating star in terms of \(\Gamma\) and \(\mathfrak{M}\).
What is the maximum magnetic field strength for a Sun-like star (\(R = 7 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{km}\), \(M = 2 \times 10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\))? Neglect factors of order unity, and give the answer in tesla and in gauss (\(1\,\mathrm{T} = 10^4\,\mathrm{G}\)).
What is the maximum magnetic field strength for a neutron star (\(R = 12\,\mathrm{km}\), \(M = 3 \times 10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}\))?

8.5 Exercises

Exercise 8.1 (Self-gravitating slab) An infinite, static slab of incompressible fluid with uniform density \(\rho_0\) fills the region \(| z | < a\) and is held together by its own gravity.

Compute the gravitational acceleration inside and outside the slab, and the pressure profile inside it. Use Poisson’s equation, \(\nabla^2 \Psi = 4 \pi G \rho\).
Model the disk of a galaxy as such a slab, with \(\rho_0 = 10^{-23}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} = 10^{-20}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\) and \(a = 10^{19}\,\mathrm{m}\). A star starts at rest at \(z = a\). How fast does it cross the mid-plane, and what is the period of its vertical oscillation?

Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 8.


Exercise 8.2 (Mass of a molecular cloud) A self-gravitating cloud of molecular hydrogen \(\left( p = nk_B T = \frac{2}{5} \rho \varepsilon \right)\) is measured to have radius \(R = 0.1\,\mathrm{pc}\) and temperature \(T = 10\,\mathrm{K}\). Estimate the mass of the cloud.


Exercise 8.3 (Temperature of the solar core) Estimate the temperature at the center of the Sun, assuming that density and pressure change over a length scale comparable to the solar radius. Make the estimate twice: first assuming that the Sun is supported by gas pressure, then assuming that it is supported by radiation pressure. Which assumption is more plausible, and why?
Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 11.


Exercise 8.4 (Numerical solution of the Lane–Emden equation) The Lane–Emden equation describes the structure of a star with a polytropic equation of state, \(p = K \rho^{1 + 1 / n}\). It reads \[
\frac{1}{\xi^2} \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} \xi} \left( \xi^2 \frac{\mathrm{d} \theta}{\mathrm{d} \xi} \right) = - \theta^n, \qquad \theta (0) = 1, \qquad \theta' (0) = 0,
\tag{8.38}\] where \(\theta^n\) is the density in units of the central density, and \(\xi\) is the radius in suitable units. Write a code to compute numerically the solution of the Lane–Emden equation for a given \(n\).

Validate your code by comparing numerical and analytic solution for \(n = 0, 1, 5\).
Plot the solution for \(n = 1.5\) and find the radius of the polytrope, i.e., the value \(\xi_r\) at which \(\theta (\xi_r) = 0\).

Hint: use the solve_ivp function from scipy.integrate.

title: 9  Sound Waves and the Doppler Effect
text:
9.1 Oscillation Equation
The equations of fluid mechanics are nonlinear and only few analytic solutions are known. However, significant insight into astrophysical systems can be obtained by considering small perturbations around a background flow. Typically the background is chosen to be a hydrostatic solution, e.g., the density profile of an atmosphere. However, this method can be applied to more general situations. This is the key working principle of asteroseismology (helioseismology in the case of the Sun). Sound waves are also one of the key tools to learn about the early Universe, as they generate the baryon acoustic oscillations seen in the CMB and in the distribution of galaxies.
To set the stage, consider a gas flow with density, pressure, and velocity \[
\rho_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}), \quad p_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}), \quad \mathbf{v}_0 (t
; \mathcal{V}) .
\tag{9.1}\] We describe its perturbation in terms of a small displacement vector \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t ; \mathcal{V})\) describing the offset of each fluid element from its background state.
The density, pressure, and velocity of each fluid element change according to \[
\rho (t ; \mathcal{V}) = \rho_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}) + \delta \rho (t ;
\mathcal{V}), \quad p (t ; \mathcal{V}) = p_0 (t ; \mathcal{V}) + \delta p
(t ; \mathcal{V}), \quad \mathbf{v} (t ; \mathcal{V}) =\mathbf{v}_0 (t ;
\mathcal{V}) + \frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi} (t ; \mathcal{V})}{\mathrm{d} t} .
\tag{9.2}\] The quantities with the \(\delta\) in front are the Lagrangian perturbations1. The Eulerian perturbation of a quantity is given by \[
q' (t, \mathbf{x}) = q_0 (t, \mathbf{x}-\boldsymbol{\xi}) + \delta q (t,
\mathbf{x}) - q_0 (t, \mathbf{x}) = \delta q (t, \mathbf{x}) -\boldsymbol{\xi}
\cdot \nabla q_0 .
\tag{9.3}\] The difference between Lagrangian and Eulerian perturbations is that the Lagrangian perturbations are specific to individual fluid elements, while the Eulerian perturbations record the difference in the flow at a fixed position. This distinction turns out to be crucial when perturbing non-homogeneous backgrounds, for which \(\nabla q_0 \neq 0\), as we will see in Chapter 10.
For the moment, we consider a homogeneous medium in which \(\rho_0\), \(p_0\), and \(\mathbf{v}_0 = 0\) are constant. We perturb it by displacing the fluid elements by a small amount \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) and let it evolve freely. How do the perturbations evolve? To find out, we need to insert the Lagrangian perturbations into the Lagrangian equations (Chapter 5).
The continuity equation (Equation 1.15) reads \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}
\longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} (\rho_0 + \delta \rho )}{\mathrm{d} t} = - (\rho_0
+ \delta \rho) \nabla \cdot \left( \frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t}
\right) .
\tag{9.4}\] Dropping quantities that are quadratic or higher order in the perturbation, and integrating in time with the condition that \(\delta \rho = 0\) when \(\boldsymbol{\xi} = 0\), we obtain \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \delta \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} \longrightarrow \boxed{\delta \rho = - \rho_0
\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}} .
\tag{9.5}\] To find the perturbed momentum equation, first note that \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial
t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol{\xi}= \frac{\partial
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol{\xi}+ \left(
\frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} \cdot \nabla \right) \boldsymbol{\xi}=
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} + O (| \boldsymbol{\xi} |^2),
\tag{9.6}\] so \[
\mathbf{v}= \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t}, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}
\mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} +
(\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}+ \left( \frac{\mathrm{d}
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} \cdot \nabla \right) \mathbf{v}= \frac{\partial^2
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} + O (| \boldsymbol{\xi} |^2) .
\tag{9.7}\] The momentum equation (Equation 4.12) becomes \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p \rightarrow
\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \frac{1}{\rho_0} \nabla p =
- \frac{1}{\rho_0} \nabla \delta p.
\tag{9.8}\] Here we have used the fact that, for a homogeneous background, the Eulerian and Lagrangian perturbations are the same, \(p' = \delta p\) (Equation 9.3). This is not true in a stratified atmosphere, as we will see in Chapter 10.
We will consider only the case of adiabatic perturbations, for which \[
p = p (\rho) .
\tag{9.9}\] In other words, we are taking the pressure at constant entropy. For example, for an ideal gas, we have already seen that for adiabatic processes (Equation 2.24) \[
p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon \longrightarrow p = K \rho^{\Gamma} ,
\tag{9.10}\] with \(K = (\Gamma - 1) \rho^{1 - \Gamma} \varepsilon\).
Why should sound waves be adiabatic? A sound wave compresses some regions of the fluid and expands others, so the compressed regions become hotter. Heat flows from the hot to the cold regions, but this takes time. Heat needs to diffuse over a distance comparable to the wavelength \(\lambda_w\) of the wave, which takes a time \(t_{\mathrm{diff}} \sim \lambda_w^2 / D\), where \(D \sim \lambda v_{\mathrm{th}}\) and \(\lambda\) is the mean free path (Chapter 6). The period of the wave is \(\sim \lambda_w / c_s\), where \(c_s\) is the sound speed defined below, which is comparable to the thermal velocity of the particles \(v_{\mathrm{th}}\). So we have \[
\frac{t_{\mathrm{diff}}}{\lambda_w / c_s} \sim \frac{\lambda_w}{\lambda} \gg 1,
\tag{9.11}\] whenever the fluid description is valid. In other words, heat does not have time to leave the compressed regions during one period, and the perturbations are adiabatic. The opposite limit, isothermal perturbations, happens when the gas can cool very quickly, for example by radiation. This is the case in cold molecular clouds (Chapter 8, Chapter 12).
In this case, we can use the chain rule to rewrite \(\nabla \delta p\) in terms of \(\nabla \delta \rho\): \[
\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \frac{1}{\rho_0}
\frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} \rho} \nabla \delta \rho = \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d}
\rho} \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{9.12}\] Defining the sound speed \(c_s = \sqrt{\mathrm{d} p / \mathrm{d} \rho}\), we obtain the oscillation equation: \[
\boxed{\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2 \nabla
\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}= 0.}
\tag{9.13}\] In general, the sound speed needs to be evaluated at constant entropy, that is \[
\boxed{c_s = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s} .}
\tag{9.14}\]
If, instead, the perturbations are isothermal, we need to take the derivative of the pressure at constant temperature. For an ideal gas, this gives the isothermal sound speed \[
c_{\mathrm{iso}} = \sqrt{\left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_T} = \sqrt{\frac{k_B T}{\mu m_u}} = \frac{c_s}{\sqrt{\Gamma}} .
\tag{9.16}\] This is the sound speed that appears in the equation of state of an isothermal gas, \(p = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho\) (Chapter 4, Chapter 8).
The oscillation Equation 9.13 is the fundamental equation to describe sound waves. Taking the divergence on both sides and using Equation 9.5, we find that the density perturbation \(\delta \rho\) satisfies the wave equation: \[
\frac{\partial^2 \delta \rho}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2 \nabla^2 \delta \rho =
0.
\tag{9.17}\] To solve the oscillation equation, we consider the ansatz \[
\boldsymbol{\xi}=\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \exp [\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}-
\omega t)],
\tag{9.18}\] which describes a plane sound wave propagating in the direction \(\mathbf{k}\) and having frequency \(\omega\). \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1\) is the polarization vector, describing the way in which fluid elements oscillate as the wave propagates. As usual, the physical displacement is the real part of Equation 9.18. Inserting this ansatz into Equation 9.13, we find \[
\omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = c_s^2 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}_1)
.
\tag{9.19}\] This means that plane wave solutions to Equation 9.13 exist only for specific choices of \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1, \omega\) and \(\mathbf{k}\). We see that the RHS is parallel to \(\mathbf{k}\), so solutions with \(\omega \neq 0\) can exist only if \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \parallel \mathbf{k}\). This means that sound waves are longitudinal. Displacements with \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \perp \mathbf{k}\) are also solutions, but with \(\omega = 0\). They do not compress the fluid, so there is no restoring force (recall that a fluid at rest cannot sustain shear, Chapter 4). This is opposite from electromagnetic waves in vacuum, in which the electric and magnetic fields oscillate in the plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Setting \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = \xi_1 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\), we find \[
\omega^2 = c_s^2 k^2 .
\tag{9.20}\] This is the dispersion relation for sound waves. It means that both phase and group velocity for sound waves are given by \(c_s\) \[
v_{\mathrm{phase}} = \frac{\omega}{k} = c_s, \qquad v_{\mathrm{group}} =
\frac{\mathrm{d} \omega}{\mathrm{d} k} = c_s .
\tag{9.21}\] This justifies the name sound speed for \(c_s\). Since \(v_{\mathrm{phase}}\) does not depend on \(k\), sound waves are non-dispersive: a pulse made of many waves with different wavelengths propagates without changing its shape.
What happens to fluid elements when a sound wave passes through them? They are displaced along the direction of the wave. This causes a compression of the fluid. From Equation 9.5, we find: \[
\delta \rho = - \mathrm{i} \rho_0  (\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}_1) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}
(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} .
\tag{9.22}\]
The same method can be applied to a homogeneous fluid moving with constant velocity \(\mathbf{v}_0\). In this case the sound waves are carried by the flow, and the dispersion relation becomes \[
\omega = \mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \mathbf{k} \pm c_s k .
\tag{9.25}\] This means that the frequency of the sound measured by an observer at rest is shifted with respect to the frequency \(c_s k\) measured by an observer moving with the fluid. This is the Doppler effect. We derive Equation 9.25 in the in-class worksheet (Section 9.3).
