title: 9  Sound Waves and the Doppler Effect
text:
Figure 9.1: Lagrangian displacement of a fluid element from position \(\mathbf{x}\) to position \(\mathbf{x}+\boldsymbol{\xi}\).















TipExample



For an ideal gas, with \(p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon = \frac{\rho}{\mu m_u} k_B T\), the sound speed is \[
c_s^2 = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s = \Gamma K
\rho^{\Gamma - 1} = (\Gamma - 1) \Gamma \varepsilon = \frac{\Gamma k_B
T}{\mu m_u} .
\tag{9.15}\]









TipExample



Consider air at room temperature, \(T = 293\,\mathrm{K}\). Air is mostly made of \(\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(\mathrm{O}_2\), so \(\mu \approx 29\) and \(\Gamma = 7/5\). From Equation 9.15 we find \(c_s \approx 343\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), which is the measured value. Newton was the first to compute the speed of sound, but he assumed that the perturbations were isothermal. He found \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} \approx 290\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), about 15% too small. The discrepancy was only explained a century later by Laplace, who realized that sound waves are adiabatic.
In astrophysics, sound speeds span a large range. In a cold molecular cloud with \(T = 10\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\mu \approx 2.3\), we have \(c_s \approx 0.2\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). At the center of the Sun, \(T \approx 1.6 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\mu \approx 0.85\), so \(c_s \approx 500\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). This means that sound takes about one hour to cross the Sun (Exercise 9.1).










TipExample



Consider a sound wave propagating along \(z\) with wave number \(k\). Then \(\mathbf{k}= k \hat{\mathbf{z}}\) and \(\omega = c_s k\). The only non-zero component of \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is the \(z\)-component \[
\xi_z = \mathrm{Re} \left\{ \xi_1 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} k (z - c_s t)} \right\} = A \cos [k (z - c_s t)] + B \sin [k
(z - c_s t)] \Longleftrightarrow \xi_1 = A - \mathrm{i} B
\tag{9.23}\] The density perturbation is given by \[
\frac{\delta \rho}{\rho_0} = - \frac{\partial \xi_z}{\partial z} = k \{ A
\sin [k (z - c_s t)] - B \cos [k (z - c_s t)] \} .
\tag{9.24}\] Note that the density perturbation is shifted by a quarter of a wavelength with respect to the displacement. The gas is most compressed where \(\xi_z\) changes sign, not where it is largest. This is shown in Figure 9.2.








Figure 9.2: A plane sound wave at a fixed time. Top: displacement \(\xi_z\) and density perturbation \(\delta\rho/\rho_0\). Bottom: positions of fluid elements, initially equally spaced, after being displaced by \(\xi_z\).

title: 9  Sound Waves and the Doppler Effect
text:
9.2 Wave Energy and Momentum
Sound waves also transport energy and momentum. The deposition of energy by breaking waves (Chapter 11) is thought to play an important role in phenomena such as core-collapse supernovae, stellar eruptions, and the evolution of giant molecular clouds.






NoteGoing further: Normal Modes



Before we can compute the energy carried by waves, we need to develop some general perturbation theory. In general, the oscillation equation takes the form \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\xi},
\tag{9.26}\] where \(\hat{\mathbf{F}}\) is a differential operator. For example, for sound waves in a homogeneous medium \(\hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\xi}= \rho_0 c_s^2 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}\). We can find a dispersion relation by looking for solutions such that \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i}
\omega t} .
\tag{9.27}\] Inserting this ansatz in Equation 9.26, we find an eigenvalue problem \[
- \omega^2 \rho_0 \boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) = \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) .
\tag{9.28}\] In most applications, \(\hat{\mathbf{F}}\) is self-adjoint: \[
\int \boldsymbol{\zeta} (\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\xi}
(\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{d} V = \int \boldsymbol{\xi}
(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\zeta} (\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{d} V .
\tag{9.29}\] For sound waves, this can be shown by integrating by parts: both sides are equal to \(- \int \rho_0 c_s^2 (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\zeta}) (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) \mathrm{d} V\). An important consequence of Equation 9.29 is that \(\omega^2\) is always real. So each mode either oscillates, if \(\omega^2 > 0\), or grows exponentially, if \(\omega^2 < 0\). We will use this to study instabilities later in the course (Chapter 15, Chapter 16, Chapter 17).
The general theory of linear operators then implies that Equation 9.28 has an infinite set of eigenvalues \(\{ \omega_n \}\) and eigenfunctions \(\{ \boldsymbol{\eta}_n \}\) and that any perturbation (not just plane waves) can be written as an infinite superposition of elementary solutions: \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \sum_n \boldsymbol{\eta}_n (\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{e}^{-
\mathrm{i} \omega_n t} .
\tag{9.30}\] The quantities \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_n (\mathbf{x})\) are also called the normal modes of oscillations. Note that the normal modes need not be countable. For example, for sound waves in a homogeneous infinite medium all positive sound frequencies \(\omega\) are allowed. In this case, Equation 9.30 takes the form of an integral. For plane waves in a homogeneous medium, Equation 9.30 is just the Fourier transform: \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \int \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{k}\boldsymbol{\eta}
(\mathbf{k}) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}} \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} c_s kt} ,
\tag{9.31}\] where the real part is understood. However, when we consider sound waves in a finite medium, for example a star of a given radius, standing waves must fit an integer number of half wavelengths inside the star. This makes the frequencies \(\{ \omega_n \}\) quantized.






TipExample



Consider a rigid, cylindrical pipe of length \(L\) filled with gas at constant density and temperature. The ends of the pipe are sealed. The displacement equation for sound waves propagating in the pipe is \[
\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\partial_t^2 \xi (t, z) = c_s^2 \partial_z^2 \xi (t, z), & 0 < z < L,\\
\xi (t, 0) = \xi (t, L) = 0. &
\end{array}\right.
\tag{9.32}\] If we look for solutions in the form \(\xi (t, z) = \eta (z) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t}\), we find the eigenvalue problem \[
\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
\partial_z^2 \eta (z) + \left( \frac{\omega}{c_s} \right)^2 \eta (z) =
0, & 0 < z < L\\
\eta (0) = \eta (L) = 0. &
\end{array}\right.
\tag{9.33}\] This equation is just the equation for a harmonic oscillator. The general solution is \[
\eta (z) = A \cos (k z) + B \sin (k z), \qquad k =
\frac{\omega}{c_s} .
\tag{9.34}\] However, not all solutions satisfy the boundary conditions. To satisfy the boundary conditions, we require \[
A = 0, \qquad k = k_n = \frac{n \pi}{L} \Longrightarrow \omega = c_s
\left( \frac{n \pi}{L} \right), \quad n = 1, 2, \ldots
\tag{9.35}\] For example, for a pipe of length \(L = 1\,\mathrm{m}\) filled with air, the frequency of the fundamental mode is \(\omega_1 / 2 \pi = c_s / (2 L) \approx 170\,\mathrm{Hz}\). This is how organ pipes work. The first few normal modes are plotted in Figure 9.3.






Figure 9.3: Normal modes for gas in a cylindrical pipe.



This means that all sound waves propagating along the pipe are in the form \[
\xi (t, z) = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \left[ A_n \sin \left( \frac{n \pi c_s
t}{L} \right) + B_n \cos \left( \frac{n \pi c_s t}{L} \right) \right] \sin
\left( \frac{n \pi z}{L} \right),
\tag{9.36}\] where \(A_n\) and \(B_n\) are determined by the initial velocity \(\partial_t \xi (0, z)\) and displacement \(\xi (0, z)\), respectively.










NoteGoing further: Work Integral



We might be tempted to define the energy density of a wave in the general form \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t}\) as \[
K_{\mathrm{wave}} = \frac{1}{2} \rho_0  \left\langle \left| \frac{\partial
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t } \right|^2 \right\rangle = \frac{1}{2} \rho_0  |
\boldsymbol{\eta} |^2  \omega^2 \langle \sin^2 (\omega t) \rangle =
\frac{\omega^2}{4} \rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2,
\tag{9.37}\] where \(\langle \cdot \rangle\) denotes averaging over a period \(T = 2 \pi / \omega\) of the wave. Equation 9.37 is the kinetic energy density associated with the wave. However, it turns out that the kinetic energy is just one portion of the wave energy.
The energy of the wave is related to \(\xi^2\), so it cannot be computed directly from linear theory. However, we can use a trick:

adiabatically perturb the system to create a wave with an external force;
compute the work done by the external force on the system.

To achieve this we add a source term to the oscillation equation: \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\xi}+\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{ext}} (t) .
\tag{9.38}\] Suppose we want to excite the mode \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t}\), where \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) is such that \(\hat{\mathbf{F}} \boldsymbol{\eta}= - \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\eta}\). Then we can take \(\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{ext}} (t) = F_0 \mathrm{e}^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x})\), where \(F_0\) is chosen so that for \(t \lesssim 0\), \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{e}^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta} (\mathbf{x})\). Inserting this into the oscillation equation yields \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \rho_0 \gamma^2
\mathrm{e}^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta}= \mathrm{e}^{\gamma t}  \hat{\mathbf{F}}
\boldsymbol{\eta}+ F_0 \mathrm{e}^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta}= (- \rho_0 \omega^2 + F_0)
\mathrm{e}^{\gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta}.
\tag{9.39}\] We can solve for \(F_0\) to find that \[
F_0 = \rho_0  (\omega^2 + \gamma^2) .
\tag{9.40}\] The work done by the external force per unit volume is given by the work integral \[
W_{\mathrm{ext}} = \int_{- \infty}^0 \mathrm{d} t \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t}
\cdot \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{ext}} = \int_{- \infty}^0 \mathrm{d} t \rho_0 \gamma
(\gamma^2 + \omega^2) \mathrm{e}^{2 \gamma t} \boldsymbol{\eta} \cdot \boldsymbol{\eta}=
\rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2  \int_{- \infty}^0 \mathrm{d} t \gamma (\gamma^2 +
\omega^2) \mathrm{e}^{2 \gamma t},
\tag{9.41}\] where we have used the fact that \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\) is time independent. The last integral can be computed analytically, so the previous expression yields \[
W_{\mathrm{ext}} = \rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2  \left( \frac{\gamma^2}{2} +
\frac{\omega^2}{2} \right) .
\tag{9.42}\] The energy density of the wave is obtained in the limit in which \(\gamma \downarrow 0\): \[
\boxed{E_{\mathrm{wave}} = \frac{\omega^2}{2} \rho_0  | \boldsymbol{\eta} |^2
.}
\tag{9.43}\] Note that \(E_{\mathrm{wave}} = 2 K_{\mathrm{wave}}\), meaning that half of the wave energy is potential energy. For example, for a sound wave with \(\boldsymbol{\eta}=\mathbf{A} \cos (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x})\), the mean energy density (averaging over one wave-length) is \[
E_{\mathrm{wave}} = \frac{\omega^2}{4} \rho_0 A^2 .
\tag{9.44}\] It is possible to compute the linear momentum density \(\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{wave}}\) carried by waves in a similar way. One finds \[
\boxed{\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{wave}} = \frac{\mathbf{k}}{\omega}
E_{\mathrm{wave}} .}
\tag{9.45}\]

title: 9  Sound Waves and the Doppler Effect

9.3 In-class worksheets

9.3.1 Sound waves
Consider an ideal gas with \[
p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon = \frac{\rho}{\mu m_u} k_B T.
\tag{9.46}\] What is the sound speed \(c_s\) as a function of \(\rho\) and \(T\)? Does it depend on \(\rho\)?
Show that \[
\boldsymbol{\xi}= f (z - c_s t)  \hat{\mathbf{z}}
\tag{9.47}\] is a solution of \[
\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2 \nabla \nabla \cdot
\boldsymbol{\xi}= 0.
\tag{9.48}\] Sketch the solution for different times if \(f (x) = \mathrm{e}^{- x^2 / 2}\). What is the corresponding density perturbation? Is \(f (z + c_s t) \hat{\mathbf{z}}\) also a solution? What does it describe?


9.3.2 The Doppler effect
Consider an initially homogeneous flow with \[
\rho = \rho_0 = \mathrm{const}, \qquad p = p_0 = \mathrm{const}, \qquad
\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}_0 = \mathrm{const} .
\tag{9.49}\] Introduce a small perturbation in the form of a Lagrangian displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\).

Show that the Lagrangian density perturbation is given by \[
\delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{9.50}\]
Use the results from part 1) to show that the oscillation equation reads \[
\left[ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \nabla)
\right]^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}= c_s^2 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{9.51}\]
Introduce the ansatz \(\boldsymbol{\xi}=\boldsymbol{\eta}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}\) and show that the dispersion relation is \[
\omega_{\pm} =\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \mathbf{k} \pm c_s k.
\tag{9.52}\] What is the physical meaning of the \(\pm\) solutions?
Consider a sound wave propagating at an angle \(\theta\) with respect to \(\mathbf{v}_0\). Let \(\omega_0 = c_s k\) be the frequency of sound in the fluid frame. Show that the frequency of sound in the lab frame is \[
\omega = \omega_0  \left( 1 + \frac{v_0}{c_s} \cos \theta \right),
\tag{9.53}\] where \(v_0 = | \mathbf{v}_0 |\).

9.4 Exercises

Exercise 9.1 (Helioseismology) The surface of the Sun oscillates with periods of about 5 minutes. These oscillations are due to sound waves trapped inside the Sun. In this exercise, we estimate their frequencies with a very simple model. Assume \(\Gamma = 5/3\).

Estimate the sound speed at the center of the Sun, where \(T \approx 1.6 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\mu \approx 0.85\), and at the base of the convection zone, at \(r \approx 0.7\,R_\odot\), where \(T \approx 2 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\mu \approx 0.6\).
Estimate the time \(t_s\) it takes for sound to travel from the center to the surface of the Sun. For \(r < 0.7\,R_\odot\), use the average of the two sound speeds you found in part 1. For \(r > 0.7\,R_\odot\), assume that the temperature decreases linearly to zero at the surface, and that \(\mu\) is constant.
Model the Sun as a pipe of length \(R_\odot\), closed at both ends. What is the frequency of the fundamental mode? What is the order \(n\) of a mode with a period of 5 minutes?
The observed frequencies of consecutive modes of this type differ by about \(135\,\mu\mathrm{Hz}\). Compare with your estimate. What do these observations measure?

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
10.1 Waves in Isothermal Atmospheres
Consider a stratified, static, isothermal atmosphere. We assume constant acceleration \(g\) in the negative \(z\) direction. The hydrostatic equilibrium equations are (Chapter 4) \[
\partial_z p_0 = - \rho_0 g, \qquad p_0 = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho_0,
\tag{10.1}\] where \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} = \sqrt{k_B T / (\mu m_u)}\) is the isothermal sound speed (Equation 9.16).
Combining these two we find \[
\partial_z \rho_0 = - \frac{g}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \rho_0 \Longrightarrow \rho_0 =
\tilde{\rho} \mathrm{e}^{- z / H} .
\tag{10.2}\] \(H = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 / g\) is called the scale height of the atmosphere and has units of a length.
We want to study the propagation of waves in this atmosphere. The continuity equation still gives (Equation 9.5) \[
\delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi},
\tag{10.3}\] and the velocity perturbation is \[
\mathbf{v}' = \delta \mathbf{v}- (\boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}_0 =
\delta \mathbf{v}= \frac{\mathrm{d} \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{\partial
\boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v}_0 \cdot \nabla) \boldsymbol{\xi}=
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} .
\tag{10.4}\] The sound speed is given by \[
c_s^2 = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial \rho} \right)_s = \Gamma c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 ,
\tag{10.5}\] which implies that \(\delta p = c_s^2 \delta \rho\) for adiabatic perturbations. However, \(p' \neq c_s^2 \rho'\), because the Eulerian and Lagrangian perturbations differ when \(\nabla p_0 \neq 0\) (Equation 9.3). Instead we have \[
\delta p = c_s^2 \delta \rho \Longrightarrow (p' +\boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot
\nabla p_0) = c_s^2 \delta \rho \Longrightarrow p' = c_s^2 \delta
\rho + g \rho_0 \xi_z .
\tag{10.6}\] The momentum equation reads \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p - g \rho
\hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.7}\] Setting \(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}'\), \(p = p_0 + p'\), and \(\rho = \rho_0 + \rho'\) yields \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - \nabla p_0 - g
\rho_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - \nabla p' - g \rho'  \hat{\mathbf{z}} + \ldots,
\tag{10.8}\] where the dots denote terms of second order in the perturbation. The first two terms on the RHS cancel out. Dropping the higher order terms we find \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - c_s^2 \nabla
\delta \rho + g \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - g \rho_0 \nabla
\xi_z - g \left( \delta \rho + \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z  \right)
\hat{\mathbf{z}},
\tag{10.9}\] where we have used Equation 10.6 and \[
\rho' = \delta \rho - (\boldsymbol{\xi} \cdot \nabla) \rho_0 = \delta \rho +
\frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z .
\tag{10.10}\] The second and last term on the RHS of Equation 10.9 cancel out leaving \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - c_s^2 \nabla
\delta \rho - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z - g \delta \rho \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.11}\] Using the fact that \[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla \delta \rho &= \nabla (- \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) \\
&= - \rho_0 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}- \nabla \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \\
&= - \rho_0 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}+ \frac{\rho_0}{H} \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}},
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.12}\] we obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
\rho_0 \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = {}& c_s^2 \rho_0 \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}- \rho_0 \Gamma g \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}} \\
& - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z + g \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.13}\] This can be simplified to \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = {}& c_s^2 \left( \nabla \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}- \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{c_s^2} \frac{1}{H} \nabla \xi_z \right) \\
& - \frac{(c_s^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2)}{H} \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
}
\tag{10.14}\] We are going to analyze the consequences of this equation shortly. Before we do that, we show that this equation reduces to Eq. (6.31) of Clarke and Carswell (2007) in the limit of vertical oscillations in the \(z\) direction. To do that, we take the divergence of Equation 10.14 and use \(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi} = - \delta \rho / \rho_0\) to obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial^2 \delta \rho}{\partial t^2} &= c_s^2 \left( \nabla^2 \delta \rho + \frac{2}{H} \partial_z \delta \rho + \frac{\delta \rho}{H^2} \right) \\
&\qquad + g \rho_0 \nabla^2 \xi_z \\
&\qquad - \frac{(c_s^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2)}{H} \left( \partial_z \delta \rho + \frac{\delta \rho}{H} \right) \\
&= c_s^2 \nabla^2 \delta \rho + \frac{c_s^2 + c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{H} \partial_z \delta \rho \\
&\qquad + \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{H} \rho_0 \nabla^2 \xi_z + c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \frac{\delta \rho}{H^2} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{10.15}\] Assuming that \(\delta \rho = \delta \rho (t, z)\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi}= \xi_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), we obtain, \[
\frac{\partial^2 \delta \rho}{\partial t^2} - c_s^2  \frac{\partial^2 \delta
\rho}{\partial z^2} - \frac{c_s^2}{H}  \frac{\partial \delta \rho}{\partial
z} = 0,
\tag{10.16}\] where we have used the fact that \[
\nabla^2 \xi_z = \partial_z^2 \xi_z = \partial_z  \left( - \frac{\delta
\rho}{\rho_0} \right) = - \frac{\partial_z \delta \rho}{\rho_0} -
\frac{\delta \rho}{\rho_0 H} .
\tag{10.17}\] Equation 10.16 is identical to Eq. (6.31) of Clarke and Carswell (2007). It describes the propagation of density modes in a stratified atmosphere, but neglects an entirely different class of modes, the gravity waves, in which the fluid elements move up and down, while the wave propagates mostly in the horizontal direction. We discuss them in Section 10.2.
As before, we look for traveling wave solutions \[
\boldsymbol{\xi}=\boldsymbol{\eta}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}
,
\tag{10.18}\] where now we allow the components of \(\mathbf{k}\) to be complex. Inserting this into Equation 10.14 we obtain \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\omega^2 \boldsymbol{\eta} = {}& c_s^2 \left( \mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\eta}+ \mathrm{i} \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{c_s^2} \frac{1}{H} \eta_z \right) \mathbf{k} \\
& + \mathrm{i} \frac{(c_s^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2)}{H} \mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\eta} \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
}
\tag{10.19}\]

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
In the limit \(kH \gg 1\), that is, when the wavelength is much smaller than the scale height of the atmosphere, the terms proportional to \(1/H\) can be neglected and we recover the dispersion relation for waves in a homogeneous medium, namely \(\omega^2 = c_s^2 k^2\), as expected.
Purely horizontal waves, with \(\boldsymbol{\eta}, \mathbf{k} \perp \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), cannot satisfy the dispersion relation, unless \(c_s = c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), that is for isothermal as opposed to adiabatic perturbations. Physically this means that density fluctuations become buoyant, so they acquire a \(k_z \neq 0\) component in their wave vector.
For waves with \(\boldsymbol{\eta} \parallel \mathbf{k} \parallel \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), the dispersion relation simplifies to \[
\omega^2 = c_s^2  \left( k^2 + \mathrm{i} \frac{1}{H} k \right)
\Longrightarrow k_{1, 2} = - \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2 H} \pm \sqrt{\left(
\frac{\omega}{c_s} \right)^2 - \left( \frac{1}{2 H} \right)^2} .
\tag{10.20}\] These are the so-called pressure or p-modes of the atmosphere. They are the generalization of sound waves. Note that \(k\) has a real part only if \(\omega\) is larger than the acoustic cutoff frequency \[
\omega_{\mathrm{ac}} = \frac{c_s}{2 H} .
\tag{10.21}\]

If \(\omega \gg \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\), then the dispersion relation for p-modes can be approximated as: \[
k_{1, 2} \approx - \frac{\mathrm{i}}{2 H} \pm \frac{\omega}{c_s} .
\tag{10.22}\] In this case the displacement grows exponentially with height: \[
\xi_z = \eta_z \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} =
\eta_z \exp \left[ \mathrm{i} \omega \left( \pm \frac{z}{c_s} - t \right)
\right] \exp \left( \frac{z}{2 H} \right) .
\tag{10.23}\] This makes sense, because the energy flux carried by the wave, which is the energy density (Equation 9.43) times \(c_s\), \(\sim \rho_0 \omega^2 |\boldsymbol{\xi}|^2 c_s\), must be the same at all heights. Since \(\rho_0\) decreases with height, \(|\boldsymbol{\xi}|\) must increase as \(\rho_0^{-1/2} \propto \mathrm{e}^{z / 2 H}\). The density perturbation of the wave propagating upward is \[
\delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}= - \tilde{\rho} \eta_z
\left( \frac{\mathrm{i} \omega}{c_s} + \frac{1}{2 H} \right) \exp \left[
\mathrm{i} \omega \left( \frac{z}{c_s} - t \right) \right] \exp \left( -
\frac{z}{2 H} \right) .
\tag{10.24}\] Note that the density perturbation itself decreases with height. However, the background density decreases faster, so the relative perturbation \(\delta \rho / \rho_0 \propto \mathrm{e}^{z / 2 H}\) grows. This means that waves propagating upward through an isothermal atmosphere eventually become nonlinear, \(\delta \rho \sim \rho_0\), and break, forming shocks (Chapter 11). Waves breaking in this way are thought to contribute to the heating of the solar chromosphere.
If \(\omega < \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\), then \(k\) is purely imaginary and the waves do not propagate. In the limit \(\omega \ll \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\), we find \[
k_{1, 2} \approx 0, - \frac{\mathrm{i}}{H} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad
[\xi_z]_{1, 2} = \eta_z  \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t}, \eta_z \mathrm{e}^{z / H} \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i}
\omega t} .
\tag{10.25}\] In other words, the atmosphere responds to the perturbation as a whole, rather than with a wave propagating upward.

Let us now consider the case of perturbations with horizontal displacement. We can align the \(x\)-axis with \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\), meaning that \(\boldsymbol{\eta}= \eta \hat{\mathbf{x}}\). In this case, the dispersion relation becomes \[
\omega^2 \eta \hat{\mathbf{x}} = c_s^2  (k_x \eta) \mathbf{k}+ \mathrm{i}
\frac{(c_s^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2)}{H} k_x \eta \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.26}\] This means that there are two components of \(\mathbf{k}= (k_x, 0, k_z)\). The \(x\)-component of Equation 10.26 is \[
\omega^2 = c_s^2 k_x^2 \Longrightarrow k_x = \pm \frac{\omega}{c_s} .
\tag{10.27}\] The \(z\)-component of Equation 10.26 is \[
k_z = - \mathrm{i} \left( 1 - \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{c_s^2} \right)  \frac{1}{H} .
\tag{10.28}\] The corresponding displacement is \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \eta \exp \left[ \mathrm{i} \omega \left( \pm
\frac{x}{c_s} - t \right) \right] \exp \left[ \left( 1 - \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{c_s^2}
\right)  \frac{z}{H} \right]  \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\tag{10.29}\] These are called Lamb waves. They are sound waves that propagate horizontally and are trapped near the bottom of the atmosphere. Indeed, their energy density \(\rho_0 |\boldsymbol{\xi}|^2 \propto \mathrm{e}^{(1 - 2 / \Gamma) z / H}\) decreases with height for \(\Gamma < 2\). Lamb waves generated by the eruption of the Hunga Tonga volcano in 2022 were observed to travel around the Earth several times. In the limit in which \(c_s \rightarrow c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), that is \(\Gamma \rightarrow 1\) (isothermal perturbations), these waves reduce to horizontal sound waves.







TipExample



Consider the atmosphere of the Earth. It is not isothermal, but we can estimate its properties taking \(T \approx 288\,\mathrm{K}\), \(\mu \approx 29\), and \(\Gamma = 7/5\). We find \(H = k_B T / (\mu m_u g) \approx 8\,\mathrm{km}\), \(c_s \approx 340\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and an acoustic cutoff period \(2 \pi / \omega_{\mathrm{ac}} \approx 5\,\mathrm{min}\).
For the solar photosphere, \(T \approx 5800\,\mathrm{K}\), \(\mu \approx 1.3\), \(g \approx 2.7 \times 10^2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), and \(\Gamma = 5/3\). We find \(H \approx 140\,\mathrm{km}\), \(c_s \approx 8\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\), and \(\omega_{\mathrm{ac}} / 2 \pi \approx 4.6\,\mathrm{mHz}\), corresponding to a period of about 3.6 minutes. The measured value is about \(5.3\,\mathrm{mHz}\). The solar oscillations with periods of about 5 minutes have lower frequencies, about \(3.3\,\mathrm{mHz}\), so they cannot propagate into the solar atmosphere. They are reflected at the surface and remain trapped inside the Sun. This is why the Sun rings like a pipe (Exercise 9.1).

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
10.2 Gravity Waves
To understand the second class of waves, consider a fluid element that is displaced upward by a small distance \(\xi_z\). We assume that the displacement is slow enough for the fluid element to stay in pressure equilibrium with its surroundings, and that it is adiabatic. The pressure of the fluid element changes by \(\delta p = \xi_z \partial_z p_0 = - \rho_0 g \xi_z\), so its density changes by \[
\delta \rho = \frac{\delta p}{c_s^2} = - \frac{g}{c_s^2} \rho_0 \xi_z .
\tag{10.30}\] The density of the surrounding gas at the new position is \(\rho_0 + \xi_z \partial_z \rho_0 = \rho_0 - (g / c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2) \rho_0 \xi_z\). Since \(c_s > c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), the fluid element is denser than its surroundings, by \[
\Delta \rho = \delta \rho - \xi_z \partial_z \rho_0 = g \left( \frac{1}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} - \frac{1}{c_s^2} \right) \rho_0 \xi_z .
\tag{10.31}\] So gravity pulls it back down. The equation of motion of the fluid element is \[
\rho_0 \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \xi_z}{\mathrm{d} t^2} = - g \Delta \rho = - \rho_0 N^2 \xi_z, \qquad
N^2 = g^2 \left( \frac{1}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} - \frac{1}{c_s^2} \right) = \frac{(\Gamma - 1) g^2}{c_s^2} .
\tag{10.32}\] In other words, the fluid element oscillates up and down with frequency \(N\), which is called the buoyancy frequency or Brunt–Väisälä frequency. Note that \(N = 0\) if \(\Gamma = 1\). This makes sense, because, if the perturbations are isothermal, a displaced fluid element always has the same density as its surroundings. If the atmosphere were stratified in such a way that \(N^2 < 0\), the displaced fluid element would be lighter than its surroundings and would keep rising. This is the onset of convection, which we will discuss in Chapter 15.
To find the waves associated with this oscillation, we go back to Equation 10.19 and consider a general wave vector. We can always align the \(x\)-axis with the horizontal component of \(\mathbf{k}\), so that \(\mathbf{k} = (k_x, 0, k_z)\). Equation 10.19 is a linear system of equations for \(\boldsymbol{\eta}\), which has non-trivial solutions only if its determinant vanishes. To simplify the result, it is useful to write \(k_z = K - \mathrm{i} / (2 H)\), with \(K\) real. This takes into account the growth of the amplitude with height, \(\mathrm{e}^{z / 2 H}\), that we found for the p-modes. After some algebra, we find the dispersion relation \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\omega^4 - \omega^2 \left[ c_s^2 (k_x^2 + K^2) + \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}^2 \right]& \\
{} + N^2 c_s^2 k_x^2 &= 0 .
\end{aligned}
}
\tag{10.33}\] This is a quadratic equation for \(\omega^2\), so for each wave vector there are two solutions:

The larger solution describes the acoustic waves, or p-modes. One can show that these have \(\omega > \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\). For \(c_s k \gg \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\) they reduce to sound waves, \(\omega^2 \approx c_s^2 (k_x^2 + K^2)\).
The smaller solution describes the gravity waves, or g-modes, in which the restoring force is buoyancy. These have \(\omega < N\). For \(c_s k \gg \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\) we find \[
\omega^2 \approx N^2 \frac{k_x^2}{k_x^2 + K^2} .
\tag{10.34}\] Interestingly, the frequency of gravity waves depends only on the direction of \(\mathbf{k}\), not on the wavelength. Gravity waves with \(K = 0\), propagating horizontally, have the largest frequency, \(\omega \approx N\). In these waves, the fluid elements move up and down, like the fluid element we considered above.

For an isothermal atmosphere, \(\omega_{\mathrm{ac}}^2 - N^2 = (g / c_s)^2 (\Gamma / 2 - 1)^2 \geq 0\), so \(N \leq \omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\). Waves with frequencies between \(N\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{ac}}\) cannot propagate vertically. The two branches are shown in Figure 10.1. The Lamb waves we found before lie between the two branches, because they do not propagate vertically.






Figure 10.1: Dispersion relation for waves in an isothermal atmosphere with \(\Gamma = 5/3\), for vertical wave number \(K = 0\). Acoustic waves (p-modes) can propagate in the region above the upper curve and gravity waves (g-modes) in the region below the lower curve. Waves with \(K \neq 0\) move further into these regions. The dotted line is the Lamb wave, \(\omega = c_s k_x\).

text:
10.3 In-class worksheet
We consider small disturbances in a plane parallel, isothermal atmosphere. We will assume \(z\) to be the vertical direction and \(g\) to be the gravitational acceleration, assumed to be constant and towards the negative \(z\) direction. Let \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} = \sqrt{k_B T / (\mu m_u)}\) be the isothermal sound speed.

Show that the static background density \(\rho_0\) satisfies \[
\rho_0 (z) = \tilde{\rho} \mathrm{e}^{- z / H},
\tag{10.35}\] where \(H = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 / g\) is the scale height of the atmosphere.
Let \(\delta \rho\) and \(\rho'\) be the Lagrangian and Eulerian perturbations of the density. Show that \[
\rho' = \delta \rho + \frac{\rho_0}{H} \xi_z .
\tag{10.36}\]
Let \(p'\) be the Eulerian pressure perturbation. Show that \[
p' = c_s^2 \delta \rho + g \rho_0 \xi_z,
\tag{10.37}\] where \(c_s^2 = \Gamma c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2\) is the square of the sound speed and \(\xi_z\) is the \(z\)-component of the displacement.
Use the results from the previous two points to show that \[
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = - c_s^2 \nabla
\delta \rho - g \rho_0 \nabla \xi_z - g \delta \rho \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{10.38}\]
If time allows: consider vertical waves, \(\boldsymbol{\xi} = \xi_z (t, z) \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), and look for solutions \(\xi_z \propto \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (k z - \omega t)}\). Show that \[
\omega^2 = c_s^2 \left( k^2 + \frac{\mathrm{i} k}{H} \right),
\tag{10.39}\] and that the waves can propagate, that is, \(k\) has a real part, only if \(\omega > c_s / (2 H)\).

title: 10  Waves in Stratified Atmospheres
text:
10.4 Exercises

Exercise 10.1 (Waves in a polytropic atmosphere) An isentropic atmosphere sits in a uniform gravitational field \(g\), with pressure \(p_0 = K \rho_0^{1 + 1/n}\) and \(K\) constant. Let \(x\) be the depth below the top of the atmosphere, and suppose that the unperturbed density is \(\rho_0 = (bx)^n\) with \(b\) constant.

Show that hydrostatic equilibrium requires \(g = Kb (1 + n)\).
Perturb the atmosphere with a small vertical velocity \(v\), taken positive upward, together with adiabatic perturbations \(p' \ll p_0\) of the pressure and \(\rho' \ll \rho_0\) of the density. Show that \(p' = (gx / n) \rho'\).
Show that the linearized continuity and momentum equations are \[
\frac{\partial \rho'}{\partial t} - v \frac{\partial \rho_0}{\partial x} - \rho_0 \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} = 0
\tag{10.40}\] and \[
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} + \left( \frac{\rho'}{\rho_0} \right) g - \frac{g}{n \rho_0} \frac{\partial (x \rho')}{\partial x} = 0.
\tag{10.41}\]
For \(n = 1/2\), combine these equations to show that \[
\frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial t^2} = 2 gx \frac{\partial^2 v}{\partial x^2} + 3 g \frac{\partial v}{\partial x} .
\tag{10.42}\]
Look for solutions \(v (t, x) = v_1 (x) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t}\) and change variable to \(\tau = (2 x / g)^{1/2}\). Show that Equation 10.42 becomes \[
\frac{1}{\tau} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2}{\mathrm{d} \tau^2} (\tau v_1) + \omega^2 v_1 = 0.
\tag{10.43}\] Find the solution that stays finite at \(x = 0\) and interpret it physically.

Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 22.

title: 11  Shock Waves
text:
11.1.1 Shock waves I

Consider a shock wave in an ideal gas with adiabatic index \(\Gamma\). Let \(\rho_1, p_1\), and \(T_1\) be the upstream (unshocked) gas density, pressure, and temperature. Let \(\rho_2, p_2,\) and \(T_2\) be the corresponding downstream (post-shock) quantities.

Show that the ratio of downstream to upstream temperature across the shock is \[
\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{p_2}{p_1}  \frac{(\Gamma + 1) p_1 + (\Gamma - 1)
p_2}{(\Gamma - 1) p_1 + (\Gamma + 1) p_2} .
\tag{11.1}\]
If \(T_2 = 4 T_1\), what are \(p_2\) and \(\rho_2\) as a function of \(\rho_1, p_1,\) and \(T_1\)?




11.1.2 Shock waves II

The Bullet Cluster (1E 0657-56) consists of two colliding clusters of galaxies. The name comes from the characteristic shape of a shock formed by the interaction of the gas from the two clusters, which is visible in X-ray. The image in Figure 11.1 has been obtained with the Chandra X-ray space telescope.






Figure 11.1: Chandra/ACIS 0.5–5 keV image of the Bullet Cluster. From Markevitch et al. (2002); © The American Astronomical Society, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



This data can be fitted to infer the following parameters for the upstream and downstream electron density and temperature: \[
\begin{gathered}
n_1 = 3.7 \times 10^{- 3}\, \mathrm{cm}^{- 3}, \enspace T_1 = 9.3 \times 10^7
\,\mathrm{K}, \\
n_2 = 9.3 \times  10^{- 3}\, \mathrm{cm}^{- 3}, \enspace T_2 =
2.2 \times  10^8 \,\mathrm{K}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{11.2}\] Estimate

the Mach number of the shock (defined as the Mach number of the upstream flow);
the relative velocity of approach of the two clusters of galaxies.

title: 11  Shock Waves
text:
11.2 Exercises

Exercise 11.1 (Piston-driven shock) A piston drives a strong shock wave through a cold gas that is initially at rest; similar considerations are used to describe young supernova remnants. The piston moves at speed \(v_p\) and has a mass per unit surface area \(\Sigma_p\). The gas follows a gamma-law equation of state \[
p = (\Gamma - 1) \rho \varepsilon .
\tag{11.3}\]

Express the shock speed \(s\), and the downstream density \(\rho_2\) and pressure \(p_2\), in terms of the upstream density \(\rho_1\). Keep \(\Gamma\) general (do not set \(\Gamma = 5/3\)) and do not use the expression for \(s\) given by Kulsrud, which contains a typo.
Calculate the work that the piston does on the gas and estimate when the piston begins to decelerate. Compare the mass of the piston with the mass of the gas that the shock has swept up by that time. For this estimate, take the piston velocity to stay constant until the piston has lost a significant fraction of its kinetic energy.

Exercise 12.1 (Colliding clouds) Two identical clouds, each of radius \(3 \times 10^{16}\, \mathrm{m}\) (about 1 pc) and temperature \(10\,\mathrm{K}\), collide with each other at a relative velocity of \(4\, \mathrm{km} \, \mathrm{s}^{- 1}\).

The shocked gas cools at a rate \(\dot{Q} = 10^{- 7}\, \mathrm{W} \, \mathrm{kg}^{- 1}\). Decide whether the shock is approximately adiabatic or isothermal.
Suppose the collision produces an isothermal shock. How thick is the shocked layer, \(x\), at the moment when the whole of each cloud has been shocked?
At later times the layer settles into a structure that can be approximated by a hydrostatic isothermal slab with column density \(10^{- 2}\, \mathrm{g} \, \mathrm{cm}^{- 2} = 0.1\, \mathrm{kg} \, \mathrm{m}^{- 2}\). In this hydrostatic structure, what fraction of the clouds’ mass lies within the thickness \(x\)? Neglect edge effects and variations of the column density across the plane of the slab. (Hint. Exercise 13.1 (Ionized cavities around star clusters) A cluster of ionizing stars with total luminosity \(L\) clears out a cavity in the interstellar medium, which has an undisturbed density \(\rho_0\).

Use the similarity-solution method to find how the cavity radius \(r\) grows with time \(t\). [Hint. Take \(r \propto L^{\alpha} \rho_0^{\beta} t^{\gamma}\) and determine \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\).]

title: 14  Stellar Winds and Spherical Accretion
text:
The radial velocity \(v\) for an isothermal wind with isothermal sound speed \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}\) satisfies the equation \[
(v^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2)  \frac{1}{v} \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} r} = \frac{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{r} - \frac{GM}{r^2} .
\tag{14.1}\] Find the acceleration of the wind at the sonic point \[
r_c = \frac{GM}{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} .
\tag{14.2}\]
crumbs: 14  Stellar Winds and Spherical Accretion

title: 14  Stellar Winds and Spherical Accretion
text:
14.2 Exercises

Exercise 14.1 (Radiation-driven winds) Consider an isothermal steady stellar wind. Radiation pressure in optically thin conditions produces an additional force per unit mass that can be parameterized as \[
f = \frac{A}{r^2},
\tag{14.3}\] where \(A > 0\).

Show that the momentum equation becomes \[
(v^2 - c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2)  \frac{1}{v}  \frac{\mathrm{d} v}{\mathrm{d} r} = \frac{2 c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{r} -
\frac{GM}{r^2} + \frac{A}{r^2},
\tag{14.4}\] where \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}\) is the isothermal sound speed.
Assuming \(A < GM\), how does the structure of the wind change?
How does the radial profile of the velocity change if \(A > GM\)? Give a physical interpretation of the results.



Exercise 14.2 (Isothermal Bondi accretion) Far from a star of mass \(M\) located at the origin, isothermal gas has pressure \(p_{\infty} = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho_{\infty}\) and density \(\rho_{\infty}\). This gas is steadily accreted onto the star.

Find the accretion rate, assuming that the gas remains isothermal. At what radius does the infalling gas reach the sound speed?
Let \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} = 1\, \mathrm{km} /\mathrm{s}\) and \(n_{\infty} = 10^3\) hydrogen atoms per \(\mathrm{cm}^{3}\), and take the mass of the hydrogen atom to be \(1.66 \times 10^{- 27}\, \mathrm{kg}\). Express this radius in units of the solar radius \(R_{\odot} = 7 \times 10^8\, \mathrm{m}\).
Calculate the time that a star of mass \(M\) needs to double its mass.

A heavy fluid with density \(\rho_2\) is layered on top of a lighter fluid with density \(\rho_1\) in a constant vertical gravitational field \(g\) (\(\rho_2 > \rho_1\)). The system is perturbed by rotating a cylinder of fluid of radius \(r\), as shown in Figure 16.1.






Figure 16.1: A cylinder of fluid of radius \(r\) straddling the interface between the heavy fluid (density \(\rho_2\), above) and the light fluid (density \(\rho_1\), below). The ring around the cylinder has been rotated rigidly by an angle \(\theta\).

title: 18  Diffusion and Viscous Flows
text: 18.1 In-class worksheet

title: 18  Diffusion and Viscous Flows
text:
Core-collapse supernovae inject metals, such as oxygen, into the interstellar medium (ISM). After the supernova remnant has stalled its expansion, the diffusion of these elements throughout the galaxy can be modeled through an advection-diffusion equation: \[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot (\rho \mathbf{v}) = \nabla
\cdot (D \nabla \rho),
\tag{18.1}\] where \(\rho\) is the mass density of the newly synthesized elements, \(\mathbf{v}\) is the local velocity of the ISM, and \(D\) is a diffusion coefficient.

Show that, under suitable assumptions, \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \int_V \rho \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{r}= 0.
\tag{18.2}\]
Assume that \(\mathbf{v}= \mathrm{const}\), \(D = \mathrm{const} > 0\), and look for solutions in the form \[
\rho (t, \mathbf{x}) = \rho_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}-
\omega t)} .
\tag{18.3}\] Sketch the solution for different times and give a physical interpretation of the results.
How do the results change if \(D < 0\)?
Show that Equation 18.1 can be written as \[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left[ \rho \left(
\mathbf{v}- D \frac{\nabla \rho}{\rho} \right)  \right] = 0.
\tag{18.4}\] Interpret the term in round brackets as an effective propagation velocity \(\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}}\). How does \(\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{eff}}\) depend on the wave number \(\mathbf{k}\) if \(\rho\) is as in Equation 18.3?

title: 18  Diffusion and Viscous Flows
text:
18.2 Exercises

Exercise 18.1 (Steady viscous vortex) Consider a steady-state, axisymmetric solution of the incompressible, viscous, Navier–Stokes equations in cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\) in the form \[
v_R = - \alpha R, \qquad v_{\phi} = \frac{\mathcal{C}}{2 \pi R} g (R), \qquad
v_z = 2 \alpha z,
\tag{18.5}\] where \(\alpha > 0\) and \(\mathcal{C} > 0\) are given constants, while \(g (R)\) is a function satisfying \[
\lim_{R \rightarrow 0} g (R) = 0, \qquad \lim_{R \rightarrow \infty} g (R)
= 1.
\tag{18.6}\] Let \(\nu > 0\) be the kinematic viscosity.

Show that the flow is incompressible.
Derive an equation for \(g (R)\) assuming the flow to be steady state.
Compute the vorticity \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) of the flow.

crumbs: 19  Accretion Disks I: Structure and Viscous Evolution

title: 19  Accretion Disks I: Structure and Viscous Evolution
text:
Cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\) are defined as follows \[
x = R \cos \phi, \qquad y = R \sin \phi, \qquad z = z.
\tag{19.1}\] The unit vectors in the \(R, \phi\), and \(z\) directions are \[
\begin{gathered}
\hat{\mathbf{R}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}}  \left(\begin{array}{c}
x\\
y\\
0
\end{array}\right), \\
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2 +
y^2}}  \left(\begin{array}{c}
- y\\
x\\
0
\end{array}\right), \\
\hat{\mathbf{z}} = \left(\begin{array}{c}
0\\
0\\
1
\end{array}\right) .
\end{gathered}
\tag{19.2}\]

Given the fluid velocity written as \(\mathbf{v}= v_R \hat{\mathbf{R}} + v_{\phi} \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + v_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), find its Cartesian components \(v_x, v_y,\) and \(v_z\).
Use the chain rule for derivatives to show that \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial R} = \frac{x}{R}  \frac{\partial}{\partial x}
+ \frac{y}{R}  \frac{\partial}{\partial y}, \qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial \phi} = - y \frac{\partial}{\partial x} + x
\frac{\partial}{\partial y} .
\tag{19.3}\]
Using the results from the previous points show that \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}= \frac{1}{R}  \frac{\partial (Rv_R)}{\partial
R} + \frac{1}{R}  \frac{\partial v_{\phi}}{\partial \phi} +
\frac{\partial v_z}{\partial z} .
\tag{19.4}\]
Conclude that the continuity equation in cylindrical coordinates is \[
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{R}  \left[ \frac{\partial
(\rho Rv_R)}{\partial R} + \frac{\partial (\rho v_{\phi})}{\partial
\phi} \right] + \frac{\partial (\rho v_z)}{\partial z} = 0.
\tag{19.5}\]
crumbs: 19  Accretion Disks I: Structure and Viscous Evolution

title: 19  Accretion Disks I: Structure and Viscous Evolution
text:
19.2 Exercises

Exercise 19.1 (α-disks: scale height, viscosity, Reynolds number)  

Consider gas in an accretion disk that is in hydrostatic equilibrium in the vertical direction, with the vertical pressure gradient balancing the vertical component of the gravitational acceleration due to the central object. Show that the angular frequency of rotation \(\Omega\), the sound speed \(c_s\), and the vertical scale height \(H\) of the disk satisfy \(c_s \sim H \Omega\).
Suppose now that the \(R \phi\) component of the viscous stress tensor equals a factor \(\alpha\) times the thermal pressure. Show that (i) \(\nu \sim \alpha c_s H\) and (ii) the Reynolds number is \(\mathrm{Re} \sim \frac{1}{\alpha} \left( \frac{R}{H} \right)^2\).

Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 47.


Exercise 19.2 (Similarity form of the disk equation)  

Show that the viscous evolution equation of a Keplerian accretion disk, \[
\frac{\partial \Sigma}{\partial t} = \frac{3}{R}
\frac{\partial}{\partial R} \left[ R^{1 / 2}  \frac{\partial}{\partial
R} (\nu \Sigma R^{1 / 2}) \right],
\tag{19.6}\] can be recast as \[
\frac{\partial S}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial^2 Y}{\partial X^2},
\tag{19.7}\] with \(S = \Sigma R^{3 / 2}\), \(Y = 3 \nu \Sigma R^{1 / 2}\), and \(X = 2 R^{1 / 2}\).
Obtain also a partial differential equation for \(S (t, X)\) when \(Y = Y_0 + \beta (S - S_0)\), where \(Y_0\), \(S_0\), and \(\beta\) are constants.
Describe how \(S\) evolves in the two cases (a) \(\beta > 0\) and (b) \(\beta < 0\).

Adapted from Clarke and Carswell (2007), Problem 49.


Exercise 19.3 (Numerical evolution of an accretion disk)  

Show that Equation 19.6 can be written as \[
\frac{\partial S}{\partial T} = \frac{\partial^2 (SX^{- 2})}{\partial
X^2},
\tag{19.8}\] where \(S\) and \(X\) are defined as in Exercise 19.2 and \(T = 12 \nu t\).
To solve Equation 19.8 numerically, introduce a grid \[
\{ (T_n, X_k) = (n \Delta T, X_{\min} + k \Delta X) : n = 0, 1, \ldots,
N_T, k = 0, 1, \ldots, N_X \},
\tag{19.9}\] where \(\Delta T\), \(X_{\min}\), and \(\Delta X\) are fixed parameters. Let \(S^n_k\) be the approximation of \(S\) at \((T_n, X_k)\)1. Then \(S_k^n\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, N_X - 1\) can be written as \[
\frac{S^{n + 1}_k - S^n_k}{\Delta T} = \frac{S^{n + 1}_{k + 1} X_{k +
1}^{- 2} - 2 S^{n + 1}_k X_k^{- 2} + S^{n + 1}_{k - 1} X_{k - 1}^{-
2}}{\Delta X^2} .
\tag{19.10}\] The boundary conditions for this problem are \[
S_0 = S_{N_X} = 0,
\tag{19.11}\] corresponding to Dirichlet boundary condition for \(S\).
Show that Equation 19.10 can be written as \[
(I - \Delta TA) \mathbf{S}^{n + 1} =\mathbf{S}^n,
\tag{19.12}\] where \(\mathbf{S}^n = (S_1^n, S_2^n, \ldots, S^n_{N_X - 1})\) is a vector of values, \(I\) is the identity matrix, and \(A\) is a tridiagonal matrix. Find the explicit form of \(A\).
Write code to evolve in time the density in the disk by repeatedly solving Equation 19.12 starting from some initial condition \(\mathbf{S}^0\). You can use scipy.linalg.solve_banded to solve the linear equations.
Consider as initial conditions \[
S (t = 0, X) = \mathrm{e}^{- (X - 10)^2},
\tag{19.13}\] with \(X_{\min} = 1\). Plot the numerical solutions at successive times. Interpret the results in a few sentences.

title: 20  Accretion Disks II: Steady Disks and Spectra
text:
Viscous instability in accretion disks. The equation describing the evolution of the surface density \(\Sigma\) in an accretion disk is given by \[
\partial_t \Sigma = \frac{3}{R} \partial_R  [R^{1 / 2} \partial_R (\nu
\Sigma R^{1 / 2})] .
\tag{20.1}\] Assume that the viscosity \(\nu\) is in the form \(\nu = \nu (\Sigma, R)\).

Introduce the quantity \(\psi = \nu \Sigma\) and consider a small perturbation \(\delta \Sigma\) in the surface density of the disk. Find the equation describing the evolution of the corresponding perturbation \(\delta \psi\) of \(\psi\).
Under what condition is the disk stable?
crumbs: 20  Accretion Disks II: Steady Disks and Spectra

title: 20  Accretion Disks II: Steady Disks and Spectra
text:
20.2 Exercises

Exercise 20.1 (Accretion-disk spectrum) Model an accretion disk as a set of concentric rings \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, N\), each with median radius \(R_i\) and radial extent \(\Delta R\). Let the disk extend from an inner radius \(R_{\mathrm{in}}\) to an outer radius \(R_{\mathrm{out}}\) and the temperature be \[
T (R) = T_{\mathrm{in}}  \left( \frac{R_{\mathrm{in}}}{R} \right)^{3 / 4} .
\tag{20.2}\] Assume that the \(i\)th ring emits as a blackbody with a fixed temperature \(T_i = T (R_i)\) \[
B_{\nu} (T) = \frac{2 h \nu^3}{c^2}  \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^{h \nu / k_B T} - 1},
\tag{20.3}\] where \(h\) is the Planck constant, \(c\) the speed of light, and \(k_B\) the Boltzmann constant.

Write a code to compute and plot the emergent spectrum from a single ring at radius \(R_i\). Plot the emergent spectrum for several radii. You can work in units in which \(k_B = h = c = 1\). You can take \(T_{\mathrm{in}} = 1\) in these units.
Write a code to compute the emergent spectrum from the full disk by summing up the contribution from each ring. Plot the resulting spectrum and discuss its physical interpretation. Verify that the spectrum approximately scales as \(\nu^{1 / 3}\) for \(T_{\mathrm{out}} \lesssim \nu \lesssim T_{\mathrm{in}}\). You can work in the same units as in the previous point. Additionally assume that \(R_{\mathrm{out}} / R_{\mathrm{in}} = 10^4\), so that \(T_{\mathrm{out}} = 10^{-3}\, T_{\mathrm{in}}\).

title: 21  Turbulence
text:
21.1 What is Turbulence?
Turbulence is the chaotic, complex motion observed in fluids across all scales, from the chaotic motion of the quark–gluon plasma produced in heavy-ion collisions (fm scale) to the motion of gas in the intracluster medium (Mpc scale). Turbulence plays an important role in many terrestrial and astrophysical flows. For example, turbulence in the interstellar medium is thought to generate overdensities that eventually grow up to become stars. Turbulence also shapes the evolution and death of stars. Turbulent flows efficiently mix fluid: think of the way in which milk and coffee mix once turbulence is generated with a spoon. Turbulent flows also efficiently dissipate kinetic energy and develop large effective shear viscosity, e.g., triggering angular momentum transport.
Despite its importance for a number of applications, including many of practical, industrial impact, and despite the fact that turbulence has been studied for more than 500 years, we still lack a rigorous theory of turbulence. The closest thing we have to a theory is Kolmogorov’s 1941 theory (K41). These notes contain an introductory-level description of K41 and some example applications. For a more in depth description, I would recommend Landau–Lifshitz Vol. 6 (Landau and Lifshitz 1987) and Pope, Turbulent Flows, 2000 (Pope 2000).

title: 21  Turbulence
text:
21.2 Kolmogorov’s Theory
Fluid motion is driven by external forces, such as gravity, which have a characteristic scale \(\ell_0\) comparable to the size of the system of interest. For example, for a star \(\ell_0 \sim R_*\), the radius of the star. The starting point of Kolmogorov’s theory is to decompose the flow velocity in some patch of the fluid \(\mathbf{v}\) into a mean flow \(\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle\) and a fluctuating component \(\mathbf{v}'\), not necessarily assumed to be small. The theory then assumes that, if the size \(\ell\) of the region under consideration is sufficiently small, \(\ell \ll \ell_0\), \(\mathbf{v}'\) is universal, at least in a statistical sense, meaning that it does not depend on the particular system, but that is set by the equations of motion.
To keep our notation simple, we set \(\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0\), meaning that \(\mathbf{v}' =\mathbf{v}\). Note that we can always set \(\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0\) by working in the appropriate reference frame, so this is not a restriction on the theory we are developing. We are also going to assume that the flow is incompressible, which is a good approximation if the velocity fluctuations are small compared to the sound speed (Chapter 9). As we will see, the velocity fluctuations become smaller at smaller scales, so this is always true at sufficiently small scales, except in shocks. The flow is then described by the Navier–Stokes equations (Chapter 18) \[
\partial_t \mathbf{v}+ (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{g}-
\frac{\nabla p}{\rho} + \nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{v}, \qquad \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{v}= 0,
\tag{21.1}\] where \(\mathbf{g}\) is some external acceleration field, typically gravity in astrophysical applications.
The equation for the evolution of the kinetic energy is obtained by multiplying Equation 21.1 by \(\mathbf{v}\): \[
\frac{1}{2}  [\partial_t v^2 + (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2] =\mathbf{g}
\cdot \mathbf{v}- \frac{1}{\rho} \nabla p \cdot \mathbf{v}+ \nu \nabla^2
\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\tag{21.2}\] Consider the first term on the RHS, representing the work done by the external force on the flow. If \(\ell \ll \ell_0\), then we can take \(\mathbf{g} \sim \mathrm{const}\) over this region and \[
\langle \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v} \rangle \sim \mathbf{g} \cdot \langle
\mathbf{v} \rangle = 0.
\tag{21.3}\] This suggests that the evolution of \(v\) for \(\ell \ll \ell_0\) is independent of the details of the external force \(\mathbf{g}\), so \(v\) can be universal. Of course, if \(\ell \sim \ell_0\), then \(\langle \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v} \rangle > 0\) in general, meaning that kinetic energy is injected at the scale \(\ell_0\) by gravity and then evolves according to Equation 21.2.
Let’s now consider the role of pressure (note that \(\rho = \mathrm{const}\)): \[
\langle \nabla p \cdot \mathbf{v} \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V \nabla p
\cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V = \frac{1}{V} \int_V [\nabla \cdot (p
\mathbf{v}) - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}] \mathrm{d} V = \frac{1}{V} \oint_S
p\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n} \mathrm{d} S = 0.
\tag{21.4}\] In the last equation we have assumed that \(\mathbf{v}\) is isotropic (no preferred direction), so \(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{n}\) is zero on average.
In a similar way, we can rewrite the average of the last term in the RHS of Equation 21.2 as \[
\int_V \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V = \oint_S \mathbf{n}
\cdot (\nabla \mathbf{v}\mathbf{v}) \mathrm{d} S - \int_V \nabla \mathbf{v}:
\nabla \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V = - \int_V | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 \mathrm{d} V .
\tag{21.5}\] This means that, on average, we can simplify the kinetic energy equation to read \[
\partial_t v^2 = 2\mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{v}- (\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2
- 2 \nu | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 .
\tag{21.6}\] As already mentioned, the first term on the RHS is responsible for energy injection. The last term describes kinetic energy dissipation. We can estimate this term as \[
\nu | \nabla \mathbf{v} |^2 \sim \nu \left( \frac{v (\ell)}{\ell} \right)^2,
\tag{21.7}\] where \(v (\ell)\) is the characteristic velocity fluctuation on a length scale \(\ell\): \[
v (\ell) = \langle | \mathbf{v} (\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{l}) -\mathbf{v}
(\mathbf{x}) | \rangle = \frac{1}{V} \int_V | \mathbf{v}
(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{l}) -\mathbf{v} (\mathbf{x}) | \mathrm{d} V.
\tag{21.8}\] We use the notation \(A \sim B\) to signify that two quantities, \(A\) and \(B\), are equal up to factors of order unity.
The quantity on the RHS of Equation 21.7 has units of power per unit mass, as expected, since it is the rate at which the kinetic energy per unit mass is dissipated. Equation 21.7 suggests that the energy is dissipated at a scale \(\ell_d\) (the dissipation or Kolmogorov scale) at which the dissipation rate is equal to the mean power of the global flow: \[
\nu \left( \frac{v (\ell_d)}{\ell_d} \right)^2 \sim \frac{v^3
(\ell_0)}{\ell_0} \Longrightarrow \ell_d \sim \ell_0  \left[
\frac{\nu}{\ell_0 v (\ell_0)} \right]^{1 / 2}  \left[ \frac{v (\ell_d)}{v
(\ell_0)} \right] = \frac{\ell_0}{\mathrm{Re}^{1 / 2}}  \left[ \frac{v
(\ell_d)}{v (\ell_0)} \right] .
\tag{21.9}\] In the previous equation, we have introduced the Reynolds number \[
\mathrm{Re} = \frac{\ell_0 v (\ell_0)}{\nu} .
\tag{21.10}\] Experimental observations of fluids in pipes suggest that turbulence sets in when \(\mathrm{Re} \gtrsim 10^3\). In astrophysical situations, \(\mathrm{Re}\) can be much larger. For example, in the interstellar medium \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 10^9\). In neutron star mergers we contend with flows having \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 10^{15}\). Consequently, Equation 21.9 implies that \(\ell_d \ll \ell_0\) for turbulent flows.
Summarizing, in our analysis of Equation 21.6 we have found that kinetic energy is injected at large scale \(\ell_0\) (first term on the RHS) and dissipated at the dissipation scale \(\ell_d \ll \ell_0\) (last term on the RHS). This means that there is a range of scales \(\ell_d \ll \ell \ll \ell_0\), the so-called inertial range, in which the dynamics is dominated by the nonlinear term \((\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2\). We can estimate it as \[
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2 \sim \frac{v^3 (\ell)}{\ell} .
\tag{21.11}\] Note that, for an incompressible flow, the nonlinear term can also be written as a divergence, \((\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2 = \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{v} v^2)\). So, by the same argument we used for the pressure, its average over a region vanishes. In other words, the nonlinear term does not create or destroy kinetic energy. Instead, it moves kinetic energy between different scales. In a steady state, the energy per unit mass and per unit time injected at the scale \(\ell_0\), \[
\mathcal{P} = \frac{v^3 (\ell_0)}{\ell_0},
\tag{21.12}\] must flow through all the scales in the inertial range, without losses, until it reaches the dissipation scale, where it is dissipated. At the scale \(\ell\), the kinetic energy per unit mass \(v^2 (\ell)\) is passed on to smaller scales in a time \(\ell / v (\ell)\), so the flux of energy is \(v^3 (\ell) / \ell\). Since this must be the same at all scales, we have \[
\frac{v^3 (\ell)}{\ell} \sim \mathcal{P} \Longrightarrow \boxed{v
(\ell) \sim (\mathcal{P} \ell)^{1/3} = v (\ell_0)  \left( \frac{\ell}{\ell_0} \right)^{1 / 3}} .
\tag{21.13}\] This result is key to the theory of turbulence and is called Kolmogorov’s second similarity hypothesis1. It has been verified many times through direct numerical simulations and experiments. Note that \(v (\ell)\) decreases at smaller scales, so the flow is subsonic at sufficiently small scales, as we anticipated.
Often this hypothesis is formulated in terms of the energy spectrum \(E (k)\). This is defined so that \(E (k) \mathrm{d} k\) is the kinetic energy per unit mass in eddies with wave numbers between \(k\) and \(k + \mathrm{d} k\): \[
\frac{1}{2} \langle | \mathbf{v} |^2 \rangle = \int_0^{\infty} E (k) \mathrm{d} k .
\tag{21.14}\] Eddies of size \(\ell\) have wave numbers \(k \sim 1 / \ell\). The kinetic energy per unit mass in eddies of size \(\sim \ell\) is the energy in a range of wave numbers of width \(\sim k\) around \(k\), so \[
v^2 (\ell) \sim k E (k) \Longrightarrow E (k) \sim \frac{v^2 (1 / k)}{k} \sim \mathcal{P}^{2/3} k^{- 5 / 3} .
\tag{21.15}\] This is the famous Kolmogorov \(k^{- 5 / 3}\) spectrum. A comparison between data and theory over about 16 orders of magnitude in scale is shown in Figure 21.2. The figure collects measurements of density fluctuations in the interstellar medium from several types of observations, with spacecraft data, including Voyager 1, at the smallest scales. It shows the three-dimensional spectrum of density fluctuations, which in Kolmogorov’s theory scales as \(k^{- 11 / 3}\). The extra factor \(k^{- 2}\) with respect to \(E (k)\) comes from the area of a shell of radius \(k\) in Fourier space. Deviations from the Kolmogorov scaling only appear at very small scales, when plasma kinetic effects become important.






Figure 21.2: Power spectrum of electron density fluctuations in the interstellar medium from several types of observations, including Voyager 1 (points), and Kolmogorov spectrum (dashed). From Lee and Lee (2019); © Springer Nature, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



A physical interpretation of the K41 model is given by the Richardson cascade (which actually predates K41). In this model, energy is injected at large scale by \(\mathbf{g}\) and dissipated at small scales by the viscosity. The nonlinear term \((\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) v^2\) couples different scales and is responsible for the transport of energy from large scale to small scale, as illustrated in Figure 21.3.






Figure 21.3: The Richardson cascade. Redrawn after Frisch (1995).



The main mechanisms for the transport of energy are vortex stretching and shear (Kelvin–Helmholtz) instabilities (Chapter 16).
We can interpret \(v^3 (\ell) / \ell\) as a term that controls the kinetic energy dissipation: \[
\frac{v^3 (\ell)}{\ell} = \frac{v^2 (\ell)}{\tau}, \qquad \tau =
\frac{\ell}{v (\ell)},
\tag{21.16}\] where \(\tau\) is the eddy turnover time, the time over which the specific kinetic energy \(v^2 (\ell)\) is transferred to smaller scales. To see this, notice that for \(\ell_d \ll \ell \ll \ell_0\), Equation 21.6 reduces to \[
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm{d} v^2 (\ell)}{\mathrm{d} t} \sim - \frac{v^2 (\ell)}{\tau}
.}
\tag{21.17}\] The constancy of \(v^3 (\ell) / \ell\) implies that the rate at which turbulence dissipates kinetic energy is independent of \(\nu\) or of the detailed form of the physical processes responsible for dissipation! Instead, it is set by the dynamics at large scale. In other words, when kinetic energy is injected by mechanical work at large scale in a turbulent flow, turbulence efficiently transports this energy to small scales (generating large velocity gradients) at which point it is dissipated. This is the reason why turbulence theory applies equally well to the flow of water around the propeller of a ship and to the motion of rarefied gas in the intergalactic medium. This finding also justifies turbulence modeling approaches used in simulations.
With Kolmogorov’s second similarity law, we can provide a better estimate for \(\ell_d\). Using Equation 21.13 into Equation 21.9, we can eliminate \(v (\ell_d)\) to find \[
\boxed{\ell_d \sim \left( \frac{\nu}{\ell_0 v (\ell_0)} \right)^{3 / 4}
\ell_0 = \mathrm{Re}^{- 3 / 4} \ell_0} .
\tag{21.18}\] This shows that the scale separation in developed turbulence can be enormous. A direct numerical simulation needs to resolve all scales between \(\ell_d\) and \(\ell_0\), so it needs \((\ell_0 / \ell_d)^3\) grid cells. It also needs a number of time steps \(\sim \ell_0 / \ell_d\), because the time step must be smaller than the time it takes for the flow to cross one cell. So the cost of a direct numerical simulation scales as \[
\mathrm{cost} \sim \left( \frac{\ell_0}{\ell_d} \right)^4 \sim \mathrm{Re}^3,
\tag{21.19}\] which makes it impossible to directly simulate very turbulent flows. The largest simulations today have about \(10^4\) grid cells in each direction, so they can reach \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 10^5\). To study flows with higher Reynolds numbers, it is necessary to give up the idea of simulating all scales in the flow and instead resort to modeling the dynamics below the numerical grid scale using turbulence theory.






TipExample



Consider the wind in the atmosphere of the Earth, with \(\ell_0 \sim 1\,\mathrm{km}\) and \(v (\ell_0) \sim 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\). The kinematic viscosity of air is \(\nu \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\), so \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 7 \times 10^8\). The dissipation scale is \(\ell_d \sim \mathrm{Re}^{-3/4} \ell_0 \sim 0.2\,\mathrm{mm}\), and a direct numerical simulation would cost \(\sim \mathrm{Re}^3 \sim 10^{26}\), many orders of magnitude beyond what is possible. Even a cup of coffee stirred with a spoon, with \(\ell_0 \sim 3\,\mathrm{cm}\), \(v (\ell_0) \sim 0.1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and \(\nu \approx 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\), has \(\mathrm{Re} \sim 3000\) and \(\ell_d \sim 70\,\mu\mathrm{m}\).


Before we discuss some applications of Kolmogorov’s theory, it is worth mentioning its limitations. Astrophysical flows are often supersonic and highly magnetized. Compressibility and magnetic fields can have a profound role on the turbulent cascade. Shocks can dissipate kinetic energy directly at large scales (Chapter 11). Magnetic fields can give rise to inverse cascade whereby small magnetic field structures self-organize into large scale ordered fields (turbulent dynamo process, Chapter 24). The study of compressible, magnetized turbulence is still an active area of research and beyond the scope of this course. However, even for compressible, magnetized flows, Kolmogorov’s theory provides a good starting point and can often be applied directly.

title: 21  Turbulence
section: 21.3 Shredding of Clouds in a Turbulent Flow
text:
21.3 Shredding of Clouds in a Turbulent Flow
Consider a cloud of gas of radius \(R\), for example a patch of material enriched by a supernova, that is carried by the turbulent flow of the interstellar medium. We want to compute the evolution of \(R\) with time. We will consider three cases, illustrated in Figure 21.4.






Figure 21.4: Distortion of a cloud in a turbulent medium. The three different cases are \(R \sim \ell_d\) (case A), \(\ell_d \ll R \ll \ell_0\) (case B), and \(R \sim \ell_0\) (case C).



If \(R \sim \ell_d\) the particles in the cloud will undergo Brownian random motion, so, as in the case of the random diffusion of photons (Chapter 6), we have \(R \sim t^{1 / 2}\). If \(R \sim \ell_0\), then the cloud is primarily advected by the mean flow. The edges of the cloud will still experience random diffusion, so \(R \sim t^{1 / 2}\), but with an effective diffusion coefficient \(\sim \ell_0 v (\ell_0)\), which is much larger than the molecular one. Indeed, eddies of size \(\ell_0\) act like particles with mean free path \(\ell_0\) (compare with Equation 1.1) moving with velocity \(v (\ell_0)\). We will see that this is the same estimate used for the turbulent viscosity.
The more interesting case is when \(\ell_d \ll R \ll \ell_0\). In this case, the cloud undergoes rapid distortion: \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} R}{\mathrm{d} t} \sim v \sim R^{1 / 3} \Longrightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d}
R^2}{\mathrm{d} t} \sim Rv \sim R^{4 / 3} .
\tag{21.20}\] This is Richardson’s 4/3-law. We can use the second Kolmogorov similarity hypothesis to find the time dependence for \(R\): \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} R}{\mathrm{d} t} \sim v (\ell_0)  \left( \frac{R}{\ell_0} \right)^{1 / 3}
\Longrightarrow R^{2 / 3} \sim \frac{v (\ell_0)}{\ell_0^{1 / 3}} t
\Longrightarrow R^2 \sim \mathcal{P} t^3 .
\tag{21.21}\] In other words, \(R \propto t^{3 / 2}\): the cloud grows faster and faster, because, as it grows, it is torn apart by larger and faster eddies.
Turbulence significantly accelerates the mixing of new elements produced in supernovae with the interstellar medium, where they can subsequently form new stars, planets, and people.






TipExample



Consider the metals ejected by a supernova into the warm interstellar medium, with \(T \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(n \sim 1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). The turbulence in the interstellar medium is driven on scales \(\ell_0 \sim 100\,\mathrm{pc}\), with \(v (\ell_0) \sim 10\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). So turbulence mixes the metals over \(\sim 100\,\mathrm{pc}\) in a time \(\sim \ell_0 / v (\ell_0) \sim 10\,\mathrm{Myr}\). How long would it take without turbulence? The mean free path of the particles in this gas is \(\lambda \sim 10^{10}\,\mathrm{m}\), and their thermal velocity is \(v_{\mathrm{th}} \sim 10\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\), so the diffusion coefficient is \(D \sim \lambda v_{\mathrm{th}} / 3 \sim 3 \times 10^{13}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\) (Chapter 6). Molecular diffusion would take \(\sim \ell_0^2 / D \sim 10^{16}\,\mathrm{yr}\), much longer than the age of the Universe. Note also that the ratio of the two timescales is \(\ell_0 v (\ell_0) / D \sim 10^9\), which is the Reynolds number of the interstellar medium.

title: 21  Turbulence
text:
21.4 Turbulence Modeling: Reynolds Stress
Directly simulating turbulent flows is impossible, so one of the goals of turbulence theory is to develop effective strategies to deal with unresolved turbulence in simulations. Commonly used models are the Reynolds averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) and Large-Eddy Simulations (LES) frameworks. Without going into the details, both approaches are based on the general idea of coarse graining the fluid equations. That is, we replace \(\mathbf{v}\) with a suitable average \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\) and try to come up with equations for it. If we coarse grain the Navier–Stokes equations, we find: \[
\partial_t \mathbf{v}+ \nabla \cdot \left(\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ \frac{p}{\rho} \mathbf{I} \right)
=\mathbf{g}+ \nu \nabla^2 \mathbf{v} \longrightarrow \partial_t
\bar{\mathbf{v}} + \nabla \cdot \overline{\left(\mathbf{v} \otimes
\mathbf{v}+ \frac{p}{\rho} \mathbf{I} \right)} = \bar{\mathbf{g}} + \nu \nabla^2 \bar{\mathbf{v}}
.
\tag{21.22}\] These equations are exact, but unfortunately not closed, because we do not have a way to compute \(\overline{\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}}\) from \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\). This is the so-called turbulence closure problem. To work around this, we define the Reynolds stress tensor \[
\mathbf{R}= \overline{\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}} - \bar{\mathbf{v}}
\otimes \bar{\mathbf{v}}
\tag{21.23}\] and the momentum equation becomes: \[
\partial_t  \bar{\mathbf{v}} + \nabla \cdot \left(\bar{\mathbf{v}}
\otimes \bar{\mathbf{v}} +\mathbf{R}+ \frac{\bar{p}}{\rho} \mathbf{I} \right) =
\bar{\mathbf{g}} + \nu \nabla^2 \bar{\mathbf{v}} .
\tag{21.24}\] Equation 21.24 is the momentum equation for a fluid that has velocity equal to \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\), pressure \(\bar{p}\), and a new component of the stress tensor \(\mathbf{R}\). Because \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\) is some average of the true velocity, Equation 21.24 can be solved on a coarse computational mesh. The problem of modeling turbulence is now reduced to that of finding a good model for \(\mathbf{R}\). There are many such models in the literature.
The simplest model, which is also the most commonly used for astrophysical applications, is the turbulent (or eddy) viscosity model. Accordingly, one takes \[
\mathbf{R}= \frac{1}{3} (\mathrm{tr} \mathbf{R}) \mathbf{I} - \nu_T  (\nabla \bar{\mathbf{v}}+ \nabla^T \bar{\mathbf{v}}) .
\tag{21.25}\] The first term is needed because \(\mathrm{tr} \mathbf{R} = \overline{|\mathbf{v} - \bar{\mathbf{v}}|^2}\) is positive, while the trace of the second term vanishes for an incompressible flow. The first term is isotropic, so it acts like an additional pressure, the turbulent pressure \(\rho \mathrm{tr} \mathbf{R} / 3\), which we include in \(\bar{p}\). We will meet the turbulent pressure again in the in-class worksheet. With this choice, and using \(\nabla \cdot \bar{\mathbf{v}} = 0\), Equation 21.24 becomes \[
\partial_t  \bar{\mathbf{v}} + \nabla \cdot \left(\bar{\mathbf{v}}
\otimes \bar{\mathbf{v}} + \frac{\bar{p}}{\rho} \mathbf{I} \right) = \bar{\mathbf{g}} + (\nu
+ \nu_T) \nabla^2 \bar{\mathbf{v}} .
\tag{21.26}\] That is, turbulence is described simply as a dissipative process and \(\nu_T\) is an effective turbulent viscosity. The turbulent viscosity, in turn, is often obtained using dimensional analysis arguments: \[
\nu_T = \ell_{\mathrm{mix}} V,
\tag{21.27}\] where \(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\) is a characteristic length, also called the mixing length, and \(V\) is a characteristic velocity. For example, in accretion disk theory (Chapter 19), \(V = c_s\) and \(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\) is taken to be proportional to the scale-height of the disk \(H\): \[
\ell_{\mathrm{mix}} = \alpha H = \alpha \frac{c_s}{\Omega} \Longrightarrow
\nu_T = \alpha \frac{c_s^2}{\Omega},
\tag{21.28}\] where \(\Omega\) is the angular velocity of the flow. This is the so-called \(\alpha\)-viscosity model.
For shear flows along \(x\) with shear in the \(y\)-direction, one can use the velocity gradient instead of \(V\): \[
\nu_T = \ell_{\mathrm{mix}}^2  \left| \frac{\partial \bar{v}_x}{\partial
y} \right| .
\tag{21.29}\] This is Prandtl’s mixing-length model. The Smagorinsky model, which is often used in large-eddy simulations, is a generalization of this model, in which \(\ell_{\mathrm{mix}}\) is proportional to the size of the grid cells and \(| \partial \bar{v}_x / \partial y |\) is replaced by the magnitude of the rate of strain of \(\bar{\mathbf{v}}\).
For industrial applications, a popular strategy is to solve additional equations for \(\partial_t \mathbf{R}\), with coefficients calibrated to experimental (wind tunnel) results. More sophisticated “subgrid” models have also been proposed for astrophysical applications, but their detailed description is beyond the scope of this course. See Brandenburg and Nordlund (2011) for more information.
Another popular approach is the Implicit Large-Eddy Simulations (ILES) method, in which \(\mathbf{R}\) is not included explicitly in the equations. Instead, a numerical scheme is chosen that has a numerical viscosity \(\nu_{\mathrm{num}} \approx \nu_T\). This approach is often effective, but ILES simulations need to be accompanied by careful resolution studies to assess their reliability, because accurate results can only be obtained if a sufficient portion of the inertial range is resolved by the simulations.






Figure 21.5: Density in a high-resolution simulation of compressible turbulence in the interstellar medium (Federrath et al. 2021), as shown on the cover of Nature Astronomy, April 2021. © Springer Nature, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.

title: 21  Turbulence
text:
21.5 In-class worksheet
Turbulence in Core-Collapse Supernovae. We construct here a simplified model showing the role of turbulence in aiding shock revival in core-collapse supernovae.

Consider a steady accretion shock near the protoneutron star. Assume that the in-falling material is cold and that the velocity downstream of the shock is small. Show that the Rankine–Hugoniot conditions (Chapter 11) simplify to \[
p_2 \approx \rho_1 v_1^2, \qquad \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = \frac{\Gamma +
1}{\Gamma - 1},
\tag{21.30}\] where all quantities have their usual meaning.
Find the equilibrium pressure \(p_2\) needed to support the accretion shock at a fixed radius \(r_s\), given the mass of the protoneutron star \(M\), and the accretion rate \(\dot{M}\). Assume that the gas upstream of the shock falls freely from rest at infinity.
Consider angular averages of the flow, e.g., \[
\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle = \frac{1}{4 \pi} \oint \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d}
\Omega .
\tag{21.31}\] Decompose the velocity downstream of the shock as the sum of an average (laminar) component \(\langle \mathbf{v} \rangle\) and a turbulent fluctuating component \(\delta \mathbf{v}\), \(\mathbf{v}= \langle \mathbf{v} \rangle + \delta \mathbf{v}\). Assume that \(\rho\) depends only on radius, so that \(\langle \rho \mathbf{v} \rangle = \rho \langle \mathbf{v} \rangle\). Define the Reynolds stress as \[
\mathbf{R}= \langle \delta \mathbf{v} \otimes \delta \mathbf{v} \rangle
.
\tag{21.32}\] Show that the conservation of momentum across the shock can be written as \[
\rho_2  \langle v_2 \rangle^2 + \rho_2 R_{r r} + p_2 = \rho_1 v_1^2 .
\tag{21.33}\]
Define the specific turbulent kinetic energy as \[
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{turb}} = \frac{1}{2}  | \delta \mathbf{v} |^2 =
\frac{1}{2}  (R_{rr} + R_{\theta \theta} + R_{\phi \phi}) .
\tag{21.34}\] Assume that \(R_{rr} = R_{\theta \theta} + R_{\phi \phi}\) and show that with this definition Equation 21.33 can be written as \[
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_2  \langle v_2 \rangle^2 \\
& \quad + \rho_2  [(\Gamma_{\mathrm{turb}} - 1)
\varepsilon_{\mathrm{turb}} + (\Gamma - 1) \varepsilon_2] \\
& \quad = \rho_1 v_1^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{21.35}\] What is the effective adiabatic index of turbulence \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{turb}}\)?
At early times, before the turbulence develops, the accretion shock is stalled at a radius \(r_s\). What happens to the shock, once turbulence develops?

title: 21  Turbulence
text:
21.6 Exercises

Exercise 21.1 (Brownian and Lévy random walks) Consider the random walk of a particle. At each step \(i\) a particle at position \(\mathbf{x}_i\) jumps to position \[
\mathbf{x}_{i + 1} =\mathbf{x}_i + R_i \mathbf{d}_i,
\tag{21.36}\] where \(\mathbf{d}_i\) is a random direction on the sphere (uniform in \(\phi\) and \(\cos \theta\)) and \(R_i\) is either

a fixed constant (Brownian random walk); or
it has a Pareto distribution \(p (R) \sim R^{- 1 - \beta}\), for a given \(\beta\) (Lévy random walk).

The Brownian random walk can be used to model ordinary diffusion process, while Lévy random walks can be used to model effective diffusion and mixing in a turbulent flow (superdiffusion).
Write a code to simulate Brownian and Lévy random walks with \(\beta = 2 / 3\), then compute the median of the traveled distance \(D_N = | \mathbf{x}_N -\mathbf{x}_0 |\) as a function of \(N\) for the two. For \(\beta < 1\) the mean length of a step is infinite, so the median is a better measure than the mean.
Show that \(D_N \sim N^{\gamma}\) and estimate \(\gamma\) in the two cases. Compare the results with the predictions from Kolmogorov theory for diffusion in a turbulent flow (\(R \sim t^{3 / 2}\)). Explain why the Lévy random walk gives \(D_N \sim N^{1 / \beta}\).
[You can use numpy.random.uniform and numpy.random.pareto to generate \(R_i\) and \(\mathbf{d}_i\).]
