This is not relevant to astrophysical applications, because astrophysical plasmas become collisionless at small scale, i.e., they do not behave like a fluid anymore. However, Kolmogorov’s theory still applies for \(\ell \gg \ell_d\).↩︎

title: 22  Introduction to Plasma
text: 22.1 Electromagnetism Refresher

title: 22  Introduction to Plasma
text:
22.1.1 Lorentz Force and Maxwell Equations
Most of the baryonic matter in the Universe is in the form of plasma, a state of matter characterized by large electrical conductivity and charge mobility. Not surprisingly, plasma physics plays an important role in many astrophysical systems. Before we are ready to discuss plasmas, or even before we can precisely state what plasma is, it is a good idea to refresh some key concepts from electromagnetism. We will write the equations of electromagnetism in SI units, as in the rest of these notes.
The starting point for electromagnetism is the observation that some particles, electrons and protons, are endowed with electric charge, which is an intrinsic property, like mass. When two lumps of matter with net charge \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) are placed at a distance \(r\), the two experience a force \[
F = \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2} .
\tag{22.1}\] The force is repulsive if \(Q_1 Q_2 > 0\) and attractive if \(Q_1 Q_2 < 0\). In SI units, charge is measured in coulomb (\(1\,\mathrm{C} = 1\,\mathrm{A\,s}\)), and the constant \(\epsilon_0\), called the vacuum permittivity, is \[
\epsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{- 12}\,\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}} .
\tag{22.2}\] The charge of the electron is \[
e = 1.602176634 \times 10^{- 19}\,\mathrm{C} .
\tag{22.3}\] The Coulomb force on particle 2 can also be thought of as the effect on particle 2 of an electrostatic field produced by particle 1. In a system of coordinates centered on particle 1, the electrostatic field produced by particle 1 is \[
\mathbf{E}= \frac{Q_1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2}  \hat{\mathbf{r}}
\tag{22.4}\] and the force on particle 2 is given by \[
\mathbf{F}= \frac{Q_1 Q_2}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2}  \hat{\mathbf{r}} = Q_2 \mathbf{E}.
\tag{22.5}\] In general, a charged particle with charge \(Q\) moving in an electromagnetic field experiences the so-called Lorentz force: \[
\mathbf{F}= Q ( \mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} ) .
\tag{22.6}\] The electric \(\mathbf{E}\) and magnetic \(\mathbf{B}\) fields are defined by Equation 22.6, as the force per unit charge on a particle at rest, and the additional force on a moving particle. Their units are \[
[\mathbf{E}] = \mathrm{N\,C^{-1}} = \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}, \qquad [\mathbf{B}] = \mathrm{N\,s\,C^{-1}\,m^{-1}} = \mathrm{T}\ (\mathrm{tesla}) .
\tag{22.7}\] In astronomy, magnetic fields are customarily measured in gauss, with \(1\,\mathrm{G} = 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{T}\). We will give field strengths in tesla, followed by their value in gauss. Note that \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(c \mathbf{B}\), where \(c\) is the speed of light, have the same units. This makes sense, because electric and magnetic fields are different manifestations of a single field: the electromagnetic field, as is revealed by special relativity. The electromagnetic field can be found as solution of the Maxwell’s field equations \[
\begin{array}{ll}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= \dfrac{q}{\epsilon_0}, & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}= 0,\\
\nabla \times \mathbf{E}= - \dfrac{\partial
\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}, & \nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \mu_0
\mathbf{j}+ \mu_0 \epsilon_0 \dfrac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} .
\end{array}
\tag{22.8}\] In the previous equation, \(q\) is the charge density, \(\mathbf{j}\) the current density, and \(\mu_0 \approx 4 \pi \times 10^{- 7}\,\mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}\) is the vacuum permeability. The two constants are related to the speed of light by \(\mu_0 \epsilon_0 = 1 / c^2\). The equations in the first row are called the Gauss law for electric and magnetic fields. The second two equations are the Faraday, or induction, equation (left column), and the Ampère–Maxwell law (right column).






NoteGaussian units



Most astrophysics texts and papers, including Kulsrud (2005), write the equations of electromagnetism in Gaussian (CGS) units. In these units there is no \(\epsilon_0\) or \(\mu_0\), charge is measured in statcoulomb, and \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) have the same units. To translate a formula from Gaussian to SI units, replace \(B / \sqrt{4 \pi}\) with \(B / \sqrt{\mu_0}\), \(e^2\) with \(e^2 / (4 \pi \epsilon_0)\), and \(\mathbf{E}\) with \(\sqrt{4 \pi \epsilon_0}\, \mathbf{E}\), and write every \(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} / c\) as \(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}\). For example, the Gaussian plasma frequency \(\sqrt{4 \pi n e^2 / m_e}\) becomes \(\sqrt{n e^2 / (\epsilon_0 m_e)}\) (Equation 22.50), and the Gaussian magnetic pressure \(B^2 / 8 \pi\) becomes \(B^2 / 2 \mu_0\).




22.1.2 Electrostatics
If the fields do not depend on time, the Maxwell equations for \(\mathbf{E}\) simplify to \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= \frac{q}{\epsilon_0}, \qquad \nabla \times \mathbf{E}= 0.
\tag{22.9}\] The second equation tells us that \(\mathbf{E}= - \nabla \Phi\), where \(\Phi\) is the electrostatic potential. The latter satisfies the Poisson equation \[
\nabla^2 \Phi = - \frac{q}{\epsilon_0} .
\tag{22.10}\] Apart from a minus sign and the constant, \(1 / \epsilon_0\) instead of \(4 \pi G\), this is the same equation satisfied by the gravitational potential (Chapter 7).
The force experienced by a charge \(Q\) in an electrostatic field is \[
\mathbf{F}= Q\mathbf{E}= - Q \nabla \Phi .
\tag{22.11}\]






TipExample



Consider the electrostatic potential generated by a spherical distribution of charge density \(q\) and the force experienced by an electron outside the sphere, as illustrated in Figure 22.1.






Figure 22.1: Spherical distribution of charge.



The radial component of the force experienced by an electron, which has charge \(- e\), at a distance \(r\) from a charged sphere, with charge density \(q\), is given by: \[
F_r = e \partial_r \Phi .
\tag{22.12}\] From the Poisson equation \[
\nabla \cdot \nabla \Phi = - \frac{q}{\epsilon_0} .
\tag{22.13}\] Integrating both sides over a sphere of radius \(r\), we find \[
- \frac{1}{\epsilon_0} \int_V q \mathrm{d} V = - \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0} = \int_V \nabla \cdot \nabla \Phi
\mathrm{d} V.
\tag{22.14}\] The RHS gives (using the divergence theorem) \[
\int_V \nabla \cdot \nabla \Phi \mathrm{d} V = \int_S \nabla \Phi \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{r}} \mathrm{d} S = 4 \pi r^2 \partial_r \Phi \Longrightarrow
\partial_r \Phi = - \frac{Q}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2} \Longrightarrow F_r = - \frac{Qe}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r^2} .
\tag{22.15}\] So the electron is attracted by the sphere if \(Q > 0\), and repelled if \(Q < 0\).


Even though electrostatic and gravitational forces have a similar mathematical structure, these forces are very different for two reasons. First, gravity is always attractive, because no forms of matter are known to possess negative mass, while electric charge can be positive or negative and objects of similar charge repel each other. Second, gravity is a very weak force, as we explore with the next example.






TipExample



Consider a proton on the surface of the Sun. It is subject to an attractive gravitational force: \[
F_g = - \frac{GM_{\odot} m_p}{R_{\odot }^2} .
\tag{22.16}\] The proton is also subject to an electrostatic force: \[
F_e = \frac{Q_{\odot} e}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 R_{\odot}^2},
\tag{22.17}\] where \(Q_{\odot} \approx \frac{M_{\odot}}{m_p} \delta e\) is the net charge of the Sun, and \(\delta = (N_p - N_e) / N_p\) is the fractional charge imbalance. Gravity and electrostatic forces balance each other when \[
\delta = \frac{4 \pi \epsilon_0 G m_p^2}{e^2} \sim 10^{- 36} .
\tag{22.18}\] The Sun must be very close to neutral, because even a small charge imbalance would cause particles of the same charge as the Sun to be evaporated from the surface.


The argument we have just made for the Sun applies to most astrophysical systems. This implies that the charge imbalance in astronomical objects must be very small. In other words, they are quasi-neutral. As we will see shortly, quasi-neutrality is one of the key characteristics an ionized gas must have to be considered to be plasma. At this point, it is important to remark that, while we will be concerned only with systems that have zero net charge, these systems can still contain electric currents, which give rise to magnetic fields and internal stresses via the Lorentz force.






NoteGoing further: Conservation Laws in Electrodynamics



If we take the divergence of Ampère’s law we find \[
\epsilon_0 \frac{\partial \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} +
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}= 0.
\tag{22.19}\] Using Gauss’ law \[
\frac{\partial q}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}= 0.
\tag{22.20}\] So the charge density satisfies a continuity equation, just like the mass density for a fluid (Equation 1.15). In other words, the Maxwell equations imply charge conservation.
It is also possible to show that the Maxwell equations imply conservation of the energy in the electromagnetic field. To see this, consider the work done by the electromagnetic field on a fluid with charge density \(q\) and velocity \(\mathbf{v}\). The Lorentz force per unit volume is \[
\mathbf{f}= q ( \mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} ) .
\tag{22.21}\] So the work per unit volume is (using \(\mathbf{j}= q\mathbf{v}\) and Ampère’s law) \[
w =\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}= q\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{v}=\mathbf{E}
\cdot \mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{\mu_0} (\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot
\mathbf{E}- \epsilon_0 \mathbf{E} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} .
\tag{22.22}\] Using the vector identity \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot (\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) =\mathbf{B} \cdot (\nabla \times
\mathbf{E}) - \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B})
\tag{22.23}\] and \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} = \frac{1}{2}
\dfrac{\partial E^2}{\partial t},
\tag{22.24}\] we can write \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{\mu_0} [\mathbf{B} \cdot
(\nabla \times \mathbf{E}) - \nabla \cdot (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B})] -
\frac{\epsilon_0}{2}  \frac{\partial E^2}{\partial t} .
\tag{22.25}\] We can use Faraday’s law to get rid of \(\nabla \times \mathbf{E}\) to rewrite the last equation as \[
\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left( \frac{\epsilon_0 E^2}{2} + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right) + \nabla \cdot
\left( \frac{1}{\mu_0} \mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B} \right) = -\mathbf{E}
\cdot \mathbf{j}.
\tag{22.26}\] We can recognize that this is a conservation law in the form \[
\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{EM}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{S}=
-\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{j}.
\tag{22.27}\] The last term is the work done by the electric field, so we can interpret \(u_{\mathrm{EM}} = \tfrac{1}{2} \epsilon_0 E^2 + \tfrac{B^2}{2 \mu_0}\) as the energy in the electromagnetic field and the vector \(\mathbf{S}= \frac{1}{\mu_0} \mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\), called the Poynting flux, as the flux of electromagnetic energy. Equation 22.26 is also called the Poynting theorem. As we will see in Chapter 23, the equation for energy conservation for a plasma is just the sum of the energy conservation equations for the matter, which we already know as the energy equation (Chapter 6), and the energy conservation equation for the electromagnetic field.




22.1.3 Electromagnetic Waves
The propagation of electromagnetic waves in vacuum can be studied with a similar formalism as that used to study sound waves (Chapter 9). Actually, since Maxwell equations are linear, the derivation of the dispersion relation for electromagnetic waves is simpler than that for sound waves. The starting point are the Maxwell equations in vacuum: \[
\begin{array}{lll}
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= 0, &  & \nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}= 0,\\
\nabla \times \mathbf{E}= - \dfrac{\partial
\mathbf{B}}{\partial t}, &  & \nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \dfrac{1}{c^2}
\dfrac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} .
\end{array}
\tag{22.28}\] We look for solutions in the form \[
\mathbf{E} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k}
\cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}, \qquad \mathbf{B} (t, \mathbf{x}) =
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} .
\tag{22.29}\] Inserting this ansatz into the first row of Equation 22.28, we obtain \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= 0 \Longrightarrow \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} = 0
\Longrightarrow \mathbf{k} \perp \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0
\tag{22.30}\] and, similarly, \(\mathbf{k} \perp \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0\). This means that, differently from sound waves, electromagnetic waves in vacuum are transverse, meaning that \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are perpendicular to the direction of propagation of the wave.
From Faraday’s law, we obtain that \[
\mathrm{i} \omega  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot
\mathbf{x}- \omega t)} = \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0
\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)} \Longrightarrow
\omega  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 =\mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\tag{22.31}\] This implies that \(\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 \perp \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0\). From Ampère’s law, we obtain \[
\mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = - \frac{\omega}{c^2}
\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\tag{22.32}\] Substituting Equation 22.32 into Equation 22.31, we obtain (using the properties of the double vector product) \[
\omega  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = - \frac{c^2}{\omega} \mathbf{k} \times
(\mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0) = \cancel{- \frac{c^2}{\omega} \mathbf{k}
(\mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0)} + \frac{c^2}{\omega} k^2
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = \frac{c^2}{\omega} k^2  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0
\Longrightarrow \boxed{\omega^2 = c^2 k^2} .
\tag{22.33}\] So electromagnetic waves satisfy the same dispersion relation as sound waves (Equation 9.18), but with \(c\), the speed of light, instead of the sound speed \(c_s\).

title: 22  Introduction to Plasma
text:
22.2 Plasma

22.2.1 What is a Plasma?
Consider a quasi-neutral gas made of electrons and ions. Assume that, due to a thermal fluctuation, a small overdensity of electrons \(\delta n\) is created in a region with characteristic size \(L\). How large can this fluctuation be?






Figure 22.2: Schematic representation of an overdensity of electrons.



The electrostatic potential created by this overdensity is of order \[
\delta \Phi \sim \frac{L^2 e \delta n}{\epsilon_0} .
\tag{22.34}\] The potential energy of each electron is \[
e \delta \Phi \sim \frac{L^2 e^2 \delta n}{\epsilon_0} .
\tag{22.35}\] Their thermal energy is \(\sim k_B T\) (in thermodynamic equilibrium). Thermal fluctuations should have potential energy comparable to the thermal energy, so \[
\frac{L^2 e^2 \delta n}{\epsilon_0} \sim k_B T \Longrightarrow \frac{\delta n}{n} \sim
\frac{1}{L^2}  \left( \frac{\epsilon_0 k_B T}{ne^2} \right) =: \left(
\frac{\lambda_D}{L} \right)^2,
\tag{22.36}\] where \(n\) is the density of free electrons (we will also write it as \(n_e\)) and we have introduced the Debye length \[
\boxed{\lambda_D = \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon_0 k_B T}{ne^2}} .}
\tag{22.37}\] The Debye length is a characteristic length scale for charge fluctuations in the gas. Over scales \(L \gg \lambda_D\), one can assume that the medium is neutral, if the density of the gas is sufficiently high.
To see this, consider again a uniform gas of electrons and ions. The ion masses are of order \(A m_p \approx 1836 A m_e\), so if ions and electrons have on average the same kinetic energy, as would be expected in equilibrium, \(v_{\mathrm{ions}} \ll v_e\). To a first approximation, we can consider the ions to be static and immersed in a sea of electrons. If electrons are abundant, each ion will then be surrounded by a sea of electrons, which effectively shield its charge hiding it from the other ions, as shown in Figure 22.3.






Figure 22.3: Electron cloud around an ion of charge \(Q\).



It turns out that, in this situation, the electrostatic potential around the ion is \[
\Phi (r) = \frac{Q}{4 \pi \epsilon_0 r} \mathrm{e}^{- r / \lambda_D},
\tag{22.38}\] where \(\lambda_D\) is the Debye length (see the box below). In other words, the Debye length is also the characteristic screening length. However, screening can only take place if electrons are sufficiently mobile to screen each ion. To quantify this, we define the plasma parameter: \[
\Lambda = \frac{4}{3} \pi n \lambda_D^3 = \frac{4 \pi}{3 e^3}  (\epsilon_0 k_B
T)^{3 / 2} n^{- 1 / 2} .
\tag{22.39}\] The plasma parameter is just the number of electrons in each Debye sphere. We say that an ionized gas for which \(\lambda_D \ll L\) and \(\Lambda \gg 1\) is a plasma. Typical plasma parameters for astrophysical systems are given in Table 22.1. As we can see, astrophysical plasmas span a tremendous range in scales.



Table 22.1: Temperature, free electron density, Debye length, and plasma parameters for various systems. The electrons in protoneutron stars and white dwarfs are degenerate (and, in protoneutron stars, relativistic), so for these systems the values computed with the classical formulas are only indicative.

NoteGoing further: Debye Screening



We can derive Equation 22.38 as follows. Consider an ion of charge \(Q\) at the origin, surrounded by electrons with temperature \(T\) and average density \(n_e\), and by other ions, which we assume to have uniform charge density \(e n_e\), so that the plasma is neutral on average. In thermal equilibrium, the electrons follow the Boltzmann distribution. An electron has potential energy \(- e \Phi\), so \[
n (r) = n_e \mathrm{e}^{e \Phi / k_B T} \approx n_e \left( 1 + \frac{e \Phi}{k_B T} \right),
\tag{22.40}\] where we have assumed \(| e \Phi | \ll k_B T\), which is true sufficiently far from the ion. The charge density is then \[
q = e n_e - e n (r) = - \frac{n_e e^2}{k_B T} \Phi ,
\tag{22.41}\] and the Poisson equation (Equation 22.10) becomes \[
\nabla^2 \Phi = \frac{n_e e^2}{\epsilon_0 k_B T} \Phi = \frac{\Phi}{\lambda_D^2} .
\tag{22.42}\] For a spherically symmetric potential, \(\nabla^2 \Phi = \frac{1}{r} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 (r \Phi)}{\mathrm{d} r^2}\), so \(r \Phi\) satisfies \(\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 (r \Phi)}{\mathrm{d} r^2} = \frac{r \Phi}{\lambda_D^2}\). The solution that does not grow at large \(r\) is \(r \Phi = A \mathrm{e}^{- r / \lambda_D}\). Close to the ion, the potential must be that of the ion alone, \(\Phi \approx Q / (4 \pi \epsilon_0 r)\), so \(A = Q / (4 \pi \epsilon_0)\), and we recover Equation 22.38.




22.2.2 When is a Plasma a Fluid?
In Chapter 1 we have seen that a gas can be treated as a fluid if the mean free path \(\lambda\) of its particles is small compared to the scales of interest. In a plasma, the particles interact via the Coulomb force. Two particles are strongly deflected if they come so close that their electrostatic energy is comparable to their thermal energy, \(e^2 / (4 \pi \epsilon_0 r) \sim k_B T\). This gives a cross section \(\sigma \sim \pi [e^2 / (4 \pi \epsilon_0 k_B T)]^2\), and a mean free path \(\lambda \sim 1 / (n \sigma)\). Many weak collisions at larger distances make the particles lose their direction somewhat faster, and a more careful calculation gives \[
\lambda \approx 100\,\mathrm{m} \left( \frac{T}{1\,\mathrm{K}} \right)^2 \left( \frac{n}{1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}} \right)^{-1} .
\tag{22.43}\] Note that \(\lambda\) increases very quickly with temperature: hot plasmas are almost collisionless.
Magnetic fields change this picture. A particle with charge \(Q\) and mass \(m\) moving with velocity \(v\) perpendicular to a magnetic field \(B\) experiences a Lorentz force \(|Q| v B\) perpendicular to its velocity. So it moves on a circle around the field lines, with radius \(r_L\) given by \[
\frac{m v^2}{r_L} = | Q | v B \Longrightarrow r_L = \frac{m v}{| Q | B} .
\tag{22.44}\] \(r_L\) is called the Larmor radius, or gyroradius. In other words, particles cannot move freely across the magnetic field lines, even if they never collide. On scales much larger than \(r_L\), a magnetized plasma behaves like a fluid in the directions perpendicular to the magnetic field. Along the field lines, instead, particles can travel a distance \(\sim \lambda\). This is why magnetohydrodynamics (Chapter 23) works well even in plasmas in which collisions are rare. However, processes along the field lines, such as heat conduction, can be very different from those in an ordinary gas.






TipExample



Consider the warm interstellar medium, with \(T \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\), \(n \sim 1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), and \(B \sim 0.3\,\mathrm{nT}\) (\(3\,\mu\mathrm{G}\)). From Equation 22.43, \(\lambda \sim 10^{10}\,\mathrm{m}\), which is much smaller than the scales of interest, \(\sim 1\,\mathrm{pc} \approx 3 \times 10^{16}\,\mathrm{m}\). A thermal proton has velocity \(v \sim \sqrt{k_B T / m_p} \approx 9\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\), so its Larmor radius is \(r_L \approx 300\,\mathrm{km}\), even smaller.
The solar wind close to the Earth is different. It has \(T \sim 10^5\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(n \sim 5\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), so \(\lambda \sim 2 \times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}\), about the distance between the Earth and the Sun. The solar wind is essentially collisionless! However, the magnetic field is \(B \sim 5\,\mathrm{nT}\) (\(5 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{G}\)), so a thermal proton has \(r_L \approx 60\,\mathrm{km}\). On large scales, the solar wind can still be described as a magnetized fluid.




22.2.3 Cold Plasma Approximation
The cold plasma approximation is used to study the propagation of electromagnetic waves, particularly radio waves, in the interstellar medium. As the name suggests, in the cold plasma approximation we ignore the thermal motion of the electrons. We also take the ions to be stationary. Let’s consider the propagation of an electromagnetic wave through such a medium, as illustrated in Figure 22.4.






Figure 22.4: Lorentz force experienced by an electron due to a passing electromagnetic wave.



The Lorentz force experienced by an electron is (assuming \(v \ll c\)): \[
\mathbf{F}= - e ( \mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} ) \approx - e\mathbf{E}.
\tag{22.45}\] So, if we take \(\mathbf{E}= \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}\) and \(\mathbf{v}= \hat{\mathbf{v}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}\), we have \[
\hat{\mathbf{v}}_0 = \frac{e \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0}{\mathrm{i} \omega m_e} .
\tag{22.46}\] The induced current density in the plasma is \[
\hat{\mathbf{j}} = - ne \hat{\mathbf{v}}_0 = \left( \frac{\mathrm{i}
ne^2}{\omega m_e} \right)  \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = : \sigma \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0,
\tag{22.47}\] where we have introduced the conductivity \(\sigma\). Charge conservation is \[
\frac{\partial q}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{j}= 0 \Longrightarrow -
\mathrm{i} \omega \hat{q}_0 + \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{j}}_0 = 0
\Longrightarrow \hat{q}_0 = \frac{\mathbf{k} \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{j}}_0}{\omega} = \frac{\sigma}{\omega} \mathbf{k} \cdot
\hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\tag{22.48}\] Gauss’ law reads \[
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = \frac{\hat{q}_0}{\epsilon_0} \Longrightarrow
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \left( 1 - \frac{\sigma}{\mathrm{i} \omega \epsilon_0}
\right) \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = 0.
\tag{22.49}\] Introducing the dielectric constant \[
\begin{aligned}
\epsilon &= 1 - \frac{\sigma}{\mathrm{i} \omega \epsilon_0} = 1 - \left(
\frac{\omega_p}{\omega} \right)^2, \\
\omega_p &= \sqrt{\frac{ne^2}{\epsilon_0 m_e}} \\
&\approx 5.6 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{s^{-1}} \left( \frac{n}{1\,\mathrm{cm}^{- 3}} \right)^{1 /
2} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{22.50}\] To evaluate \(\omega_p\), we have used \(1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}} = 10^6\,\mathrm{m^{-3}}\). The corresponding frequency is \(f_p = \omega_p / 2 \pi \approx 9\,\mathrm{kHz}\,(n / 1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}})^{1/2}\). \(\omega_p\) is called the plasma frequency, and \(\epsilon\) (not to be confused with the internal energy \(\varepsilon\), or with the vacuum permittivity \(\epsilon_0\)) is the dielectric constant. The plasma frequency has a simple physical meaning: if the electrons are displaced with respect to the ions, the electric field pulls them back, and they oscillate around their equilibrium positions with angular frequency \(\omega_p\) (Exercise 22.1). Note also that \(\lambda_D = v_{\mathrm{th}} / \omega_p\), where \(v_{\mathrm{th}} = \sqrt{k_B T / m_e}\) is the thermal velocity of the electrons. In other words, the Debye length is the distance traveled by a thermal electron during one plasma oscillation.
With these definitions, we find that the Maxwell equations reduce to \[
\begin{array}{lll}
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \epsilon \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = 0, &  & \mathrm{i}
\mathbf{k} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = 0,\\
\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 = \mathrm{i} \omega
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_0, &  & \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times \hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = -
\mathrm{i} \frac{\omega}{c^2} \epsilon \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 .
\end{array}
\tag{22.51}\] These can be solved in the same way as the vacuum Maxwell equations to find the dispersion relation for electromagnetic waves in a cold plasma \[
c^2 k^2 = \epsilon \omega^2 \Longrightarrow k = \frac{\omega}{c}  \sqrt{1 -
\left( \frac{\omega_p}{\omega } \right)^2} \Longrightarrow \boxed{k =
\frac{1}{c}  \sqrt{\omega^2 - \omega_p^2} .}
\tag{22.52}\] For example, if the wave is propagating in the \(z\)-direction, \(\mathbf{k}= k \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). Then

If \(\omega < \omega_p\), then \(k\) is imaginary and the wave cannot propagate. Its amplitude decays exponentially over a distance \(\sim c / \omega_p\): \[
\mathbf{E}= \hat{\mathbf{E}}_0 \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \omega t} \mathrm{e}^{- \frac{z}{c}
\sqrt{\omega_p^2 - \omega^2}} .
\tag{22.53}\] Note that this is not due to dissipation. The electrons respond to the wave fast enough to cancel its electric field, so the wave is reflected by the plasma. This is the same mathematics we found for sound waves below the acoustic cutoff frequency (Equation 10.21).
If \(\omega > \omega_p\) the wave can propagate, but different frequencies propagate at different speeds: \[
v_g = \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial k} = c \sqrt{1 -
\frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega^2}} .
\tag{22.54}\] This leads to the phenomenon of dispersion, which can be used to measure the column density of free electrons between us and sources of radio pulses, such as pulsars and fast radio bursts, and hence to estimate their distance, as illustrated in Figure 22.5.






Figure 22.5: Different arrival time of a fast radio burst at different frequencies as a result of dispersion in the ISM: the first fast radio burst, FRB 010724. From Lorimer (2018) (figure by E. Keane); © Springer Nature, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.










TipExample



Consider the ionosphere of the Earth, which has \(n_e \sim 10^6\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Its plasma frequency is \(f_p \approx 9\,\mathrm{MHz}\). AM radio, with \(f \sim 1\,\mathrm{MHz}\), is reflected by the ionosphere. This is why AM stations can be received beyond the horizon, especially at night. FM radio and TV, with \(f \sim 100\,\mathrm{MHz}\), pass through the ionosphere. For the same reason, radio astronomy at frequencies below \(\sim 10\,\mathrm{MHz}\) is only possible from space.

title: 22  Introduction to Plasma
text:
22.3 In-class worksheet
Fast radio bursts are thought to be millisecond-long broad-band radio flares, produced during particularly violent magnetar flares, and possibly other astrophysical events. As the radio waves propagate from the source to Earth through the interstellar medium, the signal is dispersed, as shown in Figure 22.6:






Figure 22.6: Time-frequency signal for FRB 010724. Adapted from Lorimer (2018) (figure by E. Keane); © Springer Nature, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



The time of arrival of the peak of the burst at angular frequency \(\omega\), \(t_p (\omega)\) is given by \[
t_p = \int_0^d \frac{\mathrm{d} s}{v_g (\omega)},
\tag{22.55}\] where \(d\) is the distance to the source and \(v_g (\omega)\) is the group velocity at frequency \(\omega\). The approximate arrival times for FRB 010724 are tabulated below:

\omega_p = \sqrt{\frac{ne^2}{\epsilon_0 m_e}},
\tag{22.56}\] where \(n\) is the number density of free electrons, and that \(\omega \gg \omega_p\). Show that \[
t_p (\omega) \approx \frac{d}{c} + \frac{1}{2 c \omega^2}  \int_0^d
\omega_p^2 \mathrm{d} s.

\tag{22.58}\] where DM is the dispersion measure: \[
\mathrm{DM} = \int_0^d n \mathrm{d} s.
\tag{22.59}\]
Compute the DM for FRB 010724. In the direction of this source, the DM due to free electrons within the Milky Way is estimated to be \(\mathrm{DM} = 25\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}\,pc}\). Is this source extragalactic? [Remember that \(\omega = 2 \pi f\). It is convenient to plot \(t_p\) against \(1 / f^2\).]

title: 22  Introduction to Plasma
text:
22.4 Exercises

Exercise 22.1 (Plasma oscillations and the Debye length) Consider a slab of plasma with uniform electron density \(n_e\). The ions are at rest and have uniform charge density \(e n_e\). At \(t = 0\), all electrons in the slab are displaced by a small distance \(x\) in the direction perpendicular to the slab.

Show that the displacement creates an electric field \(E = n_e e x / \epsilon_0\) inside the slab.
Show that the electrons oscillate around their equilibrium positions with angular frequency \(\omega_p = \sqrt{n_e e^2 / (\epsilon_0 m_e)}\).
Show that \(\lambda_D = v_{\mathrm{th}} / \omega_p\), where \(v_{\mathrm{th}} = \sqrt{k_B T / m_e}\). Interpret this result.
Compute \(\omega_p\), \(f_p = \omega_p / 2 \pi\), and \(\lambda_D\) for the ionosphere of the Earth (\(n_e \sim 10^6\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), \(T \sim 10^3\,\mathrm{K}\)) and for the warm interstellar medium (\(n_e \sim 1\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), \(T \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\)).

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text:
23.1 Lorentz Force
These notes present a concise derivation of the equations of magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and a discussion of the underlying assumptions. We consider a quasi-neutral gas of ions and electrons immersed in a magnetic field. Let \(\mathbf{w}_e\) and \(\mathbf{w}_i\) be the drift velocities of electrons and ions, respectively. The Lorentz force experienced by each electron is \[
\mathbf{F}_e = - e \mathbf{w}_e \times \mathbf{B}.
\tag{23.1}\] The force experienced by the ions is \[
\mathbf{F}_i = Ze \mathbf{w}_i \times \mathbf{B}.
\tag{23.2}\] So the total force per unit volume is \[
\mathbf{f}= n_e \mathbf{F}_e + n_i \mathbf{F}_i = e (n_i
Z\mathbf{w}_i - n_e \mathbf{w}_e) \times \mathbf{B} =: \mathbf{j}
\times \mathbf{B}.
\tag{23.3}\] Here \(\mathbf{j}\) is the electric current density, measured in \(\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}\). Note that we have not included the electric force. The electric force per unit volume is \(q \mathbf{E}\), where \(q\) is the charge density, and it is negligible because the plasma is quasi-neutral, \(q \approx 0\) (Chapter 22).
The equations of MHD are just the “usual” hydrodynamics equations with the addition of the Lorentz force on the RHS: \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \boxed{\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}} - \nabla p, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{23.4}\] These equations look deceptively simple. The real complication is that \(\mathbf{j}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are not prescribed, but are self-consistently produced by the fluid. We have also implicitly made the following assumption:
This assumption is satisfied in most situations encountered in terrestrial and astrophysical applications, because the currents are sufficiently weak and the charge densities sufficiently large that we can treat the plasma as being a single fluid. This can be violated in very tenuous plasmas, for example in the magnetosphere of dying pulsars, in which the field and spin have decayed to the point that pair production is no longer efficient. In this case, one needs to go beyond magnetohydrodynamics and use the multi-fluid magnetohydrodynamics equations, or employ a fully kinetic treatment. Another situation in which this assumption can fail is if the degree of ionization of the plasma is small, so there is drift between the charged component of the gas and the neutrals, ambipolar diffusion. As we will see in Chapter 24, ambipolar diffusion plays an important role, for example, in star formation.

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text: Assumption 23.1 (Negligible drift momentum) The drift motion of the charged particles in the plasma that gives rise to the current is sufficiently small that we can neglect its contribution to the macroscopic momentum \(\rho \mathbf{v}\). In other words, in a frame in which \(\mathbf{v}= 0\), we have \(m_i n_i \mathbf{w}_i + m_e n_e \mathbf{w}_e \approx 0\).

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text:
23.2 Ohm’s Law
We need two more equations, in addition to the equation of state, to close Equation 23.4. A first equation is the equation prescribing how currents \(\mathbf{j}\) arise in the plasma. The simplest model for the current is to assume that it is proportional to the electric field.

Assumption 23.2 (Ohm’s law) The electric current in the plasma \(\mathbf{j}\) is proportional to the electric field \(\mathbf{E}'\) in the frame of the plasma (in which \(\mathbf{v}= 0\)): \(\mathbf{j}= \sigma \mathbf{E}'\).

The quantity \(\sigma\) is called the electrical conductivity, it is the inverse of the electrical resistivity \(1 / \sigma\), which you might be familiar with from electromagnetism. In SI units1 \[
[\mathbf{E}] = \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}},
\qquad [\mathbf{j}] = \mathrm{A\,m^{-2}},
\tag{23.5}\] so the units of electrical conductivity are \[
[\sigma] = \mathrm{A\,V^{-1}\,m^{-1}} = \mathrm{S\,m^{-1}} .
\tag{23.6}\] Here \(\mathrm{S} = \mathrm{A\,V^{-1}}\) is the siemens, the inverse of the ohm. Again, note that in SI units the current is an independent quantity, measured in ampere, so the Maxwell and MHD equations contain the constants \(\epsilon_0\) and \(\mu_0\). Be very careful not to mix Gaussian and SI units, because the equations are different in the two cases (Chapter 22).
One subtlety with the new assumption is what we mean for the “electric field in the frame of the plasma”. The hydrodynamics equations are invariant with respect to Galilean transformations, that is, if \(\mathbf{u}\) is a velocity in the Eulerian frame, then in the fluid frame we have \[
\mathbf{u}' =\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}.
\tag{23.7}\] On the other hand, Maxwell equations are invariant with respect to Lorentz transformations. As such, Maxwell equations and the equations of non-relativistic hydrodynamics are fundamentally incompatible. To be able to put them together in a consistent way, we need to assume that \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) transform according to Lorentz transformations in the nonrelativistic limit.

Assumption 23.3 (Nonrelativistic limit) We assume \(v \ll c\), \(| \mathbf{E} | \ll c | \mathbf{B} |\), and \(\left| \epsilon_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}}{\partial t} \right| \ll | \mathbf{j} |\). The second two assumptions are needed to ensure that charges are not relativistic and the plasma quasi-neutral.

Under these assumptions, it is possible to show that \[
\mathbf{B}' =\mathbf{B}, \qquad \mathbf{E}' =\mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v}
\times \mathbf{B}, \qquad \mathbf{j}' =\mathbf{j}.
\tag{23.8}\] Accordingly, Ohm’s law becomes \[
\mathbf{j}' = \sigma \mathbf{E}' \Longrightarrow \mathbf{j}= \sigma \left(
\mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \right) .
\tag{23.9}\] In Ampère’s law, \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \mu_0 \mathbf{j}+ \frac{1}{c^2}  \frac{\partial
\mathbf{E}}{\partial t},
\tag{23.10}\] where we have used \(\mu_0 \epsilon_0 = 1 / c^2\), we can drop the displacement current (Assumption 23.3). This makes sense, because \(E \sim v B\), so if the fields change over a length \(L\) and a time \(T \sim L / v\), the displacement current is of order \(v B / (c^2 T) \sim (v / c)^2 B / L\), while \(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}\) is of order \(B / L\). So we obtain \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \mu_0 \mathbf{j}.
\tag{23.11}\] Then the Lorentz force becomes \[
\boxed{\mathbf{f}=\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{1}{\mu_0}  (\nabla
\times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}.}
\tag{23.12}\] With this, we have completely eliminated the current from the MHD equations: \[
\boxed{\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \frac{1}{\mu_0}
(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}- \nabla p.}
\tag{23.13}\] We still need another equation for \(\mathbf{B}\) to completely close the MHD equations.

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text:
23.3 Faraday’s Law
The missing equation is given by Faraday’s law, also known as the induction equation: \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = - \nabla \times \mathbf{E}.
\tag{23.14}\] Here, we use again Ohm’s law to eliminate \(\mathbf{E}\): \[
\frac{1}{\sigma} \mathbf{j} =\mathbf{E}+
\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \Longrightarrow \mathbf{E}= \frac{1}{\sigma}
\mathbf{j}- \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} .
\tag{23.15}\] We use again Ampère’s law to remove \(\mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{\mu_0} \nabla \times \mathbf{B}\): \[
\mathbf{E}= \frac{1}{\mu_0 \sigma} \nabla \times \mathbf{B}- \mathbf{v}
\times \mathbf{B} =: \eta \nabla \times \mathbf{B}- \mathbf{v}
\times \mathbf{B} .
\tag{23.16}\] Inserting this back into the induction equation yields: \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} &= - \nabla \times \mathbf{E} \\
&= \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) - \nabla \times
(\eta \nabla \times \mathbf{B}) .
\end{aligned}
\tag{23.17}\] If \(\eta\) is constant, then \[
\nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) = \nabla (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B})
- \nabla^2 \mathbf{B},
\tag{23.18}\] so we find \[
\boxed{\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times
(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) + \eta \nabla^2 \mathbf{B}.}
\tag{23.19}\] The coefficient \(\eta = 1 / (\mu_0 \sigma)\) has units of \(\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\) and is called the magnetic diffusivity. Note that some texts use \(\eta\) for the resistivity \(1 / \sigma\) instead. The magnetic diffusivity is extremely small in most astrophysical systems.






TipExample



Consider the warm interstellar medium, with \(T \approx 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\). Its magnetic diffusivity is \(\eta \approx 500\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\) (Equation 24.27). Consider a region of size \(L \sim 1\,\mathrm{pc}\) in which the gas moves with velocity \(v \sim 10\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). The ratio between the time it takes for the magnetic field to diffuse over the region, \(L^2 / \eta\), and the time it takes for the gas to cross it, \(L / v\), is \[
\mathrm{R}_M = \frac{L v}{\eta} \sim 6 \times 10^{17} .
\tag{23.20}\] This is the magnetic Reynolds number, which we will discuss in Chapter 24. For comparison, copper has a conductivity of about \(6 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{S\,m^{-1}}\), so its magnetic diffusivity is \(1 / (\mu_0 \sigma) \approx 1.3 \times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}\). A copper bar of length \(1\,\mathrm{m}\) moving with velocity \(1\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) has \(\mathrm{R}_M \sim 100\). In other words, resistivity is negligible in astrophysics, but not in the laboratory. Even liquid-metal experiments designed to study the generation of magnetic fields struggle to reach \(\mathrm{R}_M \sim 10^3\).


This is the last equation. The full set of MHD equations is \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} \rho}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - \rho \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v}, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \frac{1}{\mu_0}  (\nabla
\times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}- \nabla p - \rho \nabla \Psi, \\
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \varepsilon}{\mathrm{d} t} &= - p \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} + \frac{j^2}{\sigma}, \\
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} &= \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) + \eta \nabla^2 \mathbf{B}, \\
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} &= 0,
\end{aligned}
\tag{23.21}\] where \(\mathbf{j} = \nabla \times \mathbf{B} / \mu_0\). The last term in the energy equation, \(j^2 / \sigma = \mu_0 \eta j^2\), describes the heating of the plasma by the electric currents, also known as Joule (or Ohmic) heating. It vanishes in ideal MHD. The last equation, \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\), is a constraint on the initial data. If it is satisfied at \(t = 0\), the induction equation guarantees that it is satisfied at all times, because the divergence of a curl vanishes (see the in-class worksheet).
The first three equations can be converted to the Eulerian frame with the usual substitution \[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \longrightarrow \frac{\partial}{\partial t} +
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) .
\tag{23.22}\] If \(\eta = 0\), these are known as the ideal-MHD equations. If \(\eta > 0\), these are called the resistive-MHD equations.

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text:
23.4 Conservation Laws
It is possible to rearrange the terms of the momentum equation to obtain an equation that shows the conservation of the linear momentum: \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} \\
& \quad + \nabla \cdot \biggl[ \rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}+ \Bigl( p + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0}
\Bigr) \mathbf{I} \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} \biggr]
=\mathbf{f},
\end{aligned}}
\tag{23.23}\] where \(\mathbf{f}\) is some external force, e.g., gravity. To derive this equation, we use the vector identity \[
(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B} = (\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} - \nabla \left( \frac{B^2}{2} \right)
\tag{23.24}\] and the fact that, since \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\), \[
\nabla \cdot (\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}) = (\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{B} (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B}) = (\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} .
\tag{23.25}\] So the Lorentz force can be written as the divergence of a tensor, \(\frac{1}{\mu_0} (\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B} = - \nabla \cdot \left[ \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \mathbf{I} - \frac{\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} \right]\), and the rest of the derivation is the same as in Chapter 6. Here, we limit ourselves to discuss a couple of the consequences of this equation. The first is that the magnetic field does not contribute to the momentum \(\rho \mathbf{v}\), consistently with Assumption 23.1. This is not the case in relativistic MHD, in which the inertia of the electromagnetic field is also taken into account. Second, we see that the Lorentz force splits into two components: one that resembles an additional pressure term \(B^2 / 2 \mu_0\), plus a term proportional to \(\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}\). We will discuss these terms in more detail in Chapter 25.
The energy conservation equation now takes into account both the gas energy and the energy in the electromagnetic field and can be obtained by combining the gas-dynamics energy equation with the Poynting theorem. For simplicity, we consider ideal MHD (\(\eta = 0\)). The equation describing the energy conservation for the gas (Equation 6.22) is \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 \right) \right] + \nabla \cdot \left[ \left( \rho \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right) \mathbf{v} \right] \\
& \qquad =\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}+ (\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot
\mathbf{v} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{23.26}\] This is just the usual energy equation, with the inclusion of a new term representing the work done by the Lorentz force. The latter can be rewritten using Equation 23.16 as \[
(\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \mathbf{v}= - (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) \cdot \mathbf{j}= \mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{j}.
\tag{23.27}\] You might recognize this as being the energy sink term in the Poynting theorem (Equation 22.26), which reads \[
\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{EM}}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \mathbf{S}= -
\mathbf{j} \cdot \mathbf{E},
\tag{23.28}\] where \(u_{\mathrm{EM}}\) is the electromagnetic field energy, which in our case is: \[
u_{\mathrm{EM}} = \frac{\epsilon_0 E^2}{2} + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \approx \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} =
u_{\mathrm{B}},
\tag{23.29}\] consistently with our assumption that the dynamics is nonrelativistic. The Poynting vector is, using again Equation 23.16: \[
\mathbf{S}= \frac{1}{\mu_0}  (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}) =
\frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})}{\mu_0} .
\tag{23.30}\] Combining Equation 23.26 and Equation 23.28, we obtain \[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} v^2 \right) + u_{\mathrm{B}} \right] \\
& \quad + \nabla \cdot \left[ \left( \rho \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right) \mathbf{v}+\mathbf{S} \right] =\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{23.31}\] In full form: \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
& \partial_t  \left[ \rho \left( \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} v^2
\right) + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right] \\
& \quad + \nabla \cdot \biggl[ \left( \rho \varepsilon + \tfrac{1}{2} \rho v^2 + p \right)
\mathbf{v} \\
& \qquad\qquad + \frac{\mathbf{B} \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})}{\mu_0}
\biggr] =\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{23.32}\] This equation highlights the fact that magnetic and fluid energies are not separately conserved, but their sum is. In other words, it is possible to convert gas kinetic energy into magnetic energy (dynamo effect) or magnetic energy into kinetic and internal energy (magnetic reconnection, Chapter 24). In resistive MHD, Equation 23.32 still holds. In this case, Equation 23.27 has an additional term, \(- j^2 / \sigma\), and the Poynting flux has an additional term proportional to \(\eta\). However, these are exactly compensated by the Joule heating in the energy equation of the gas. In other words, the magnetic energy dissipated by the electric currents is transferred to the internal energy of the gas.

title: 23  The MHD Equations
text:
23.6 Exercises

Exercise 23.1 (Angular momentum of the solar wind)  

Starting from the equations of ideal MHD, show that the angular momentum of the plasma, \[
\mathbf{J} = \int_V \mathbf{r} \times \rho \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V,
\tag{23.34}\] subject to an external force per unit volume \(\mathbf{f}\), satisfies \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{J}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \int_V \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{f} \mathrm{d} V
- \oint_S \left[ (\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S})  (\mathbf{r} \times
\rho \mathbf{v}) + (p + B^2 / 2 \mu_0) \mathbf{r}
\times \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}- (\mathbf{r} \times
\mathbf{B})  (\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}) / \mu_0 \right] .
\tag{23.35}\] [Hint. Follow the steps of Exercise 6.1.]
Assume that the magnetic field is stationary in a frame rotating with the angular velocity of the Sun. Show that if the solar wind is infinitely conducting, then (in cylindrical coordinates \(R, \phi, z\)) \[
B_{\phi} v_R = (v_{\phi} - \Omega R) B_R,
\tag{23.36}\] where \(\Omega\) is the angular velocity of the Sun.
Let \(\dot{J}\) be the \(z\)-component of the torque across a cylinder of radius \(R\) and height \(2 R\). Assume that \(\dot{J}\) does not depend on \(R\), and neglect the flux of angular momentum through the top and bottom of the cylinder. Show that \(\dot{J}\) can be written as \[
- \dot{J} = 2 \pi \int_{- R}^R \left( R \rho v_R v_{\phi} - R
\frac{B_{\phi} B_R}{\mu_0} \right) R \mathrm{d} z.
\tag{23.37}\] Assume that the expression in parentheses is independent of \(z\), and that \(4 \pi \rho R^2 v_R\), the mass flux of the solar wind through the cylinder, is a constant. Show that \[
- \frac{\dot{J}}{4 \pi \rho R^2 v_R} = Rv_{\phi}  \left( 1 - \frac{B_R^2}{\mu_0 \rho v_R^2} \right) + \frac{B_R^2}{\mu_0 \rho v_R^2} \Omega R^2 .
\tag{23.38}\]
There is a radius, \(R_A\), called the Alfvén radius where the radial Alfvén speed \(v_A = B_R / \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}\) is equal to \(v_R\). Evaluate the angular momentum loss per unit mass at this radius and show that it is equal to \(\Omega R_A^2\).
If \(R_A\) is 10 \(R_{\odot}\), approximately what fraction of its mass must the Sun lose to slow its rotation down by a factor of 2? Take the moment of inertia of the Sun to be \(0.06 M_{\odot} R_{\odot}^2\). What fraction of its mass has the Sun lost in 5 billion years if the solar wind was steady and the number density at the Earth is \(10\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) and the velocity is \(300\,\mathrm{km/s}\)?

title: 24  Flux Freezing
text:
24.1 The Ideal-MHD Limit
Flux freezing is an important phenomenon in highly conducting plasmas. In these notes, we derive flux freezing in ideal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD), however it is important to remark that flux freezing also applies beyond ideal MHD, at least in an approximate way. We also discuss the role of flux freezing in the context of some important astrophysical systems. The key equation we will consider is the induction equation (or Faraday’s Law), which reads (when \(\eta = \mathrm{const}\), see Equation 23.19): \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) + \eta \nabla^2 \mathbf{B}.
\tag{24.1}\]
Let \(L\) and \(V\) be characteristic length and velocity scales for the plasma. We can introduce the dimensionless time and space coordinates and velocity \[
\hat{t} = t \frac{V}{L}, \qquad \hat{x} = \frac{x}{L}, \qquad
\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{V} .
\tag{24.2}\] Faraday’s law can be written as \[
\frac{V}{L}  \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial \hat{t}} = \frac{V}{L}
\hat{\nabla} \times (\hat{\mathbf{v}} \times \mathbf{B}) + \frac{\eta}{L^2}  \hat{\nabla}^2 \mathbf{B}.
\tag{24.3}\] That is \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial \hat{t}} = \hat{\nabla} \times
(\hat{\mathbf{v}} \times \mathbf{B}) + \left( \frac{\eta}{LV}
\right)  \hat{\nabla}^2 \mathbf{B}= \hat{\nabla} \times (\hat{\mathbf{v}}
\times \mathbf{B}) + \frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_M}  \hat{\nabla}^2 \mathbf{B}.
\tag{24.4}\] We have introduced the magnetic Reynolds number, by analogy with the Reynolds number of Equation 21.10, \[
\mathrm{R}_M = \frac{LV}{\eta} .
\tag{24.5}\] The magnetic Reynolds number measures the relative importance of advection and resistivity in the evolution of the magnetic field. It is analogous to the “usual” Reynolds number, which measures the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a fluid. When \(\mathrm{R}_M \gg 1\), we say that we are in the ideal-MHD limit. As we have seen in Chapter 23, \(\mathrm{R}_M\) is enormous in most astrophysical systems, for example \(\mathrm{R}_M \sim 6 \times 10^{17}\) in the warm interstellar medium.
In the ideal-MHD limit, the Faraday law simplifies to \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times
\mathbf{B}) \Longrightarrow \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} + \nabla
\times (\mathbf{B} \times \mathbf{v}) = 0.
\tag{24.6}\] Remarkably, this is identical to the vorticity equation for a barotropic, inviscid fluid: \[
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}}{\partial t} + \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\omega}
\times \mathbf{v}) = 0.
\tag{24.7}\] The analogy between vorticity and magnetic field plays an important role in our understanding of MHD phenomena such as dynamos and is sometimes known as the Batchelor’s analogy.
Consider now a surface \(S (t)\) that moves with the fluid, and the magnetic flux across it \[
\Phi (t) = \int_{S (t)} \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} .
\tag{24.8}\] The flux can change for two reasons: because \(\mathbf{B}\) changes with time, and because the surface moves. In a time \(\mathrm{d} t\), each element \(\mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}\) of the boundary \(C (t)\) of the surface sweeps an area \(\mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} t \times \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}\), so the boundary adds a flux \(\mathbf{B} \cdot (\mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} t \times \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l}) = - (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l} \, \mathrm{d} t\). Using Stokes’ theorem, we find \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d} \Phi}{\mathrm{d} t} &= \int_{S (t)} \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} - \oint_{C (t)} (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l} \\
&= \int_{S (t)} \left[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} - \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \right] \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A} = 0,
\end{aligned}
}
\tag{24.9}\] where we have used Equation 24.6 in the last step. In other words, the magnetic flux across any surface co-moving with the flow is constant in ideal MHD. The same argument applied to the vorticity gives Kelvin’s circulation theorem: the circulation \(\mathcal{C} = \oint_{C (t)} \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{l} = \int_{S (t)} \boldsymbol{\omega} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{A}\) around a curve moving with a barotropic, inviscid fluid is conserved.
This fact is called flux freezing and is one of the most important properties of MHD. To understand this consider a magnetic flux tube. As the name suggests, a flux tube is an imaginary bundle of magnetic field lines dragged by the plasma. This is illustrated in Figure 24.1.
Consider the surface bounding the flux tube on the sides. This surface is such that the magnetic flux across it is zero, since there is no component of the field perpendicular to it. If we let this surface move with the plasma velocity, the flux freezing condition requires the magnetic field to deform to stay always parallel to it, as illustrated in Figure 24.1. In other words, the magnetic field is dragged by the plasma as if it was painted on the fluid elements. As we will see shortly, flux freezing has other important consequences.
At the microscopic level, the reason why flux freezing occurs in highly conducting plasmas is that the charged particles are “stuck” to the magnetic field lines1. Another way to think about flux freezing is in terms of induced currents. In order for the magnetic field lines to drift with respect to the plasma with velocity \(\mathbf{v}_d\), one would need to induce an electric field (in the plasma frame) \[
\mathbf{E}' = \mathbf{v}_d \times \mathbf{B}
\tag{24.10}\] which corresponds to a current \(\mathbf{j}' = \sigma \mathbf{E}'\). However, \(\sigma \rightarrow \infty\) (that is, \(\eta \rightarrow 0\)) in the ideal-MHD limit, meaning that an infinite current is required to cause the field lines to slip.

title: 24  Flux Freezing
text:
Figure 24.1: Effect of flux freezing.






24.1.1 Magnetic Field Amplification
Flux freezing also implies that, if a flux tube is compressed by the flow, then its magnetic field intensity is amplified. To see this, consider the situation illustrated in Figure 24.2.






Figure 24.2: Field amplification from the compression of a magnetic flux tube: a wide tube of cross-section \(A_1\) and field \(\mathbf{B}_1\) is squeezed from the sides by a velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) into a thinner tube of cross-section \(A_2\) and field \(\mathbf{B}_2\). Redrawn after Kulsrud (2005).



When a flux tube is compressed and its area changes from \(A_1\) to \(A_2\), the B-field strength needs to change in such a way so that the magnetic flux remains unchanged: \[
A_1 B_1 = A_2 B_2 .
\tag{24.11}\] So the magnetic field strength must be amplified: \[
B_2 = \frac{A_1}{A_2} B_1 .
\tag{24.12}\] It is instructive to compare this with the rate at which the plasma density is changed during the same process. In this case, the quantity that is conserved is the mass of the plasma in the flux tube, so \[
\rho A \ell = \mathrm{const} \Longrightarrow \rho_1 A_1 \ell = \rho_2 A_2 \ell
\Longrightarrow \rho_2 = \frac{A_1}{A_2} \rho_1 .
\tag{24.13}\] In this situation, we find that the ratio of magnetic field strength to density in the plasma stays constant: \[
\frac{B}{\rho} = \mathrm{const} .
\tag{24.14}\] Things are very different if the magnetic flux tube is compressed in the direction parallel to the magnetic field, as illustrated in Figure 24.3.






Figure 24.3: Compression along a flux tube.



In this case, the density of the plasma changes according to \[
\rho A \ell = \mathrm{const} \Longrightarrow \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} =
\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_2} .
\tag{24.15}\] However, \(B\) remains constant, because the cross-section of the flux tube, \(A\), is unchanged.






TipExample: Stellar collapse



A star with radius \(r_1 \sim 10^9\,\mathrm{m}\) collapses to form a neutron star with radius \(r_2 \sim 10\,\mathrm{km}\), and all its magnetic flux ends up in the neutron star.

By what factor does the magnetic field increase?
By what factor does the density increase?
If the initial field is \(B_1 \sim 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(100\,\mathrm{G}\)), what will be the field of the neutron star?

Answer. The density evolves according to \(\rho r^3 = \mathrm{const}\), while the magnetic field evolves according to \(Br^2 = \mathrm{const}\) (assuming the field to be approximately radial), this means that \[
\begin{gathered}
B_2 = \left( \frac{r_1}{r_2} \right)^2 B_1, \qquad \rho_2 = \left(
\frac{r_1}{r_2} \right)^3 \rho_1, \\
B \sim \rho^{2 / 3} .
\end{gathered}
\tag{24.16}\] For example, an initial field of \(10^{-2}\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(100\,\mathrm{G}\)) is amplified to \(10^{8}\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(10^{12}\,\mathrm{G}\)) as result of the collapse of the star. The strong amplification of the magnetic field during the collapse of a star is the reason why neutron stars have extremely strong magnetic fields, up to \(10^{11}\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(10^{15}\,\mathrm{G}\)).




24.1.2 Resistive Evolution
If the resistivity \(1/\sigma\) is finite, \(\eta > 0\), then the magnetic field lines are not stuck to the plasma, but can drift. To understand how this process operates, we consider the evolution of a magnetic field under the sole influence of Ohmic diffusion: \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \eta \nabla^2
\mathbf{B}.
\tag{24.17}\] If the typical curvature radius of the field lines is \(L\), then we can approximate the previous equation as \[
\frac{\partial B}{\partial t} \sim \frac{\eta}{L^2} B =
\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{decay}}} B, \qquad T_{\mathrm{decay}} = \frac{L^2}{\eta} .
\tag{24.18}\] For many astrophysical applications \(L\) is very large, so \(T_{\mathrm{decay}}\) is very long. We will put actual numbers for \(\eta\) and \(L\) when we discuss the problem of star formation below. If the magnetic field has more than one characteristic scale, then the smaller scales will be dissipated more rapidly by the resistivity. This has the effect of “smoothing” the field lines. To quantify this, we can use the Fourier transform. Accordingly, we represent the magnetic field as a superposition of plane waves \[
\mathbf{B} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \int \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{k}
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} (t) \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}},
\qquad \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^3} \int \mathbf{B} (t, \mathbf{x}) \mathrm{e}^{- \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot
\mathbf{x}} \mathrm{d} V .
\tag{24.19}\] Note that the \(\mathbf{k}= 0\) mode of the B-field is proportional to the average value of the field in the volume \(V\): \[
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_0 = \frac{1}{(2 \pi)^3} \int \mathbf{B} (t,
\mathbf{x}) \mathrm{d} V = \frac{V}{(2 \pi)^3} \langle \mathbf{B} \rangle .
\tag{24.20}\] Inserting Equation 24.19 into Equation 24.17, we obtain: \[
\int \mathrm{d}^3 \mathbf{k}\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}}  \left[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}}{\mathrm{d} t} + \eta k^2  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} \right] = 0
\tag{24.21}\] The integral vanishes for all \(\mathbf{x}\) only if the quantity in square brackets vanishes for every \(\mathbf{k}\): \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \eta k^2  \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} .
\tag{24.22}\] So we have transformed Equation 24.17 into a simple system having an infinite number of decoupled equations, with solutions \[
\hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} (t) = \hat{\mathbf{B}}_{\mathbf{k}} (0) \exp
\left( - \eta k^2 t \right) .
\tag{24.23}\] We can see that different modes of the B-field decay exponentially and that large \(k\) modes are damped exponentially more quickly than smaller \(k\) modes. On the other hand, the \(k = 0\) mode is not affected at all and stays constant for all times. This means that the action of the resistivity is not really to make the field decay, but rather to straighten out all field lines, as illustrated in Figure 24.4.






Figure 24.4: Evolution of the magnetic field under the effect of resistivity.

title: 24  Flux Freezing
text:
24.2 Star Formation
One situation in which flux freezing must be violated is star formation. Consider the collapse of a region of a molecular cloud to form a star. If flux freezing were to hold, using the same approach as for the stellar collapse example, we would find \[
\begin{array}{clcc}
\rho : & 10^{- 24}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} & \to &
1\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}\\
B : & 10^{- 10}\,\mathrm{T}\ (1\,\mu\mathrm{G}) & \to & 10^{6}\,\mathrm{T}\ (10^{10}\,\mathrm{G})
\end{array}
\tag{24.24}\] That is, the protostar would be embedded with a pulsar-like magnetic field. This is actually impossible. Indeed, the gravitational binding energy of the protostar would be \[
W \sim - \frac{3 GM^2}{5 R} \sim 2 \times 10^{48} M_1^2\,\mathrm{erg},
\tag{24.25}\] where \(M_1\) is the protostar mass in solar masses. The magnetic energy would be \[
U_B \sim \frac{4}{3} \pi R^3 \cdot \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \sim 8 \times 10^{51}\,
\mathrm{erg} \gg | W | !
\tag{24.26}\] The protostar would be unbound, meaning that the magnetic stresses would tear it apart. In reality, the magnetic field halts the collapse of an ideal-MHD cloud well before these levels of magnetic field strength can be achieved. To see why, note that both the gravitational binding energy and the magnetic energy scale as \(1 / R\) during the collapse (see the in-class worksheet). So, if flux freezing holds, the ratio \(U_B / | W |\) does not change during the collapse. With the numbers above, the cloud already has \(U_B \gg | W |\) before it starts to collapse. In other words, if flux freezing holds, a cloud for which the magnetic energy exceeds the binding energy can never collapse. To form a star, the cloud must get rid of most of its magnetic flux. Obviously, Nature has a way to form stars from magnetized clouds, so how does it defeat flux freezing?
It turns out that resistivity is not sufficient to do the trick. The magnetic diffusivity \(\eta = 1/(\mu_0 \sigma)\) of ionized hydrogen plasma depends weakly on density and can be approximated as (Kulsrud 2005) \[
\eta \approx \frac{420}{T_{\mathrm{eV}}^{3 / 2}}\,
\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}.
\tag{24.27}\] For a star \(T_{\mathrm{eV}} \approx 10^2\) and \(L \sim R_{\odot} \approx 7 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{m}\), so the decay time is \[
T_{\mathrm{decay}} = \frac{L^2}{\eta} \approx 1.2 \times 10^{18}\,\mathrm{s} \approx
40\,\mathrm{Gyr} .
\tag{24.28}\] This is longer than the age of the Universe, so the magnetic fields of stars are also frozen in the plasma. For a molecular cloud core, with \(T \approx 10\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(L \approx 0.1\,\mathrm{pc}\), the decay time is even longer, \(\sim 10^{16}\,\mathrm{yr}\). So resistivity is clearly not sufficient to release the magnetic flux and allow stars to form.
The mechanism currently thought to be responsible for the drift between magnetic fields and the plasma is ambipolar diffusion. The details go beyond the scope of this course, but the key observation is that molecular clouds are only weakly ionized. The neutral component of the gas is not affected by the Lorentz force, so it can flow perpendicular to field lines. The Lorentz force on the ions, on the other hand, is orders of magnitude larger than gravity, so the ions are stuck on the field lines. The mutual friction between ions and neutrals has the effect of regulating the rate of collapse and determines the time for the formation of protostars. This physics is illustrated in Figure 24.5.






Figure 24.5: Ambipolar diffusion.



Magnetic fields do not just regulate the collapse of clouds into protostars. They also play a key role enabling it. Indeed, magnetic fields allow the protostar to lose angular momentum and prevent the gas from getting stuck at the centrifugal barrier (see Exercise 26.1). This happens because the collapsing cloud forces a large column of gas, parallel to the mean magnetic field, to corotate with it. This allows the forming protostar to dissipate angular momentum. We explore this in a more quantitative way in Exercise 23.1, for the case of the solar wind.

title: 24  Flux Freezing
text:
24.3 Io and Jupiter
The unipolar-inductor model for the interaction between Jupiter and its moon Io is one of the early successes of plasma astrophysics. This model has also been adopted to explain a variety of other astrophysical systems, including the launching of electromagnetic waves by black holes moving through plasma. The main idea of this model is that the motion of a conductor, in this case Io, in an external magnetic field, in this case Jupiter’s field, generates an electric current.
The original motivation for this model was the discovery in the 1960s of radio flares from Jupiter in phase with the rise and setting of Io. More precisely, Jupiter has a rotation period of about 10 hours, while Io has an orbital period of about 42 hours. Radio flares are preferentially detected when Io has a longitude of \(90^{\circ}\) or \(240^{\circ}\) with respect to Jupiter, as shown in Figure 24.6, taken from Duncan (1965).






Figure 24.6: Number of radio bursts detected from Jupiter as a function of the phase of Io. From Duncan (1965); © Elsevier, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



In 1969, Goldreich and Lynden-Bell (Goldreich and Lynden-Bell 1969) proposed a model to explain:

the mechanism generating the radiation;
the reason for the phase difference between the rising and setting of Io and the radiation bursts.

We explain this model in a qualitative way and then build a semi-quantitative simplified model below.
Io is primarily composed of silicates and iron, so it has a good electrical conductivity. This means that there is no electric field inside Io, in Io’s frame of reference, and the magnetic field lines of Jupiter are stuck to it (flux freezing). However, because in Jupiter’s frame of reference Io completes a revolution every 13 hours, the field lines cannot be frozen everywhere, otherwise the magnetic energy in the magnetosphere would grow without bound2. This means that the field lines must slip somewhere. It turns out that this happens in Jupiter’s atmosphere, where the gas resistivity is the highest, due to the presence of a neutral gas. The geometry of the magnetic flux tube connecting Jupiter and Io is illustrated in Figure 24.7.






Figure 24.7: Magnetic flux tube connecting Io and Jupiter. Redrawn after Goldreich and Lynden-Bell (1969).



The slippage of the field lines on Jupiter’s surface drives a current along the flux tube connecting the planet to the moon. Electrons gyrate in the field lines producing cyclotron radiation, which is beamed primarily in the direction perpendicular to the field lines, explaining the offset between Io’s rises and settings and the radio bursts. This is illustrated in more detail in Figure 24.8.






Figure 24.8: Left panel: footprint of the magnetic-flux tube connecting Io and Jupiter on Jupiter’s atmosphere. Right panel: cross-section of the magnetic-flux tube connecting Jupiter and Io and direction in which the current \(I\) flows between the planet and the moon. Redrawn after Goldreich and Lynden-Bell (1969).



A strong electric field is created in the direction perpendicular to the \(B\)-field, in the \(Y\)-direction shown in the figure. The potential difference across the flux tube is \(\Delta \Phi \sim v B D\), where \(v \approx 57\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\) is the velocity of Io with respect to Jupiter’s corotating magnetic field, \(B \approx 2\,\mu\mathrm{T}\) (\(0.02\,\mathrm{G}\)) is the magnetic field at Io, and \(D \approx 3600\,\mathrm{km}\) is the diameter of Io. This gives \(\Delta \Phi \sim 4 \times 10^5\,\mathrm{V}\)3. However, the motion of electrons perpendicular to the field lines is suppressed by the Lorentz force, so a current is driven along the field lines, through the moon, and back to the planet, as shown in the right panel of Figure 24.8. The current intensity is \(I \sim 10^6\,\mathrm{A}\), which is sufficient to produce cyclotron and synchrotron radiation.
Here, we consider a toy model in which we see how the electric field is created by the slippage of the field lines. We consider a conductor moving in an external B-field anchored in a wall with infinite conductivity, as shown in Figure 24.9.






Figure 24.9: Toy model for the Io and Jupiter problem.



In our analogy, the conductor is Jupiter’s atmosphere, while the wall represents Io. We imagine that initially the field is vertical and the conductor is at rest. At \(t = 0\), we start moving the conductor with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) in the \(x\)-direction. The field is dragged up to a distance \(L\) and then starts to slip, realizing the configuration shown in Figure 24.9.
There is no external electric field, so the electric field in the frame of the conductor is \[
\mathbf{E}' =\mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} =
\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} = v_x B_y
\hat{\mathbf{z}},
\tag{24.29}\] and the associated current is \(\mathbf{j}= \sigma (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) = \sigma v_x B_y \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). The current is responsible for the creation of the \(x\)-component of the \(B\)-field (with \(\eta = 1 / \mu_0 \sigma\)): \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \mu_0 \mathbf{j} \Longrightarrow - \partial_y B_x
= \mu_0 j_z \Longrightarrow B_x = - \mu_0 j_z y = - \frac{1}{\eta} v_x
B_y y.
\tag{24.30}\] On the other hand, from the geometry of the system, we have: \[
B_x = \left. \frac{B_y L}{D} \right|_{y = d} \Longrightarrow L = \frac{v_x
Dd}{\eta} = v_x T_{\mathrm{decay}} ,
\tag{24.31}\] where now \(T_{\mathrm{decay}}\) is computed as in Equation 24.18, with \(L^2\) replaced by \(D d\).
This shows the two key features of the system. The relative motion of the conductor and the walls generates an electric field (a consequence of Faraday’s law). The electric field drives a current in the system. The current, in turn, causes the field lines to bend and slip (from Ampère’s law).






NoteGoing further: Pulsars



Pulsars were discovered by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish in 1967. It was later realized that pulsars are rotating neutron stars endowed with strong magnetic fields. In 1969, Goldreich and Julian (Goldreich and Julian 1969) developed the first model of a pulsar. Like the unipolar induction model, Goldreich and Julian’s model applies to a variety of astrophysical systems and shows another key physical effect associated with flux freezing. Namely, the fact that rotating neutron stars fill their surroundings with a dense plasma, creating the so-called magnetosphere.






Figure 24.10: Schematic illustration of a pulsar magnetosphere. Redrawn after Goldreich and Julian (1969).



In this model, shown in Figure 24.10, we neglect the misalignment between magnetic North pole and rotational axis, which would be needed to produce the pulsed emission. However, this model contains all required physical ingredients. We assume at first that the pulsar is a neutron star with a dipole magnetic field in vacuum. The magnetic field is then given by \[
\mathbf{B}= B_0  \left( \tfrac{R}{r} \right)^3  (2 \cos \theta
\hat{\mathbf{r}} + \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) .
\tag{24.32}\] The angular velocity of the star is given by \[
\boldsymbol{\Omega}= \Omega \hat{\mathbf{z}}, \qquad \hat{\mathbf{z}} = \cos
\theta \hat{\mathbf{r}} - \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} .
\tag{24.33}\] In the previous equation \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\) is the unit vector in the \(z\)-direction. Since neutron stars are essentially perfect conductors, there should be no electric field in their frame \(\mathbf{E}' = 0\). This means that in the inertial frame there is an electric field inside the star given by \[
\mathbf{E}= - \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} = -
(\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{r}) \times \mathbf{B}= B_0 \Omega
r  \left( \frac{R}{r} \right)^3 (\sin^2 \theta \hat{\mathbf{r}} - 2 \cos
\theta \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) .
\tag{24.34}\] In the previous equation we have used the fact that \[
\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times \mathbf{r}= \Omega r \sin \theta
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
\tag{24.35}\] and \[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \times (2 \cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{r}} + \sin \theta
\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) = 2 \cos \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}} - \sin \theta
\hat{\mathbf{r}} .
\tag{24.36}\] If there is vacuum in the exterior (and assuming axisymmetry), then the external electric potential is \[
\Phi (r, \theta) = \sum_{\ell = 0}^{\infty} \frac{\phi_{\ell}}{r^{\ell + 1}}
P_{\ell} (\cos \theta), \qquad r > R
\tag{24.37}\] where \(\phi_{\ell}\) are fixed by the fact that the tangential component of the electric field should be continuous on the surface of the star4 \[
[\![ \mathbf{E}_{\parallel} ]\!] = 0 \Longrightarrow E_{\theta} (r =
R) = - \frac{1}{R} \partial_{\theta} \Phi (r = R) .
\tag{24.38}\] Inside the star, \(E_{\theta} \propto \sin \theta \cos \theta \propto \partial_{\theta} P_2 (\cos \theta)\), so only the \(\ell = 2\) term can match it (the \(\ell = 0\) term is fixed by the total charge of the star, which we assume to be zero). So the external field is quadrupolar, meaning that \[
\Phi (r, \theta) = \frac{\phi_2}{r^3} P_2 (\cos \theta),
\tag{24.39}\] then Equation 24.38 implies \[
\boxed{\Phi = - \frac{2 B_0 \Omega R^5}{3 r^3} P_2 (\cos \theta) .}
\tag{24.40}\] So we find that there is an enormous electrostatic potential at the surface of the star: \[
| \Phi | \approx 4
\times 10^{16}  (B_8 R^2_4 / P)\,\mathrm{V},
\tag{24.41}\] where \(B_8 = B_0 / 10^8\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(10^{12}\,\mathrm{G}\)), \(R_4 = R / 10^4\,\mathrm{m}\), and \(P = 2 \pi / \Omega\) is the period in seconds. For example, the ratio of electrostatic to gravitational force for a neutron star with \(M = 1.4\,M_{\odot}\) is \[
\frac{| \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{EM}} |}{| \mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{G}} |} \sim
\frac{\Phi e}{\frac{GM}{R} m} = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}
2 \times 10^8, & \text{protons},\\
4 \times 10^{11}, & \text{electrons} .
\end{array}\right. \gg 1.
\tag{24.42}\] The electromagnetic forces are strong enough to pull charges out of the surface of the neutron star and fill all the region around it with plasma. The field is so strong that electron-positron cascade production is triggered once the first particles are extracted. This is the so-called magnetosphere. The magnetosphere creates currents that to leading order short out the electric potential to infinity.
In the extreme conditions found in pulsar or black-hole magnetospheres, the electromagnetic energy density is so large compared to the plasma inertia that the plasma is forced to move in such a way as to cancel the Lorentz force, \(q \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B} = 0\). This is the so-called force-free electrodynamics approximation. Electrons, positrons, and ions can flow freely along the \(B\)-field lines, so they short out any electric field along \(\mathbf{B}\). If, in addition, the plasma moves with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\), the electric field is given by the ideal-MHD condition: \[
\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{B}= 0, \qquad \mathbf{E}+ \mathbf{v}
\times \mathbf{B}= 0.
\tag{24.43}\] From the first condition, if the system is axisymmetric, we have that \[
\mathbf{E}= E_0  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \times \mathbf{B} \Longrightarrow
\mathbf{E}= - \Omega r \sin \theta  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \times
\mathbf{B}.
\tag{24.44}\] From the last two equations, we find \[
0 = (\mathbf{v}- \Omega r \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}) \times \mathbf{B}
\Longrightarrow \mathbf{v}= \Omega r \sin \theta \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}
+ v_d  \hat{\mathbf{B}} .
\tag{24.45}\] So the plasma velocity has two components. The plasma is forced to co-rotate with the pulsar (first term in the first equation). However, when \(\Omega r \sin \theta \geq c\), the drift velocity \(v_d\) of plasma along the field lines must be non-zero so that \(| \mathbf{v} | < c\). The region at which \(\Omega r \sin \theta = c\) is called the light cylinder. It is the boundary of the region in which magnetic field lines can be closed. Outside the light cylinder, the \(B\)-field lines bend and reach infinity so that plasma can flow away from/to the pulsar (depending on its charge) creating a current.
The plasma charge density is given by Gauss’ law of electrodynamics: \[
q = \epsilon_0 \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E} .
\tag{24.46}\] Note that \[
\frac{q}{\epsilon_0} = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}= \nabla \cdot \left[ -
\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \right] = - \mathbf{B} \cdot
(\nabla \times \mathbf{v}) + \mathbf{v} \cdot (\nabla \times
\mathbf{B}) .
\tag{24.47}\] This can be computed using \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{v}= \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\Omega} \times
\mathbf{r}) =\boldsymbol{\Omega} (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{r}) -
(\boldsymbol{\Omega} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{r}= 2\boldsymbol{\Omega}
\tag{24.48}\] and \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \mu_0 \mathbf{j}= \mu_0 q \mathbf{v}
\tag{24.49}\] So the charge density is \[
\frac{q}{\epsilon_0} = - 2 \mathbf{B} \cdot \boldsymbol{\Omega}+ \frac{q}{\epsilon_0}
\frac{v^2}{c^2} \Longrightarrow q_{\mathrm{GJ}} = - 2 \epsilon_0 \boldsymbol{\Omega}
\cdot \mathbf{B}  \frac{1}{1 - v^2 / c^2} .
\tag{24.50}\] Note that \(\boldsymbol{\Omega} \cdot \mathbf{B}\) changes sign across a critical line in the magnetosphere. This means that there is charge separation in the magnetosphere.
The minimum electron number density is the so-called Goldreich–Julian density \[
n_{\mathrm{GJ}} = \frac{| q_{\mathrm{GJ}} |}{e} \approx 7 \times 10^{10}  (B_8 / P)\,\mathrm{cm}^{-
3} .
\tag{24.51}\] This is \(\sim 10\) orders of magnitude larger than the typical density of electrons in the ISM. More recent theoretical models show that the plasma number density can be several orders of magnitude larger than the Goldreich-Julian density. This is because the plasma is rich in electron-positron pairs and \(n_{\mathrm{GJ}}\) only measures the net density of charges. For example, see Figure 24.11.






Figure 24.11: \(\log_{10} (n / n_{\mathrm{GJ}})\) in a particle-in-cell simulation with approximate treatment of pair creation. Coherent plasma waves are thought to be responsible for the production of the radio pulses. From Philippov et al. (2015); © The American Astronomical Society, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.
