title: 24  Flux Freezing
text:
24.5 Exercises

Exercise 24.1 (Flux freezing in an Alfvén wave) In this exercise we check, for a simple wave, that the magnetic field lines move together with the plasma. Consider a plasma with uniform density \(\rho\) and pressure \(p\), in the uniform magnetic field \(B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). We perturb it with a transverse wave travelling along the field, with velocity and magnetic field \[
\mathbf{v}= \epsilon v_A \sin (kz - \omega t)  \hat{\mathbf{x}}, \qquad
\mathbf{B}= B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - \epsilon B_0 \sin (kz - \omega t)
\hat{\mathbf{x}} ,
\tag{24.52}\] where \(\epsilon \ll 1\) and \(v_A = B_0 / \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}\).

Show that Equation 24.52 solves the ideal-MHD equations to first order in \(\epsilon\), provided that \(\omega = k v_A\). In other words, we neglect all terms of order \(\epsilon^2\) and higher.
The ideal-MHD equations neglect the displacement current. Use the ideal-MHD electric field to compute the displacement current of this wave, and compare it with the term \(\mu_0 \mathbf{j}\) in Ampère’s law. Show that the displacement current is negligible when \(v_A \ll c\).
Now consider a plasma with finite resistivity, that is, with magnetic diffusivity \(\eta > 0\). Compare the resistive term in the induction equation with the term \(\nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\), and show that the resistive term is negligible when \(\omega T_{\mathrm{decay}} \gg 1\), where \(T_{\mathrm{decay}} = 1 / (k^2 \eta)\) is the decay time of Equation 24.18 for \(L = 1/k\).
To first order in \(\epsilon\), the field lines are the curves \(x (z)\) that solve \[
\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{\mathrm{d} z} = \frac{B_x}{B_0} .
\tag{24.53}\] Find these curves. Then compute the displacement of the fluid elements, \[
x (z, t) = \int v_x \mathrm{d} t ,
\tag{24.54}\] and show that it gives the same curves. This is what we expect if the field lines are frozen into the plasma.

Adapted from Kulsrud (2005), Problem 3.1.

title: 25  Magnetic Tension and Hydromagnetic Equilibria
text:
25.1 Magnetic Tension Force
Up to now we have been primarily concerned with the consequences of the induction equation (Faraday’s law). We have seen that, in the ideal-MHD limit, the magnetic field lines are frozen in the flow and explored some of the consequences of this fact. Now, we consider the feedback of the magnetic field on the plasma, that is the impact of the \(\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}\) term in the momentum equation.
A first somewhat obvious, but important remark is that the magnetic force \(\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}\) is always perpendicular to the magnetic field, as is obvious from the cross product. In other words, there is no impediment to the plasma flow along field lines. On the other hand, the field might resist or drive plasma motion perpendicular to the field lines. The latter, in turn, causes the field lines to move, in accordance with the induction equation. It is important to keep this in mind, because we are now going to rewrite the Lorentz force in a form in which this constraint is not manifest. Using the vector identity \[
\nabla (\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}) =\mathbf{A} \times (\nabla \times
\mathbf{B}) +\mathbf{B} \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{A}) + (\mathbf{A}
\cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}+ (\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{A}
\tag{25.1}\] (see also Equation 23.24) and Ampère’s law (\(\mu_0 \mathbf{j}= \nabla \times \mathbf{B}\)), we can rewrite the Lorentz force as \[
\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times
\mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} = \frac{(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} -
\nabla \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} .
\tag{25.2}\] The second term is often improperly referred to as the magnetic pressure, because it is reminiscent of the \(- \nabla p\) term in the momentum equation, while the first term is improperly referred to as magnetic tension. However, remember that magnetic pressure is only effective perpendicular to the field lines, as we have already remarked. To better understand the nature of the Lorentz force in MHD, we factor \[
\mathbf{B}= B \hat{\mathbf{b}},
\tag{25.3}\] where \(\hat{\mathbf{b}}\) is a unit vector. Accordingly, we can write \[
\begin{aligned}
(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} &= B (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)
(B \hat{\mathbf{b}}) \\
&= B^2  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) \hat{\mathbf{b}}
+ B \hat{\mathbf{b}}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) B \\
&= B^2  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} + \frac{1}{2}
\hat{\mathbf{b}}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) B^2 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{25.4}\] The last term on the RHS is, apart from a factor 1/2, the projection of \(\nabla B^2\) parallel to \(\mathbf{B}\): \[
[\hat{\mathbf{b}}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla) B^2]_i = \sum_{j = 1}^3
\hat{b}_i  \hat{b}_j \partial_j  (B^2) = [(\hat{\mathbf{b}} \otimes
\hat{\mathbf{b}}) \nabla (B^2)]_i =: \nabla_{\parallel} B^2 .
\tag{25.5}\] Plugging this back into Equation 25.2 yields \[
\mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}= \frac{B^2}{\mu_0}  (\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot
\nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} - [\mathbf{I}- \hat{\mathbf{b}} \otimes
\hat{\mathbf{b}}]  \frac{\nabla B^2}{2 \mu_0} = \frac{B^2}{\mu_0}
(\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} - \nabla_{\perp}
\frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} .
\tag{25.6}\] The last term is the component of \(\nabla (B^2 / 2 \mu_0)\) perpendicular to the field lines. This is the correct form of the magnetic pressure, while the first term on the RHS is the proper form of the magnetic tension.
We remark that \(u_B = B^2 / 2 \mu_0\) is the energy density of the magnetic field, so the magnetic pressure is \[
p_B = (\Gamma_B - 1) u_B,
\tag{25.7}\] which has the same form as the equation of state of an ideal gas (Equation 2.16), with an effective adiabatic index \(\Gamma_B = 2\). This makes sense, because, if we compress a flux tube perpendicular to the field, flux freezing (Chapter 24) gives \(B \propto \rho\), so \(p_B \propto \rho^2\). For ionized hydrogen \(\Gamma = 5 / 3\), so magnetic energy is more effective at resisting compression than gas internal energy. Of course, magnetic pressure can only resist compression perpendicular to the field lines.
To understand the meaning of the first term on the RHS of Equation 25.6, note that \[
(\hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \nabla)  \hat{\mathbf{b}} =\boldsymbol{\kappa},
\tag{25.8}\] where \(1 / | \boldsymbol{\kappa} |\) is the curvature radius of the field lines and \(\boldsymbol{\kappa}\) points towards the centre of curvature. In other words, \(\boldsymbol{\kappa}= 0\) for straight field lines. For a circular field line, \(1 / | \boldsymbol{\kappa} |\) is the radius of the circle spanned by the line. This means that the magnetic field lines back-react on the plasma as if they were elastic strings under a tension \(B^2 / \mu_0\) per unit area.
Summarizing, we find that there are two components of the Lorentz force. The first is the magnetic pressure, according to which the magnetic field lines resist being bundled together. The second is the magnetic tension, according to which the magnetic field lines resist bending. This situation is illustrated in Figure 25.1. We will see that magnetic tension is the restoring force for Alfvén waves (Chapter 26) and the driver of the magnetorotational instability (Chapter 27).
As we have already anticipated (see Equation 23.23), the Lorentz force can be rewritten as the divergence of the magnetic stresses: \[
\frac{(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} - \nabla \frac{B^2}{2
\mu_0} = \nabla \cdot \left[ \frac{\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} -
\frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \mathbf{I} \right] =: \nabla \cdot
\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{EM}} .
\tag{25.9}\] This follows from Equation 23.25. Including both the fluid stresses \(\mathbf{T}\) and the magnetic stresses, the momentum equation reads: \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = \nabla \cdot
[\mathbf{T}+\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{EM}}] .
\tag{25.10}\] For an ideal fluid \(\mathbf{T}= - p\mathbf{I}\), however shear and bulk viscosity can also be included in \(\mathbf{T}\) to obtain the viscous MHD equations. In conservation form, the momentum equation reads \[
\frac{\partial (\rho \mathbf{v})}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot [\rho
\mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}-\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{EM}}] = 0,
\tag{25.11}\] where \(\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes \mathbf{v}\) is the flux of momentum carried by the flow1.

title: 25  Magnetic Tension and Hydromagnetic Equilibria
text:
Figure 25.1: Left panel: effect of the magnetic pressure force. Right panel: effect of the magnetic tension force.










TipExample: Solar prominence



Solar prominences are plasma arches which rise above the solar photosphere and are supported by the magnetic tension, as illustrated by Figure 25.2 and Figure 25.3. Prominences are made of cool gas, \(T \sim 10^4\,\mathrm{K}\), with densities \(n \sim 10^{10}\)–\(10^{11}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), about 100 times denser than the surrounding corona, which has \(T \sim 10^6\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(n \sim 10^9\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). The scale height of a gas at \(10^4\,\mathrm{K}\) in the gravity of the Sun is only a few hundred km, while prominences extend for tens of thousands of km above the photosphere. So the gas pressure alone cannot support them against gravity.






Figure 25.2: Solar prominence in UV. Credit: NASA (What is a solar prominence?); not covered by the license of these notes.









Figure 25.3: Force diagram for a Solar prominence.



To understand how prominences are supported against gravity, let us consider the balance of forces on the region in the volume \(V\) with boundary surface \(S\): \[
\begin{aligned}
0 &= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} \int_V \rho \mathbf{v} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= - \int_V \nabla \cdot [\rho \mathbf{v} \otimes
\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{T}-\mathbf{T}_{\mathrm{EM}}] \mathrm{d} V \\
& \quad + \int_V \rho \mathbf{g} \mathrm{d} V \\
&= - \int_S \rho \mathbf{v}\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} \\
& \quad - \int_S \left( p + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right) \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} \\
& \quad + \int_S \frac{\mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} \mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}+ \int_V \rho
\mathbf{g} \mathrm{d} V.
\end{aligned}
\tag{25.12}\] For a prominence at rest, \(\mathbf{v} = 0\) and the first term vanishes. Note that the field lines enter \(V\) going down on the left and leave it going up on the right. In other words, the prominence sits in a dip of the field lines, like a weight on a hammock. The main force balancing gravity is the magnetic tension, arising from the \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}\) term. On the left, \(\mathbf{B}\) points into \(V\), so \(\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} < 0\) and the force is opposite to \(\mathbf{B}\). Since \(\mathbf{B}\) points down, the force points up. On the right, \(\mathbf{B}\) points out of \(V\), so \(\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} > 0\) and the force is along \(\mathbf{B}\), which also points up. The horizontal components cancel. The magnetic pressure, arising from the squeezing of the field lines below the prominence, also contributes, but is subdominant. We work out a simple model of this configuration in Exercise 25.1.
The attentive reader might have noticed that the term \(\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S}\) gives a force along \(\mathbf{B}\), with magnitude \(B^2 | \hat{\mathbf{b}} \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbf{S} | / \mu_0\). How can this be possible? We have seen that the magnetic force is always perpendicular to \(\mathbf{B}\). The point is that this term represents the net force from the magnetic tension on the whole volume \(V\), not the force at a specific point. In other words, we should not confuse the force on individual fluid elements, which is always perpendicular to \(\mathbf{B}\), with the net force on a control volume, which can be in any direction.

title: 25  Magnetic Tension and Hydromagnetic Equilibria
text:
25.2 Hydromagnetic Equilibria
Consider the hydrostatic equilibrium of a plane-parallel, magnetized atmosphere in a gravitational potential \(\Psi (z)\), as illustrated in Figure 25.4. This equilibrium configuration could be representative of the disk in a spiral galaxy, or of the photosphere of the Sun.






Figure 25.4: Force diagram for a plane-parallel magnetized atmosphere.



The force-balance equation for hydromagnetic equilibrium is \[
- \nabla p - \rho \nabla \Psi + \frac{1}{\mu_0} (\nabla \times \mathbf{B})
\times \mathbf{B}= 0.
\tag{25.13}\] We will make two simplifying assumptions.

The gas is isothermal, so \(p = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho\). This means that, in absence of magnetic fields, \[
\rho (z) = \rho_0 \exp (- \Psi / c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2) .
\tag{25.14}\]
We assume that the magnetic field is planar and does not depend on \(x\), meaning that \[
\mathbf{B}= B_y (y, z)  \hat{\mathbf{y}} + B_z (y, z)  \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{25.15}\] This means that there exists a vector potential \(\mathbf{A}= A (y, z) \hat{\mathbf{x}}\) such that \(\nabla \times \mathbf{A}=\mathbf{B}\). In particular, \[
B_y = \partial_z A, \quad B_z = - \partial_y A \qquad \Longleftrightarrow
\qquad \mathbf{B}= \nabla A \times \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\tag{25.16}\] Note that \(\mathbf{A} \perp \mathbf{B}\) and that the function \(A (y, z)\) is constant along the field lines, because \(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla A = 0\). So the isocontours of \(A (y, z)\) are the field lines.

To compute the Lorentz force we use \[
\nabla \times \mathbf{B}= \nabla \times (\nabla \times \mathbf{A}) = -
\nabla^2 \mathbf{A}+ \nabla (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{A}) = - \hat{\mathbf{x}}
\nabla^2 A
\tag{25.17}\] and \[
(\nabla \times \mathbf{B}) \times \mathbf{B}= - (\nabla^2 A)
\hat{\mathbf{x}} \times (- \hat{\mathbf{x}} \times \nabla A) = - (\nabla^2
A) \nabla A.
\tag{25.18}\] For reasons that will be more clear later, we rewrite \[
\nabla p + \rho \nabla \Psi = \mathrm{e}^{- \Psi / c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \nabla q, \qquad q = p\,\mathrm{e}^{\Psi
/ c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} .
\tag{25.19}\] The force equation finally reduces to \[
\boxed{- \frac{1}{\mu_0} (\nabla^2 A) \nabla A = \mathrm{e}^{- \Psi / c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \nabla
q.}
\tag{25.20}\] The last equation shows that \(\nabla q \parallel \nabla A\), which means that \(q = q (A)\). Since \(\nabla q = (\mathrm{d} q / \mathrm{d} A) \nabla A\), the force equation becomes \[
\nabla^2 A = - \mu_0 \mathrm{e}^{- \Psi / c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \frac{\mathrm{d} q}{\mathrm{d} A} .
\tag{25.21}\] This is a nonlinear Poisson equation for \(A\), analogous to the Grad–Shafranov equation used to model the magnetic equilibria of tokamaks and of pulsar magnetospheres. One can then find equilibrium configurations by specifying \(q = q (A)\), which encodes the amount of matter enclosed by the field lines \(A\) and \(A + \mathrm{d} A\), and solving Equation 25.21 for \(A\). We shall not follow this line of reasoning here, instead we will make two more simplifying assumptions, following Parker (1966).

We assume that the magnetic field lines are horizontal, \(\mathbf{B}= B (z) \hat{\mathbf{y}}\).
We assume that the ratio of magnetic to gas pressure is constant \[
\frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0 p} = \alpha_0 .
\tag{25.22}\]

With these simplifications, the equation for equilibrium becomes \[
(1 + \alpha_0)  \frac{\mathrm{d} p}{\mathrm{d} z} = - \frac{p}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}  \frac{\mathrm{d}
\Psi}{\mathrm{d} z} .
\tag{25.23}\] Apart from the additional factor \(1 + \alpha_0\), this is the usual equation for hydrostatic equilibrium of a plane-parallel isothermal atmosphere (Equation 10.2). The solution is \[
\begin{gathered}
p (z) = p_0 \exp \left( - \frac{\Psi (z)}{(1 + \alpha_0) c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2} \right),
\\ B (z) = B_0 \exp \left( - \frac{\Psi (z)}{2 (1 + \alpha_0) c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}
\right) .
\end{gathered}
\tag{25.24}\] For a uniform gravitational field, \(\Psi = g z\), the scale height of the gas is \(H = (1 + \alpha_0) c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 / g\). In other words, the magnetic field makes the atmosphere thicker, because part of the weight of the gas is supported by the magnetic pressure. The inverse of \(\alpha_0\), \[
\beta = \frac{2 \mu_0 p}{B^2},
\tag{25.25}\] is called the plasma beta. Plasmas with \(\beta \gg 1\) are dominated by the gas pressure, while plasmas with \(\beta \ll 1\) are dominated by the magnetic field.






TipExample: Magnetic support of the Galactic disk



Consider the gas in the disk of the Milky Way near the Sun. The magnetic field is \(B \approx 0.5\,\mathrm{nT}\) (\(5\,\mu\mathrm{G}\)), so the magnetic pressure is \(B^2 / 2 \mu_0 \approx 1 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{Pa}\). The thermal pressure of the gas is \(p / k_B \approx 3000\,\mathrm{K\,cm^{-3}}\), that is \(p \approx 4 \times 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{Pa}\). So \(\alpha_0 \approx 2\), or \(\beta \approx 0.4\). In other words, the magnetic field is as important as the gas pressure in supporting the disk against the gravity of the stars2. In the model of Equation 25.24, the field increases the scale height of the gas by a factor \(1 + \alpha_0 \approx 3\).


Remarkably, the solution in Equation 25.24 turns out to be unstable for any \(\alpha_0 > 0\) to long-wavelength perturbations, if the perturbations are also isothermal. This is the so-called Parker instability (Parker 1966). Note that, if the perturbations have adiabatic index \(\Gamma\) and are allowed to vary across the field lines, the atmosphere is unstable for \(\Gamma < 1 + \alpha_0\) (Newcomb 1961). Without magnetic field, \(\alpha_0 = 0\), this is the condition \(N^2 < 0\) for the onset of convection in an isothermal atmosphere (Section 10.2). In other words, an isothermal atmosphere is marginally stable to isothermal perturbations, \(N = 0\), and the magnetic field makes it unstable. The Parker instability is demonstrated in the MHD simulations shown in Figure 25.5.






Figure 25.5: Development of the Parker instability in 3D MHD simulations, at three times, shown in a vertical slice. From Matsumoto and Shibata (1992); © Astronomical Society of Japan, reproduced for non-commercial educational use and not covered by the license of these notes.



Imagine starting from horizontal field lines, like in the left panel of the figure, and adding a small bend to them. The gas in the regions where the field lines are inclined can now slide down along them, because the magnetic force has no component along the field. In doing so, the gas loses gravitational potential energy and collects in the valleys, as shown by the arrows in the middle panel. The crests of the field lines are now lighter, so they are pushed further up by the magnetic pressure below them, the gas drains more efficiently, and the perturbation grows. This instability is responsible, for example, for the emergence of magnetic flux tubes from the solar interior, which gives rise to the type of prominence we have discussed previously.
In the case of the solar corona, the field lines at the foot of the prominences are anchored in the outer convection layers of the Sun. The motion of plasma in this region moves the field lines in random ways and builds enormous tension in the field. When field lines of opposite polarities find themselves sufficiently close they can annihilate in a so-called reconnection event. This might seem in contradiction with flux freezing, since the magnetic Reynolds number in the corona is enormous (Chapter 24). However, reconnection takes place in thin current sheets, in which the field changes direction over a very short distance. The magnetic Reynolds number computed with this length is small, so the field lines can diffuse through the plasma. Reconnection suddenly releases the magnetic tension and generates solar flares and coronal mass ejections. Solar eruptions can significantly impact satellites and space communication and can be hazardous for astronauts. The prediction of solar eruptions using ground- and space-based observations, in conjunction with MHD simulations, is a field of its own: space weather modeling.

25.3 In-class worksheet
Explosive Reconnection. Plasma is contained in a region bounded by two perfectly conducting plates. Two magnetic flux tubes are anchored on the plates and stretched by the application of an external force \(\mathbf{f}\) as shown in panel (a) of Figure 25.6.






Figure 25.6: Explosive reconnection of two magnetic flux tubes anchored on conducting plates: (a) before and (b) after reconnection.



When \(\ell \approx D\), the field lines reconnect and snap to a new configuration shown in panel (b). This process releases energy stored in the magnetic tension of the field to accelerate the plasma to a velocity \(\mathbf{v}\), which reaches a maximum when the field lines are perfectly straight. Assume that the ideal-MHD approximation holds at all times, except when reconnection takes place.

Show that, apart from geometric factors of order unity, the force per unit volume necessary to hold the field lines bent to a height \(\ell\) is \[
| \mathbf{f} | \approx \frac{B^2}{\mu_0}  \frac{\ell}{D^2} .
\tag{25.26}\]
Show that, apart from factors of order unity, the maximum velocity of the plasma after the reconnection event is \[
v \approx v_A,
\tag{25.27}\] where \(v_A\) is the Alfvén velocity \[
v_A = \frac{B}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}} .
\tag{25.28}\]
Magnetic fields in solar active regions have strengths \(B \sim 0.03\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(300\,\mathrm{G}\)) and extend over regions of size \(L \sim 3 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{km}\). Estimate the magnetic energy available. Compare it with the energy released by a large solar flare, \(\sim 10^{32}\,\mathrm{erg} = 10^{25}\,\mathrm{J}\).

text:
25.4 Exercises

Exercise 25.1 (A model for solar prominences) Consider the model of a solar prominence of Kippenhahn and Schlüter (1957). The prominence is a vertical sheet of isothermal gas, with isothermal sound speed \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}\) (Equation 9.16), in a uniform gravitational field \(\mathbf{g} = - g \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). The magnetic field is \[
\mathbf{B} = B_x \hat{\mathbf{x}} + B_z (x) \hat{\mathbf{z}},
\tag{25.29}\] where \(B_x\) is a constant, and all quantities depend only on \(x\).

Show that \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0\) and that the horizontal component of the force balance gives \[
p + \frac{B_z^2}{2 \mu_0} = \mathrm{const} .
\tag{25.30}\]
Show that the vertical component of the force balance is \[
\rho g = \frac{B_x}{\mu_0} \frac{\mathrm{d} B_z}{\mathrm{d} x} .
\tag{25.31}\] Which component of the Lorentz force holds the gas up?
Assume that \(p \to 0\) and \(B_z \to \pm B_{\infty}\) for \(x \to \pm \infty\). Show that \[
B_z = B_{\infty} \tanh (x / w), \qquad w = \frac{2 B_x}{B_{\infty}} \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2}{g},
\tag{25.32}\] and find \(\rho (x)\). Sketch the field lines.
Show that the mass per unit area of the sheet is \[
\Sigma = \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} \rho \, \mathrm{d} x = \frac{2 B_x B_{\infty}}{\mu_0 g} .
\tag{25.33}\] Evaluate \(w\), the central number density \(n (0)\) and \(\Sigma\) for \(B_x = 1\,\mathrm{mT}\) (\(10\,\mathrm{G}\)), \(B_{\infty} = 0.2\,\mathrm{mT}\) (\(2\,\mathrm{G}\)), \(T = 7000\,\mathrm{K}\), mean molecular weight \(\mu = 0.6\), and \(g = 270\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\). Compare with observed prominences, which have widths of a few thousand km and densities \(n \sim 10^{10}\)–\(10^{11}\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\).

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.1 Waves in a Homogeneous Plasma
Waves play a very important role in the dynamics of magnetized plasmas. Particle-wave interaction with the interstellar medium regulates the propagation of cosmic rays in the Galaxy. In strong MHD turbulence (Chapter 21), the non-linear interaction between Alfvén waves acts as the main driver of the turbulence cascade. Torsional Alfvén waves extract angular momentum from proto-stellar cores allowing them to collapse and form stars (Exercise 26.1). These are just a few examples. In this chapter, we discuss the phenomenology of waves in compressible MHD.
We consider a homogeneous plasma described by the ideal-MHD equations with \[
\rho_0 = \mathrm{const}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_0 = 0, \qquad \mathbf{B}_0 = B_0
\hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{26.1}\] We proceed in the same way as when we derived the dispersion relation for sound waves in unmagnetized media (Chapter 9). However, as we will see shortly, the phenomenology of MHD waves is significantly more complex than that of sound waves. As before, we introduce a perturbation with a Lagrangian displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\), shown in Figure 26.1.
The pressure and density perturbations in the Lagrangian frame are \[
\delta \rho = - \rho_0 \nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}, \qquad \delta p =
\frac{\Gamma p_0}{\rho_0} \delta \rho = - \Gamma p_0 \nabla \cdot
\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{26.2}\] Since the background is uniform, the Lagrangian and Eulerian perturbations coincide. The magnetic field perturbations can be computed from the linearized induction equation: \[
\frac{\partial \delta \mathbf{B}}{\partial t} = \nabla \times \left(
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t} \times \mathbf{B}_0 \right)
\Longrightarrow \delta \mathbf{B}= \nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times
\mathbf{B}_0) .
\tag{26.3}\] The linearized momentum equation becomes (note that the unperturbed current vanishes \(\mathbf{j}_0 = 0\)): \[
\rho \frac{\mathrm{d} \mathbf{v}}{\mathrm{d} t} = - \nabla p +\mathbf{j} \times
\mathbf{B} \Longrightarrow \rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial
t^2} = - \nabla \delta p + \delta \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\tag{26.4}\] The perturbed current is \[
\delta \mathbf{j}= \frac{1}{\mu_0} \nabla \times \delta \mathbf{B}=
\frac{1}{\mu_0} \nabla \times [\nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times
\mathbf{B}_0)],
\tag{26.5}\] so putting everything together we get the oscillation equation \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = {} & \Gamma p_0
\nabla (\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) \\
& + \frac{1}{\mu_0} \{ \nabla \times
[\nabla \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}}
\tag{26.6}\] Of course, if \(\mathbf{B}_0 = 0\), this equation reduces to the equation for sound waves. All the new physics is in the last term on the RHS. To derive a dispersion relation, we take the usual ansatz \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) =\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot
\mathbf{x}- \omega t)},
\tag{26.7}\] which we plug into the oscillation equation. This yields \[
\begin{aligned}
- \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = {} & - \Gamma p_0 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k} \cdot
\boldsymbol{\xi}_1) \\
& - \frac{1}{\mu_0}  \{ \mathbf{k} \times [\mathbf{k} \times
(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.8}\] As we have seen for sound waves (Chapter 9), the oscillation equation gives rise to an eigenvalue problem in the form \[
- \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 =\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k}) \boldsymbol{\xi}_1,
\tag{26.9}\] where \(\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k})\) is a matrix. This equation has solutions with \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \neq 0\) if and only if \[
\det [\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k}) + \rho_0 \omega^2 \mathbf{I}] = 0.
\tag{26.10}\] The last equation defines the dispersion relation \(\omega = \omega (\mathbf{k})\). The eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k})\) define the polarization vector \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_1\) of the wave.

title: 26  MHD Waves
text: Figure 26.1: Lagrangian displacement of a fluid element from position \(\mathbf{x}\) to position \(\mathbf{x}+\boldsymbol{\xi}\).

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.2 Families of MHD Waves
In general, there are three solutions to the eigenvalue problem Equation 26.9, corresponding to three different modes. In the unmagnetized case, one of the modes is the sound wave, while the other two are the transverse modes with \(\omega = 0\) we found in Chapter 9. In the magnetized case, the magnetic field provides a restoring force also for transverse displacements, and there are three types of waves: Alfvén waves, slow-, and fast-magnetosonic waves.
Without loss of generality, we can choose the axes so that \(\mathbf{B}_0\) is along \(z\) and \(\mathbf{k}\) is in the \(x z\)-plane, at an angle \(\theta\) from \(\mathbf{B}_0\). We will see that the \(y\) component of the displacement decouples from the other two. So the eigenvalue problem splits into a \(1 \times 1\) problem (the Alfvén wave) and a \(2 \times 2\) problem (the slow and fast waves). We consider these separately below.

26.2.1 Alfvén Waves
We first consider displacements along \(y\), as depicted in Figure 26.2:

\(\mathbf{B}_0\) is along \(z\)
\(\mathbf{k}\) is in the \(x z\)-plane
\(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is along \(y\)

Note that \(\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}= 0\), meaning that \(\delta \rho = \delta p = 0\).






Figure 26.2: Geometry of the Alfvén wave: \(\mathbf{B}_0\) along \(z\), \(\mathbf{k}\) in the \(xz\)-plane at an angle \(\theta\) from \(\mathbf{B}_0\), and displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) along \(y\).



To compute the Lorentz force we proceed as follows. In Fourier space, \(\nabla \rightarrow \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k}\), so each derivative in Equation 26.3 and Equation 26.5 is replaced by a factor \(\mathrm{i} \mathbf{k}\). First we note that \[
\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0 = \xi_y B_0  \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\tag{26.11}\] Next, we compute the magnetic field perturbation as \[
\delta \mathbf{B} = \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0) = \mathrm{i} k \xi_y B_0 \cos
\theta \hat{\mathbf{y}} .
\tag{26.12}\] The current is given by \[
\begin{aligned}
\mu_0 \delta \mathbf{j} &= \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k} \times \delta \mathbf{B} = - \mathbf{k} \times [\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \\
&= k^2 \xi_y B_0 \cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{k}}_{\perp} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.13}\] Finally, the Lorentz force is \[
\mu_0 \delta \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}_0 = - k^2 B_0^2 \cos^2 \theta \xi_y
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = - (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{B}_0)^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}.
\tag{26.14}\] So \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) evolves as a mass attached to an elastic spring with spring constant \((\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{B}_0)^2 / \mu_0\). In formulas, \[
\begin{aligned}
- \rho_0 \omega^2 \xi_y &= - \tfrac{1}{\mu_0} k^2 B_0^2 \cos^2 \theta \xi_y \\
\Longrightarrow \quad & \boxed{\omega = \pm \frac{B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho_0}} k
\cos \theta = \pm \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{v}_A ,}
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.15}\] where \(\mathbf{v}_A = \mathbf{B}_0 / \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho_0}\). We call \(\omega_A = \mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{v}_A\) the Alfvén frequency. These waves are called Alfvén waves, after Alfvén (1942) (Physics Nobel Prize in 1970). Some comments are in order.

If \(\theta = 0\), these waves propagate along the field lines with velocity (Alfvén velocity): \[
v_A = \frac{B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho_0}} .
\tag{26.16}\] If \(\theta > 0\), the phase velocity is reduced to \(v_A \cos \theta\). However, the group velocity is \(\partial \omega / \partial \mathbf{k} = \pm v_A \hat{\mathbf{z}}\), for any \(\theta\). In other words, Alfvén waves always transport energy along the magnetic field lines, with velocity \(v_A\).
The displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is perpendicular to the background field \(\mathbf{B}_0\), so these waves are transverse. More precisely, Alfvén waves behave as transverse waves in an elastic string (the magnetic field). Indeed, the restoring force for these waves is magnetic tension (Chapter 25).
As already mentioned \(\delta \rho = \delta p = 0\) for these waves. As such, Alfvén waves are incompressible and exist also in incompressible flows.

Although we have derived Alfvén waves as small perturbations, it turns out that Alfvén waves with \(\delta \mathbf{B} = \mp \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho} \, \delta \mathbf{v}\), propagating in the \(\pm z\) direction, are an exact solution to the full non-linear equations, as long as the magnetic pressure \(B^2 / 2 \mu_0\) stays uniform. This means that MHD flows can support arbitrarily strong waves. We check the small-amplitude case in Exercise 24.1.


26.2.2 Magnetosonic Waves
We now consider displacements in the \(x z\)-plane, as depicted in Figure 26.3:

\(\mathbf{B}_0\) is along \(z\)
\(\mathbf{k}\) is in the \(x z\)-plane
\(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) is also in the \(x z\)-plane

Note that \(\delta p, \delta \rho\) are no longer necessarily zero.






Figure 26.3: Geometry of the magnetosonic wave: \(\mathbf{B}_0\) along \(z\), \(\mathbf{k}\) in the \(xz\)-plane at an angle \(\theta\) from \(\mathbf{B}_0\), and displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi}\) also in the \(xz\)-plane.



We can compute the current using the following vector identity \[
\mathbf{a} \times (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) =\mathbf{b} (\mathbf{a}
\cdot \mathbf{c}) -\mathbf{c} (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b})
\tag{26.17}\] and the fact that \(\mathbf{k} \perp \boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0\), since the latter is in the \(y\)-direction, we can write \[
\mathbf{k} \times [\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)]
=\mathbf{k} [\mathbf{k} \cdot (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] - k^2
(\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0) = - k^2 (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times
\mathbf{B}_0) .
\tag{26.18}\] Plugging this into the expression for the Lorentz force gives \[
\begin{aligned}
\delta \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}_0 &= - \frac{1}{\mu_0}  \{ \mathbf{k}
\times [\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times
\mathbf{B}_0 \\
&= \frac{k^2}{\mu_0}  (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)
\times \mathbf{B}_0 = - \frac{k^2 B_0^2 \xi_x}{\mu_0}  \hat{\mathbf{x}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.19}\] The pressure force is \[
- \Gamma p_0 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) = - k^2 \Gamma p_0
(\xi_x \sin \theta + \xi_z \cos \theta)  (\sin \theta \hat{\mathbf{x}} +
\cos \theta \hat{\mathbf{z}}) .
\tag{26.20}\] Using \(c_s^2 = \Gamma p_0 / \rho_0\) and \(v_A = B_0 / \sqrt{\mu_0 \rho_0}\), we find \[
\omega^2  \left(\begin{array}{c}
\xi_x\\
\xi_z
\end{array}\right) = k^2 \left(\begin{array}{cc}
c_s^2 \sin^2 \theta + v_A^2 & c_s^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta\\
c_s^2 \sin \theta \cos \theta & c_s^2 \cos^2 \theta
\end{array}\right) \left(\begin{array}{c}
\xi_x\\
\xi_z
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{26.21}\] The eigenvalues of this matrix are \(\omega^2 = T / 2 \pm \sqrt{T^2 / 4 - D}\), where \(T = k^2 (c_s^2 + v_A^2)\) and \(D = k^4 c_s^2 v_A^2 \cos^2 \theta\) are its trace and determinant. After some algebra, we find the dispersion relation \[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\left( \frac{\omega}{k} \right)^2 = {} & \frac{v_A^2 + c_s^2}{2} \\
& \pm \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{(v_A^2 - c_s^2)^2 + 4 c_s^2 v_A^2 \sin^2 \theta} .
\end{aligned}}
\tag{26.22}\] So there are two solutions and two corresponding polarization vectors \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_s\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_f\). Note that \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_s \perp \boldsymbol{\xi}_f\), since the matrix \(\mathbf{F} (\mathbf{k})\) in Equation 26.21 is self-adjoint (see Equation 9.29). Conventionally, \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_s\) is taken to be the polarization corresponding to the minus sign in Equation 26.22, i.e., to the smaller phase velocity. This is the so-called slow magnetosonic wave. Conversely, \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_f\) is called the fast magnetosonic wave. As we will see shortly, these have a mixed character of sound and magnetic waves.

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.3 Effect of Propagation Direction
We can get additional insight into the nature of the three modes by considering the properties of waves propagating along the magnetic field lines, or perpendicular to them. The general case will turn out to be intermediate between these two limits.

26.3.1 Parallel Propagating Waves (\(\theta = 0\))
Let us consider the case of waves propagating along the background magnetic field lines, that is \(\theta = 0\). In this case, the dispersion relation for Alfvén, slow, and fast modes are \[
\left( \frac{\omega}{k} \right)^2 = v_A^2, \qquad \left( \frac{\omega}{k}
\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}  [v_A^2 + c_s^2 \pm |v_A^2 - c_s^2 |] .
\tag{26.23}\] There are two different cases, depending on whether \(v_A > c_s\) or \(v_A < c_s\), shown in Figure 26.4.






Figure 26.4: Polarization diagram for MHD waves propagating along the background magnetic field.




If \(v_A > c_s\), then

The slow mode polarization is along the magnetic field, the mode propagates at speed \(c_s\) and its restoring force is pressure.
Fast and Alfvén modes are orthogonal to the magnetic field and to each other and both have the character of Alfvén waves propagating with speed \(v_A\). Magnetic tension is their restoring force.

If \(v_A < c_s\), then the situation is similar as before, but the slow and fast modes exchange character: the fast mode is now a sound wave, while the slow mode is an Alfvén wave.



26.3.2 Perpendicularly Propagating Waves (\(\theta = 90^{\circ}\))
Let us consider the case of waves propagating perpendicular to the field lines. In this case, Alfvén and slow modes cannot propagate (they have \(\omega_{A, s} = 0\)). The fast-magnetosonic wave satisfies the dispersion relation \[
\left( \frac{\omega}{k} \right)^2 = v_A^2 + c_s^2 .
\tag{26.24}\] In this case \(\boldsymbol{\xi}_f\) is parallel to \(\mathbf{k}\). The restoring force for the mode is the sum of the magnetic and gas pressures, which explains why this mode is called the “magnetosonic” mode. In other words, the field lines are compressed, as in a sound wave, but they are not bent.


26.3.3 Friedrichs Diagrams
Friedrichs diagrams show the propagation velocity of the different MHD modes as a function of a generic propagation angle \(\theta\). The special cases of \(\theta = 0, 90^{\circ}\) discussed above correspond to the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axis in Figure 26.5. In general, slow and fast modes have a mixed character between sound waves and Alfvén waves.






Figure 26.5: Friedrichs diagrams for ideal MHD, for \(v_A = 2 c_s\) (left) and \(v_A = c_s / 2\) (right). The phase speeds are in units of the smaller of \(v_A\) and \(c_s\).

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.4 Weak and Strong Field Limits
Finally, it is also instructive to compare slow- and fast-magnetosonic waves in the limits of weak magnetic field (\(c_s \gg v_A\)) and strong magnetic field \((v_A \gg c_s)\), as illustrated in Figure 26.6. Note that when \(v_A\) becomes a sizable fraction of the speed of light, we can no longer use Newtonian MHD, because the displacement current becomes important. In this limit, one needs to use the (significantly more complex) equations of relativistic magnetohydrodynamics.






Figure 26.6: Slow and fast magnetosonic waves in the limits of weak (left panel) and strong (right panel) magnetic fields.




Left panel: the fast mode is \(\sim\) a sound wave, with \(\omega \approx k c_s\), and the slow mode is nearly perpendicular to \(\mathbf{k}\), with \(\omega \approx k v_A \cos \theta\).
Right panel: the fast mode is \(\sim\) an Alfvén wave, with \(\omega \approx k v_A\), and the slow mode is nearly parallel to \(\mathbf{B}_0\), with \(\omega \approx k c_s \cos \theta\). In other words, the slow mode is a sound wave guided along the magnetic field lines. This is the situation in the solar corona.

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.5 Shock Waves
As for unmagnetized gases, MHD waves can steepen into shock waves. Alfvén waves can steepen into rotational discontinuities, in which the magnetic field direction suddenly changes across an interface. Slow- and fast-magnetosonic waves can give rise to (slow and fast) shocks and rarefaction waves. The theory of MHD shocks is very complex and beyond the scope of this course. A good overview is given in Bazer and Ericson (1959). It is important to be aware that, even in the case of shocks propagating along magnetic field lines, MHD effects can be important. For example, a shock propagating along the magnetic field can create a component of the field parallel to the shock front (a switch-on shock), and the opposite process is also possible (a switch-off shock).
We treat in detail only one case that is relevant for the interstellar medium: a shock propagating in an isothermal flow with perpendicular magnetic field, as illustrated in Figure 26.7.






Figure 26.7: Isothermal shock propagating in a medium with perpendicular magnetic field.



The shock conditions for the shock shown in Figure 26.7 are: \[
[\![ \rho u ]\!] = 0, \quad [\![ Bu ]\!] = 0,
\quad \left[\!\left[ p + \rho u^2 + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right]\!\right]
= 0,
\tag{26.25}\] where \([\![ \cdot ]\!]\) denotes the jump across the shock.
In the absence of a magnetic field, the shock conditions for an isothermal gas, \(p = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho\), are \(\rho_1 u_1 = \rho_2 u_2\) and \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho_1 + \rho_1 u_1^2 = c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 \rho_2 + \rho_2 u_2^2\). Using the first condition to eliminate \(u_2\) from the second, we find \(c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 (\rho_2 - \rho_1) = \rho_1 u_1^2 (1 - \rho_1 / \rho_2) = \rho_1 u_1^2 (\rho_2 - \rho_1) / \rho_2\). So the compression factor of an isothermal shock is \[
\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = \left( \frac{u_1}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}} \right)^2,
\tag{26.26}\] which can become arbitrarily large for large upstream Mach numbers. We discuss isothermal shocks in more detail in Chapter 12. This is dramatically different when a magnetic field is present, as long as it is sufficiently strong: \[
u_1 \gg v_A = \frac{B_1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho_1}} \gg c_{\mathrm{iso}}.
\tag{26.27}\] In this case, from \([\![ \rho u ]\!] = [\![ Bu ]\!] = 0\), we conclude that \[
\frac{B_1}{\rho_1} = \frac{B_2}{\rho_2} .
\tag{26.28}\] From the conservation of momentum, we have (using \(u_1 \gg v_A \gg c_{\mathrm{iso}}\)) \[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} &= \frac{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 + u_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} v_A^2}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 + u_2^2 +
\frac{B_2^2}{2 \mu_0 \rho_2}} \\
&\approx \frac{u_1^2}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 + u_2^2 +
\frac{B_2^2}{2 \mu_0 \rho_2^2} \rho_2} \\
&= \frac{u_1^2}{c_{\mathrm{iso}}^2 + u_2^2 +
\frac{B_1^2}{2 \mu_0 \rho_1}  \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}} \\
&\approx \frac{u_1^2}{\frac{v_A^2}{2}  \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.29}\] Solving for \(\rho_2 / \rho_1\), we obtain \[
\boxed{\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1} = \sqrt{2}  \frac{u_1}{v_A} .}
\tag{26.30}\] This shows that the compression ratio now scales with the Alfvénic Mach number of the upstream gas, \(\mathrm{Ma}_A = u_1 / v_A\), instead of the square of its Mach number. This is another example showing that magnetic fields play an important role in the dynamics of the interstellar medium and in star formation.






TipExample: Shocks in molecular clouds



Consider a molecular cloud with temperature \(T \approx 10\,\mathrm{K}\), number density \(n \approx 100\,\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) and magnetic field \(B \approx 1\,\mathrm{nT}\) (\(10\,\mu\mathrm{G}\)). The gas has \(\rho = \mu m_u n \approx 4 \times 10^{- 22}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}} = 4 \times 10^{- 19}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}\) (with \(\mu \approx 2.3\)) and \(c_{\mathrm{iso}} \approx 0.2\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\). The Alfvén velocity is \[
v_A = \frac{B}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}} \approx 1.4\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} .
\tag{26.31}\] Note that \(v_A \gg c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), so the magnetic pressure is much larger than the gas pressure. Suppose that the cloud is hit by a shock with \(u_1 = 10\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}\), for example driven by a nearby supernova remnant. Then \(u_1 \gg v_A \gg c_{\mathrm{iso}}\), and Equation 26.30 applies. Without the magnetic field, the compression factor would be \((u_1 / c_{\mathrm{iso}})^2 \approx 2500\). With the magnetic field, it is only \(\sqrt{2} u_1 / v_A \approx 10\). In other words, the magnetic field makes the shocked gas about 250 times less dense. So it is much harder to form dense cores in molecular clouds with shocks alone.

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.6 In-class worksheet
Fast Magnetosonic Waves. Consider a homogeneous plasma described by the ideal-MHD equations with \[
\rho_0 = \mathrm{const}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_0 = 0, \qquad \mathbf{B}_0 =
B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\tag{26.32}\]

Introduce a small perturbation in the form of a displacement \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x})\) of the fluid elements and show that the oscillation equation is \[
\begin{aligned}
& \rho_0  \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}}{\partial t^2} = \Gamma p_0 \nabla
(\nabla \cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}) \\
& \quad + \frac{1}{\mu_0} \{ \nabla \times [\nabla
\times (\boldsymbol{\xi} \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times \mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.33}\]
Introduce the ansatz \(\boldsymbol{\xi} (t, \mathbf{x}) = \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}- \omega t)}\) and show that Equation 26.33 reduces to \[
\begin{aligned}
& - \rho_0 \omega^2 \boldsymbol{\xi}_1 = - \Gamma p_0 \mathbf{k} (\mathbf{k}
\cdot \boldsymbol{\xi}_1) \\
& \quad - \frac{1}{\mu_0}  \{ \mathbf{k} \times
[\mathbf{k} \times (\boldsymbol{\xi}_1 \times \mathbf{B}_0)] \} \times
\mathbf{B}_0 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.34}\] [Hint. Use \(\partial_t \rightarrow - \mathrm{i} \omega\) and \(\nabla \rightarrow \mathrm{i} \mathbf{k}\).]
Consider waves with \(\mathbf{k} \parallel \hat{\mathbf{x}}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\xi} \parallel \mathbf{k}\). Find the dispersion relation \(\omega = \omega (\mathbf{k})\) and compute group and phase velocities for these waves.

title: 26  MHD Waves
text:
26.7 Exercises

Exercise 26.1 (Torsional Alfvén waves)  

Consider the torsional Alfvén wave, in cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\), \[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{v} &= \epsilon v_A g (R) f (z - v_A t)  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}, \\
\mathbf{B} &= B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} - \epsilon B_0 g (R) f (z - v_A t)
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}},
\end{aligned}
\tag{26.35}\] where \(f\) and \(g\) are arbitrary functions and \(\epsilon\) is a small parameter. Show that it is a solution of the ideal-MHD equations to first order in \(\epsilon\).
Consider a uniform plasma at rest, threaded by the magnetic field \(B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). A thin disk of radius \(a\), made of a perfectly conducting material, lies in the \(x y\)-plane with its centre at the origin. At \(t = 0\), the disk is set into rotation with a constant angular velocity \(\Omega\), with \(\Omega a \ll v_A\). The plasma just above and below the disk must move with the same tangential velocity as the disk. Use the solution of part 1 to show that, at time \(t\), the plasma with \(R < a\) and \(| z | < v_A t\) rotates with angular velocity \(\Omega\), while the rest of the plasma is still at rest.
Let \(\Sigma\) be the mass per unit area of the disk. Estimate how long it takes before the disk starts to slow down. [Hint. Compare the angular momentum of the disk with that of the plasma set in motion by the wave.]

Adapted from Kulsrud (2005), Problem 3.4.

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
27.1 Qualitative Picture
The magnetorotational instability (MRI) was first discovered by Velikhov (1959) and Chandrasekhar (1961), who studied the stability of a conducting fluid between two rotating cylinders, and then rediscovered in the context of accretion disks by Balbus and Hawley (1991). This is the instability thought to be responsible for the \(\alpha\)-viscosity (Chapter 19) in many astrophysical systems: from X-ray binaries to AGN disks. It is one of the most important, among the many instabilities operating in plasmas, so we will cover it in detail in these notes.
It was long known that a way to transport angular momentum in the disk is through magnetic stresses, that is the \(B_R B_{\phi} / \mu_0\) term in the momentum equation (Chapter 25). However, to explain the observed luminosities from accretion disks, the magnetic stresses must be similar in magnitude to the pressure in the disk \(p\) (the proportionality constant being the \(\alpha\)-viscosity coefficient). Given a small component of the field in the radial direction, flux freezing (Chapter 24) can grow \(B_{\phi}\) linearly in time. However, since \(B_R\) is small, this mechanism can transport angular momentum efficiently only if \(B_{\phi}^2 / 2 \mu_0 \gg p\). Such a strong toroidal field cannot be contained in the disk, because it is buoyant and rises out of it. The requirement for the magnetic stresses to do the job of transporting angular momentum is that \(B_R B_{\phi} / \mu_0 \approx \alpha \rho c_s^2\), with \(B_R \sim B_{\phi}\). Detailed simulations have shown that MRI is a mechanism that naturally produces the required field strengths over a short timescale. Note that a vertical field can also carry angular momentum away from the disk, through torsional Alfvén waves (Exercise 26.1).
Consider an accretion disk with Keplerian angular velocity profile \[
\Omega (R) = \Omega_0  \left( \frac{R_0}{R} \right)^{3 / 2},
\tag{27.1}\] initially threaded by a vertical magnetic field \(B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}}\). Let \(A\) and \(B\) be two fluid elements connected by a magnetic field line (initially vertical) and displace their positions according to \(\xi_r = \epsilon \cos k z\), as shown in Figure 27.1. Because inner orbits are faster, \(A\) moves ahead of \(B\), as shown in the right panel of Figure 27.1. As a result, the field line that connects them is stretched in the azimuthal direction, and a toroidal component of the field, \(B_{\phi}\), is generated.
The magnetic tension (Chapter 25) then creates an attractive force between \(A\) and \(B\), which has the effect of transporting angular momentum from \(A\) to \(B\). This causes \(A\) to lose angular momentum and sink further inwards, while \(B\) gains angular momentum and starts moving outwards. In turn, because the angular velocity decreases with radius, \(A\) increases its angular velocity, while \(B\) slows down, further separating the two points. This in turn enhances the magnetic tension force. The cycle we have just described is unstable, so the initial perturbation grows exponentially in time, until the system becomes nonlinear.
The mechanism we have just described involves the magnetic tension force, so it is natural to expect a characteristic growth rate of \[
\lambda \approx kv_A, \qquad v_A = \frac{B_z}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}} .
\tag{27.2}\] In our derivation, we have assumed the field to be sufficiently weak, so that the displaced fluid elements can acquire the angular velocity of their surroundings. This should be valid as long as \[
\omega_A = kv_A \lesssim \Omega ,
\tag{27.3}\] where \(\omega_A\) is the Alfvén frequency (Equation 26.15). We will find that the exact condition for instability is \(kv_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega\), so the maximum growth rate is achieved by taking \(k\) sufficiently large, so that \(\lambda \approx kv_A \approx \Omega\). This is a very short timescale: the amplitude of the fastest mode grows by a factor of about 100 every orbit! Moreover, the maximum growth rate is independent of the field strength, as long as \(v_A\) is not so large that the required \(k\) to satisfy \(kv_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega\) corresponds to perturbations with characteristic size larger than the vertical size of the disk. We will see that this requires \(v_A \lesssim c_s\).

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text: Figure 27.1: Qualitative description of the magnetorotational instability transporting angular momentum between fluid elements \(A\) and \(B\). Left panel: meridional view. Right panel: orbital plane.

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
27.2 Detailed Calculation
The starting point is the momentum equation of ideal MHD (Equation 23.4), with the Lorentz force written as the sum of magnetic pressure and tension (Equation 25.6). We write it in vector form. We use cylindrical coordinates \((R, \phi, z)\). \[
\rho \left[ \frac{\partial \mathbf{v}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{v} \cdot
\nabla) \mathbf{v} \right] = - \nabla \left( p + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} \right) +
\frac{(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B}}{\mu_0} +\mathbf{g} \rho .
\tag{27.4}\] We consider a disk that is Keplerian and threaded by a vertical magnetic field: \[
\mathbf{v}= R \Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} +\mathbf{u}, \qquad \mathbf{B}=
B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}} +\mathbf{b}, \qquad p + \frac{B^2}{2 \mu_0} = P_0 + P.
\tag{27.5}\] We will treat \(\mathbf{u}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) as (small) Eulerian perturbations. We will only consider modes that are axisymmetric (no \(\phi\) dependence) and incompressible \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}= \frac{1}{R}  \frac{\partial (Ru_R)}{\partial R} +
\frac{\partial u_z}{\partial z} = 0.
\tag{27.6}\] In equilibrium, the centrifugal force balances gravity, \(R \Omega^2 = G M / R^2\), and \(P_0\) is constant. We neglect the self-gravity of the disk, so that \(\mathbf{g}\) is not perturbed. To first order in \(\mathbf{u}\), and using Kepler’s law, we have \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\mathbf{v} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{v} &{}\rightarrow{} && (R \Omega)
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \cdot \nabla \mathbf{u}+\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla (R
\Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}) \\
&{}={} && - 2 \Omega u_{\phi}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \left( R \frac{\mathrm{d}
\Omega}{\mathrm{d} R} + 2 \Omega \right) u_R \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \\
&{}={} && \frac{1}{2} \Omega u_R  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} - 2 \Omega u_{\phi}
\hat{\mathbf{R}} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.7}\] Similarly, \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\mathbf{B} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{B} &{}\rightarrow{} && B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}}
\cdot \nabla \mathbf{b}+\mathbf{b} \cdot \nabla (B_0  \hat{\mathbf{z}}) =
\\
& && B_0  \dfrac{\partial b_R}{\partial z}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} + B_0
\frac{\partial b_{\phi}}{\partial z}  \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + B_0
\frac{\partial b_z}{\partial z}  \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.8}\] Since the unit vectors do not depend on \(z\), this is \(B_0 \, \partial \mathbf{b} / \partial z\). So the linearized momentum equation reads \[
\frac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2} \Omega u_R
\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} - 2 \Omega u_{\phi}  \hat{\mathbf{R}} = -
\frac{1}{\rho} \nabla P + \frac{B_0}{\mu_0 \rho} \frac{\partial \mathbf{b}}{\partial z} .
\tag{27.9}\] The induction equation, Equation 23.19 with \(\eta = 0\), can be linearized in a similar way: \[
\begin{aligned}
& \nabla \times (\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \\
& \quad \rightarrow \nabla \times \bigl[(R \Omega \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}) \times (b_R \hat{\mathbf{R}} + b_{\phi} \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + b_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}) \\
& \qquad\qquad + (u_R \hat{\mathbf{R}} + u_{\phi} \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + u_z \hat{\mathbf{z}}) \times (B_0 \hat{\mathbf{z}})\bigr] \\
& \quad = \nabla \times [- R \Omega b_R \hat{\mathbf{z}} + R \Omega b_z \hat{\mathbf{R}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - u_R B_0 \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} + u_{\phi} B_0 \hat{\mathbf{R}}] \\
& \quad = \nabla \times [ (R \Omega b_z + u_{\phi} B_0) \hat{\mathbf{R}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - u_R B_0 \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} - R \Omega b_R \hat{\mathbf{z}}] \\
& \quad = \left( \frac{\partial u_R}{\partial z} B_0 \right) \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \biggl( R \Omega \frac{\partial b_z}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\phi}}{\partial z} B_0 \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R + \Omega \frac{\partial (Rb_R)}{\partial R} \biggr) \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{1}{R} \left[ \frac{\partial (Ru_R B_0)}{\partial R} \right] \hat{\mathbf{z}} \\
& \quad = \left( \frac{\partial u_R}{\partial z} B_0 \right) \hat{\mathbf{R}} + \left( \frac{\partial u_{\phi}}{\partial z} B_0 - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R \right) \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} \\
& \qquad\qquad - \frac{1}{R} \left[ \frac{\partial (Ru_R B_0)}{\partial R} \right] \hat{\mathbf{z}} .
\end{aligned}
\tag{27.10}\] In the last equation we have also used the condition that \(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{b}= 0\).
We will consider a small patch of the disk, so that we can use the Fourier (WKB) ansatz: \[
\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t + \mathrm{i} (k_R R + k_z z)}, \qquad
\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}_0 \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t + \mathrm{i} (k_R R + k_z z)}
\tag{27.11}\] where \(k_R R, k_z R \gg 1\), so that we can neglect terms of order \(1 / R\). We also assume \(k_z \gg k_R\), which simplifies the algebra and turns out to give the fastest-growing modes. Here \(\lambda = - \mathrm{i} \omega\), so that modes with \(\lambda^2 > 0\) grow exponentially, while modes with \(\lambda^2 < 0\) oscillate. Substituting this into the linearized equations of motion yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda u_R - 2 \Omega u_{\phi} &{}={} && - \mathrm{i} k_R  \frac{P}{\rho} +
\frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 b_R}{\mu_0 \rho},  \\
\lambda u_{\phi} + \frac{\Omega}{2} u_R &{}={} && \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0
b_{\phi}}{\mu_0 \rho}, \\
\lambda u_z &{}={} && - \mathrm{i} k_z  \frac{P}{\rho} + \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 b_z}{\mu_0
\rho} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.12}\] We can eliminate \(P / \rho\) from the last equation and insert it into the first to obtain (in the limit \(k_z \gg k_R\)): \[
\lambda u_R - 2 \Omega u_{\phi} = \mathrm{i} k_z  \frac{B_0 b_R}{\mu_0 \rho} .
\tag{27.13}\] The linearized induction equation yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda b_R &{}={} && \mathrm{i} k_z B_0 u_R  \\
\lambda b_{\phi} &{}={} && - \frac{3}{2} \Omega b_R + \mathrm{i} k_z B_0
u_{\phi} .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.14}\] Eliminating \(b_R\) in the second equation yields \[
\lambda b_{\phi} = - \frac{3}{2}  \frac{\mathrm{i} k_z B_0 \Omega}{\lambda}
u_R + \mathrm{i} k_z B_0 u_{\phi} .
\tag{27.15}\] Eliminating \(b_{\phi}\) and \(b_R\) in the momentum equations above and introducing the Alfvén frequency \(\omega_A = k_z v_A\), with \(\omega_A^2 = k_z^2 B_0^2 / \mu_0 \rho\), yields \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
(\lambda^2 + \omega_A^2) u_R &{}={} && 2 \lambda \Omega u_{\phi},  \\
(\lambda^2 + \omega_A^2) u_{\phi} &{}={} && \left( - \frac{\lambda}{2} \Omega
+ \frac{3}{2}  \frac{\omega_A^2 \Omega}{\lambda} \right) u_R .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.16}\] Introducing \[
\mu^2 = \lambda^2 + \omega_A^2,
\tag{27.17}\] the dispersion relation becomes \[
f (\mu^2) = \mu^4 + \Omega^2 \mu^2 - 4 \Omega^2 \omega_A^2 = 0.
\tag{27.18}\] The product of the two roots of \(f (\mu^2)\) is negative, so there is one positive and one negative root. Since \(\lambda^2 = \mu^2 - \omega_A^2\), the instability is present when the positive root is larger than \(\omega_A^2\). Since \(f (0) < 0\), this occurs if \[
f (\omega_A^2) = \omega_A^4 - 3 \Omega^2 \omega_A^2 < 0 \Longrightarrow
\boxed{\frac{k_z B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}} = \omega_A < \sqrt{3} \Omega .}
\tag{27.19}\] We find that if \(k_z\) is sufficiently small (long wavelengths), then the mode is unstable. However, if the background field is too large, then the condition in Equation 27.19 might only be satisfied for \(k_z\) that corresponds to modes larger than the disk thickness \(H \approx c_s / \Omega\) (Exercise 19.1), so the disk is stable to the MRI. The unstable modes have wavelengths longer than \(2 \pi v_A / (\sqrt{3} \Omega)\), so they fit in the disk only if \(v_A \lesssim c_s\). In other words, the MRI operates when the plasma \(\beta\) (Equation 25.25) is larger than about one, that is, when the magnetic pressure is smaller than the gas pressure.
The growth rate of the instability is found by solving the dispersion relation to find \[
\lambda^2 = \frac{\Omega}{2}  \left( - \Omega + \sqrt{\Omega^2 + 16
\omega_A^2} \right) - \omega_A^2,
\tag{27.20}\] which is maximized when \[
\omega_A = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4} \Omega \approx \Omega,
\tag{27.21}\] which corresponds to \[
k_{\max} = \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4} \frac{\Omega}{v_A} \approx \frac{\Omega}{v_A} .
\tag{27.22}\] The growth rate of the most unstable mode is \[
\boxed{\lambda_{\max} = \frac{3}{4} \Omega .}
\tag{27.23}\]






TipExample: The MRI in a protoplanetary disk



Consider the disk of gas and dust around a young star like the Sun, at a distance \(R = 1\,\mathrm{AU}\) from the star. In the minimum-mass solar nebula, a standard model for the early solar system, the gas at this distance has \(T \approx 280\,\mathrm{K}\) and \(\rho \approx 1.4 \times 10^{- 9}\,\mathrm{g\,cm^{- 3}} = 1.4 \times 10^{- 6}\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{- 3}}\). The gas is mostly molecular hydrogen, with \(\mu \approx 2.3\), so \(c_s \approx 1\,\mathrm{km\,s^{- 1}}\). The angular velocity is \(\Omega = (G M_{\odot} / R^3)^{1 / 2} \approx 2 \times 10^{- 7}\,\mathrm{s^{- 1}}\), corresponding to an orbital period of one year, and the thickness of the disk is \(H \approx c_s / \Omega \approx 5 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{m} \approx 0.03\,\mathrm{AU}\).
Suppose that the disk is threaded by a vertical field \(B_0 \approx 10^{- 4}\,\mathrm{T}\) (\(1\,\mathrm{G}\)). The Alfvén speed is \[
v_A = \frac{B_0}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \rho}} \approx 75\,\mathrm{m\,s^{- 1}},
\tag{27.24}\] and the plasma \(\beta \approx 360\). The fastest-growing mode has wavelength \(2 \pi / k_{\max} \approx 2.5 \times 10^{9}\,\mathrm{m} \approx H / 2\), so it fits in the disk. Its growth time is \(1 / \lambda_{\max} = 4 / (3 \Omega) \approx 80\) days. In other words, even a field with magnetic pressure 360 times smaller than the gas pressure makes the disk unstable, and the perturbations grow by a factor of about 100 every year.


It is instructive to check the limit of our analysis when \(B_0 \rightarrow 0\), which corresponds to \(\omega_A \rightarrow 0\). If \(\omega_A \equiv 0\), then Equation 27.16 reduces to \[
\lambda^2 u_R = - \Omega^2 u_R, \qquad \lambda^2 u_{\phi} = - \Omega^2
u_{\phi} .
\tag{27.25}\] In other words, the perturbations oscillate with the epicyclic frequency \(\kappa\), which for a Keplerian disk equals \(\Omega\). More in general, an unmagnetized rotating fluid is stable to axisymmetric perturbations as long as its specific angular momentum \(R^2 \Omega\) increases outward. This is called the Rayleigh criterion, and it is satisfied by Keplerian disks.
In the limit of \(0 < \omega_A \ll \Omega\) (long wavelength perturbations, or weak magnetic field), we can drop all the \(\omega_A\) terms in Equation 27.16, with the exception of the term multiplied by \(\Omega\) to obtain \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\lambda^2 u_R &{}={} && 2 \lambda \Omega u_{\phi},  \\
\lambda^2 u_{\phi} &{}={} && \left( - \frac{\lambda}{2} \Omega + \frac{3}{2}
\frac{\omega_A^2 \Omega}{\lambda} \right) u_R .
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.26}\] Eliminating \(u_{\phi}\), we obtain: \[
\lambda^2 u_R = \left( \frac{3 \omega_A^2 \Omega^2}{\lambda^2} - \Omega^2
\right) u_R,
\tag{27.27}\] which has unstable solutions with \(\lambda^2 > 0\) as long as \(\omega_A > 0\). For \(\omega_A \ll \Omega\), the growing solution is \(\lambda \approx \sqrt{3} \omega_A\). This growth rate goes to zero for \(B_0 \to 0\), at fixed \(k_z\). However, the fastest-growing mode always grows at the rate \(\frac{3}{4} \Omega\), for any \(B_0 > 0\). In other words, an arbitrarily weak magnetic field makes the disk unstable, even though the disk is stable without the field. Note that the MRI only requires the angular velocity to decrease outward (see Section 27.3), while the Rayleigh criterion is about the angular momentum. This is why the MRI is so important for accretion disks.

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
27.3 In-class worksheet
There is a simple mechanical equivalent of the magnetorotational instability (MRI) in a disk with vertical magnetic field. This model is concerned with two particles of mass \(m\) orbiting a central object with angular velocity \(\Omega = \Omega (R)\) (not necessarily Keplerian). The particles are connected by a spring, as shown in Figure 27.2. The spring pulls each mass towards the common center of mass with a force equal to \(-mK\) times its displacement.






Figure 27.2: Mechanical analogue of the magnetorotational instability: two masses connected by a spring, orbiting a central object.



The coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) denote the displacement of one of the two masses from the common center of mass.

Assuming \(|x|, |y| \ll R\), show that the displacement satisfies the differential equations \[
\begin{alignedat}{2}
\ddot{x} - 2 \Omega \dot{y} &{}={} && - \left( K + \frac{\mathrm{d}
\Omega^2}{\mathrm{d} \ln R} \right) x, \\
\ddot{y} + 2 \Omega \dot{x} &{}={} && - Ky.
\end{alignedat}
\tag{27.28}\] Note that these are the same equations as those obtained for the MRI in a disk threaded by a vertical magnetic field, \(k_R = 0\), and \(K = (v_A k_z)^2 = \omega_A^2\).
Look for solutions in the form \(x (t) = x_0 \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\), \(y (t) = y_0 \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\). Find \(\lambda\).
Under what conditions is the system unstable?

title: 27  The Magnetorotational Instability
text:
27.4 Exercises

Exercise 27.1 (Dead zones in protoplanetary disks) In this exercise we estimate how much ionization is needed for the MRI to operate in a protoplanetary disk.

Consider the MRI in a disk with finite resistivity, that is, with magnetic diffusivity \(\eta > 0\). Argue that a mode with wavenumber \(k\) is damped by Ohmic diffusion on the time scale \(T_{\mathrm{decay}} = 1 / (k^2 \eta)\) (see Equation 24.18). Show that the fastest-growing mode, with \(k \approx \Omega / v_A\), grows faster than it is damped only if \[
v_A^2 \gtrsim \eta \Omega .
\tag{27.29}\]
In a weakly ionized gas, the magnetic diffusivity is approximately \[
\eta \approx 2.34 \times 10^{- 2} \left( \frac{T}{\mathrm{K}} \right)^{1 / 2} x_e^{- 1}\,\mathrm{m^2\,s^{- 1}},
\tag{27.30}\] where \(x_e = n_e / n\) is the ionization fraction. Find the minimum ionization fraction for the MRI to operate in the disk of the protoplanetary-disk Example (\(T \approx 280\,\mathrm{K}\), \(\Omega \approx 2 \times 10^{- 7}\,\mathrm{s^{- 1}}\), \(v_A \approx 75\,\mathrm{m\,s^{- 1}}\)).
Close to the star, where \(T \gtrsim 1000\,\mathrm{K}\), alkali metals such as sodium and potassium are thermally ionized, and \(x_e\) is large. Further out, the gas is ionized only by X-rays from the star and by cosmic rays. These ionize the surface layers of the disk, but they do not reach its dense midplane, unless the column density of the disk is small. Where in the disk do you expect the MRI to operate? Sketch your answer in the \(R z\)-plane.

title: Appendix A — Vector Calculus
text:
Compute the gradient of the function \[
f (x, y, z) = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}} .
\tag{A.1}\]
Consider the vector field \[
\mathbf{E}= \hat{\mathbf{r}} = \left(\begin{array}{c}
\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}}\\
\frac{y}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}}\\
\frac{z}{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}}
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{A.2}\] Compute

the gradient \[
\nabla \mathbf{E}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
\partial_x E_x & \partial_x E_y & \partial_x E_z\\
\partial_y E_x & \partial_y E_y & \partial_y E_z\\
\partial_z E_x & \partial_z E_y & \partial_z E_z
\end{array}\right) ;
\tag{A.3}\]
\(\nabla \cdot \mathbf{E}\);
\(\nabla \times \mathbf{E}\).

Prove that \[
\nabla \cdot \nabla f = \nabla^2 f = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} +
\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} .
\tag{A.4}\]
The divergence of a tensor field \[
\mathbf{T}= \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
T_{x x} & T_{x y} & T_{x z}\\
T_{y x} & T_{y y} & T_{y z}\\
T_{z x} & T_{z y} & T_{z z}
\end{array}\right)
\tag{A.5}\] is defined as \[
\nabla \cdot \mathbf{T}= \left(\begin{array}{c}
\partial_x T_{x x} + \partial_y T_{x y} + \partial_z T_{x z}\\
\partial_x T_{y x} + \partial_y T_{y y} + \partial_z T_{y z}\\
\partial_x T_{z x} + \partial_y T_{z y} + \partial_z T_{z z}
\end{array}\right) .
\tag{A.6}\] Prove that \[
\nabla \cdot (p\mathbf{I}) = \nabla \cdot \left(\begin{array}{ccc}
p &  & \\
& p & \\
&  & p
\end{array}\right) = \nabla p.
\tag{A.7}\]
